Corpus et mōtus

Body, health & movement

Scratch

scabō, scabere, scābī

Ancient Latin
  • scabō, scabere, scābī — scratch or scrape; no attested supine is supplied in Lewis & Short.
  • scalpō, scalpere, scalpsī, scalptum — scratch, scrape, carve, engrave.
  • scabiēs f. — an itching or scabby skin condition; mange. It is broader than the modern diagnosis “scabies.” The classical dictionaries give accusative scabiem and ablative scabiē, without supplying a genitive.
  • scaber, scabra, scabrum — rough, scabby.
  • Nōlī scabere. — Don’t scratch.
  • scrībō, scrībere, scrīpsī, scrīptum — write; historically associated with scratching or incising. English script belongs to this family.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: scabo · Lewis & Short: scalpo · Lewis & Short: scabies · Lewis & Short: scribo

Itch

prūriō, prūrīre

Ancient Latin
  • prūriō, prūrīre — itch; also figuratively long for something. The ancient dictionary does not supply a perfect or supine; regular-looking perfects are not presented as verified principal parts.
  • prūrītus, prūrītūs m. — itching; prūrīgō, prūrīginis f. — itching, irritation.
  • prūriēns, prūrientis — itching.
  • Mihi bracchium prūrit. — My arm itches.
  • Ubi tibi prūrit? — Where does it itch?
  • English medical pruritus derives from the Latin noun; the verb’s further etymology is uncertain.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: prurio · Lewis & Short: pruritus · Lewis & Short: prurigo

Pop / burst

crepō, crepāre, crepuī, crepitum

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • crepō, crepāre, crepuī, crepitum — crack, pop, make a sharp noise.
  • rumpō, rumpere, rūpī, ruptum — break, burst, rupture; transitive, or passive when something bursts.
  • crepitus, crepitūs m. — cracking or popping sound; crepitō, crepitāre, crepitāvī, crepitātum — crackle repeatedly.
  • vēsīca, vēsīcae f. — bladder; extended here to an inflated balloon. vēsīca īnflāta makes the image explicit.
  • follis īnflātus — balloon, from follis, a bag or inflated ball (L&S).
  • Vēsīca crepat. — The balloon pops.
  • Vēsīcam rumpe. — Burst the balloon.
  • English rupture, interrupt, corrupt belong to the rumpō family. crepō is usually treated as imitative.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: crepo · Lewis & Short: rumpo · Lewis & Short: vesica · Lewis & Short: crepito

Lewis & Short: follis

Common cold / feeling cold

gravēdō, gravēdinis f.

Ancient Latin
  • gravēdō, gravēdinis f. — heaviness, especially a cold in the head or catarrh; useful for “a cold,” without claiming an exact ancient diagnosis of a modern viral infection.
  • corȳza, corȳzae f. — catarrh; a Greek medical loan, attested in Late Latin.
  • dēstīllātiō, dēstīllātiōnis f. — dripping or discharge; catarrh in medical contexts.
  • frīgus, frīgoris n. — coldness, not normally the illness; frīgeō, frīgēre — be cold; algeō, algēre, alsī — feel cold.
  • Gravēdinem habeō. — I have a cold.
  • Gravēdine labōrō. — I’m suffering from a cold.
  • Nāsus fluit. — The nose is running.
  • Nāsus obstructus est. — The nose is blocked.
  • gravēdō is formed from gravis, “heavy”; corȳza represents Greek κόρυζα.
  • tussis, tussis f. (acc. tussim) — cough; tussiō, tussīre — cough (Traupman 63).
  • mē gravēdō frīgida et frequēns tussis quassāvit — “a cold in the head and a constant cough shook me” (Catull. 44.13–14).
  • Ecce, nunc tussīs! — See, you’re coughing now! Paucōs diēs tussiēbās. — You were coughing for a few days. Nihil jam frīgidī. — Nothing cold now.
  • For herbal teas, honey and compresses for a cold, see the Herbal remedies entry: infūsum, dēcoctum, fōmentum, mel.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: gravedo · Lewis & Short: coryza · Lewis & Short: destillatio · Lewis & Short: frigus · Lewis & Short: algeo · Bennett: hidden quantities, with later corrections

Yawn

ōscitō, ōscitāre, ōscitāvī, ōscitātum

Ancient Latin
  • ōscitō, ōscitāre, ōscitāvī, ōscitātum — yawn or gape. The deponent ōscitor, ōscitārī, ōscitātus sum is also attested.
  • ōscitātiō, ōscitātiōnis f. — yawning, a yawn; ōscitāns, ōscitantis — yawning.
  • ōs, ōris n. — mouth; the related noun has a long ō.
  • Theodōrus ōscitat. — Theo is yawning.

Jump / dive in headfirst

saliō, salīre, saluī, saltum

Ancient Latin
  • saliō, salīre, saluī, saltum — jump, leap; saltus, saltūs m. — a leap.
  • exsiliō, exsilīre — jump out or spring up; dēsiliō, dēsilīre — jump down; trānsiliō, trānsilīre — jump across.
  • Salī. — Jump.
  • Theodōrus salit. — Theo is jumping.
  • praeceps saliō; praeceps dēsiliō — dive in headfirst (Traupman 50, 305).
  • ālīsque plaudentēs praecipitēs alia post aliam in aquam dēsiliēbant ibique celerrimē natābant — and, flapping their wings, they dived headfirst into the water one after another and swam very fast there (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Body parts for washing / dressing / fingers / eyes / face / cheek / chin / thumb

manus, manūs f.

Ancient Latin
  • caput, capitis n. — head; auris, auris f. — ear; ōs, ōris n. — mouth; collum, collī n. — neck.
  • bracchium, bracchiī n. — arm; cubitum, cubitī n. — elbow; manus, manūs f. — hand.
  • pēs, pedis m. — foot; crūs, crūris n. — lower leg; genū, genūs n. — knee.
  • venter, ventris m. — belly; dorsum, dorsī n.; tergum, tergī n. — back; umerus, umerī m. — shoulder.
  • Manum mihi dā. — Give me your hand.
  • Pedes lavēmus. — Let’s wash our feet.
  • Ubi genū tuum est? — Where is your knee?
  • digitus, digitī m. — finger; oculus, oculī m. — eye; frōns, frontis f. — forehead; pectus, pectoris n. — chest.
  • vultus, vultūs m. — face, expression; vultum dūcere — pull a face; ōs contrahere — pucker one’s mouth. sūdō, sūdāre, sūdāvī, sūdātum — sweat.
  • Quīnque digitōs ostendere cōnātus, trēs ostendit. — Trying to show five fingers, he showed three. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Theodōrus manūs jūnxit et oculōs, aut alterum saltem, clausit — Theo put his hands together and closed his eyes, or one of them at least (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Theodōrus olīvam ē catīnō gustāvit, quae jam amāra nōn erat; vultum tamen dūxit — Theo tasted an olive from the dish, which was no longer bitter; he pulled a face all the same (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • gena, genae f. — cheek; usually plural genae (Traupman 58; Cic. N.D. 2.143).
  • palpebra, palpebrae f. — eyelid (Traupman 58; Cic. N.D. 2.142); pollex, pollicis m. — thumb (Traupman 58); mentum, mentī n. — chin (Traupman 58).
  • linguam exserere — stick out one’s tongue (Liv. 7.10.5).
  • cui illa, genam ejus ōsculāta, «Tālem,» inquit, «et tibi precor.» — and she kissed his cheek and said, “The same to you.” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • nam patris, quī etiam tum dormiēbat, palpebram digitō sublevāvit, ut explōrāret num vigilāret — for he lifted his sleeping father’s eyelid with a finger, to find out whether he was awake (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Theodōrus, ā pollice incipiēns, singula nōmina singulīs digitīs numerāvit — Theo, starting with his thumb, counted one name on each finger (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • lōdīcemque ad mentum puerī addūxisset — and had pulled the blanket up to the boy’s chin (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Cui imāginī cum puer linguam exseruisset, imāgō vicissim eī linguam exseruit. — When the boy stuck his tongue out at the reflection, the reflection stuck its tongue out back at him. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Move (noun) / movement / game move

mōtus, mōtūs m.; tractus, tractūs m.

Ancient nounRecorded game sense
  • mōtus, mōtūs m. — movement; our general choice for a physical or dance move when context makes the particular action clear.
  • mōtus and tractus, tractūs m. — recorded by Morgan–Owens for a move of a playing piece or checker. A game move need not be described as an ordinary bodily movement.
  • Hunc mōtum imitāre. — Copy this move. Mōtūs tuōs spectō. — I’m watching your movements. These examples are composed, not quotations.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: motus · Morgan–Owens: move of a playing piece (noun)

Flip over / flip (noun) / somersault

invertō, invertere; saltus cernuus

Ancient verbsRecorded gymnastic sense
  • invertō, invertere, invertī, inversum — turn something over or upside down; transitive. sē invertere — turn oneself over; the verb is also attested with a reflexive object.
  • cernuō, cernuāre — do a somersault; recorded by Morgan–Owens, including an Apuleius reference.
  • saltus cernuus; saltūs cernuī m. — somersault / acrobatic flip; singular nominative and genitive. Morgan–Owens lists the plural saltūs cernuī; the singular is inflected here from that expression.
  • Tabulam inverte. — Flip the plank over. Saltum cernuum fac. — Do a somersault.
  • These distinguish turning an object over from a bodily flip. They do not imply that a coin toss, switch operation, cartwheel and airborne backflip all have the same exact technical name.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: inverto · Lewis & Short: cernuo · Lewis & Short: saltus · Morgan–Owens: somersault · Morgan–Owens: somersault (verb) · Morgan–Owens: somersaults / cartwheels

Squeeze / squish / squash / crush

comprimō, comprimere; contundō, contundere

Ancient verbsSense distinctions
  • comprimō, comprimere, compressī, compressum — squeeze or press together, compress. Our practical choice for squishing something soft or squashing it down; the object supplies the soft/wet quality.
  • exprimō, exprimere, expressī, expressum — squeeze liquid out; also wring out the object containing it. Spongiam exprime. — Squeeze out the sponge. See also the food-preparation squeeze entry.
  • contundō, contundere, contudī, contūsum — pound, mash or crush by blows; Lewis & Short includes olives, roots and crushing/flattening injuries. The perfect has recorded quantity variation; contudī is left without a root-vowel macron here.
  • conterō, conterere, contrīvī, contrītum — grind or crush into small pieces; already covered in the cooking entry as well.
  • Lūtum comprime. — Squish / compress the mud. Spongiam nōlī comprimere. — Don’t squeeze the sponge.
  • Tamping and ramming: fistūcō, fistūcāre — ram down, tamp (Cato, Agr. 18.7 festūcātō; Vitruvius 7.1.1 fistūcātiōnibus); pīnsō, pīnsere — pound, beat; calcō, calcāre — tread or ram down (Pliny, NH 36.173 calcārī solum); īnferciō (īnfarciō), īnfercīre — pack or cram in (Pliny, NH 35.169 īnferciuntur, of rammed-earth walls).
  • English “squeeze,” “squish,” “squash” and “crush” overlap. These Latin choices distinguish compression, extraction, pounding and grinding; they are not four rigid one-to-one equivalents.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: comprimo · Lewis & Short: exprimo · Lewis & Short: contundo · Lewis & Short: contero · Lewis & Short: fistuco · Lewis & Short: pinso · Lewis & Short: calco · Lewis & Short: infarcio

Crash (verb) / crash (noun) / collision / crashing sound

collīdō, collīdere; collīsiō, collīsiōnis f.

Ancient wordsRecorded collision sense
  • collīdō, collīdere, collīsī, collīsum — dash or strike things together; transitive. To describe objects colliding, use the passive collīdī, with inter sē when appropriate.
  • collīsiō, collīsiōnis f. — collision; Morgan–Owens records the automobile application, citing Traupman. It also records collīsus, collīsūs m. with a Vatican Lexicon reference.
  • fragor, fragōris m. — crash or crashing sound; distinguishes the noise from the collision itself.
  • corruō, corruere, corruī — fall or collapse; useful when “crash” means coming down in a heap rather than hitting another object. Traupman also applies it to a computer crash; that is a separate modern extension.
  • Autoraedae inter sē collīduntur. — The cars crash into each other. Magnum fragōrem audīvī. — I heard a loud crash.
  • For toy cars the vehicle nouns have modern applications; the sentence is our composed description, not an ancient quotation.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: collido (dictionary transcription) · Morgan–Owens: collision (auto) · Lewis & Short: fragor · Lewis & Short: corruo · Traupman: Conversational Latin, fourth edition

Run / hurry / slowly / swim across / carry on the shoulders / tired

currō, currere, cucurrī, cursum · festīnō, festīnāre

Ancient Latin
  • currō, currere, cucurrī, cursum — run.
  • festīnō, festīnāre, festīnāvī, festīnātum; properō, properāre — hurry; lentē — slowly; celeriter — quickly.
  • trānatō, trānatāre — swim across; see the dolphin entry for natō.
  • in umerīs portāre; in umerīs vehī — carry on one’s shoulders; ride on someone’s shoulders. In umerōs. — Up on my shoulders.
  • anhēlō, anhēlāre — pant; fessus, fessa, fessum — tired.
  • Festīnā lentē. — Hurry slowly: Augustus’s maxim, which Suetonius gives in Greek, σπεῦδε βραδέως (Suet. Aug. 25, 4); for when the child dawdles and you are in a rush.
  • Theodōrus autem nōn ībat sed currēbat — Theo, though, wasn’t walking but running (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Theodōrus autem, in umerīs ejus vectus, bacillum aduncum tenēns — Theo, riding on his shoulders and holding his hooked stick (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • tolūtim — at a trot (Traupman 60; Varro; Pliny); tolūtim currere / cursitāre — trot, jog.
  • ad olīvam tolūtim cucurrit truncumque manū tangēns «Valē, olīva!» inquit — he trotted over to the olive tree and, touching the trunk, said, “Goodbye, olive tree!” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Swimming pool / swim / float / dive / bubbles / chlorine

piscīna, piscīnae f. · natō, natāre

Ancient LatinNeo-Latin
  • piscīna, piscīnae f. — swimming pool (Traupman 50); originally a fishpond, a bathing pool from the first century AD, as in Pliny’s heated pool: cohaeret calida piscīna mīrifica, ex quā natantēs mare aspiciunt — “next to it is a wonderful heated pool, from which swimmers look out at the sea” (Plin. Ep. 2.17.11).
  • natō, natāre, natāvī, natātum — swim; also float, as Cato’s test for brine: sī natābit, “if it floats” (Agr. 88). Pliny’s rule for a river: īnfrā etiam natāre concessum, “downstream you may swim too” (Ep. 8.8.6).
  • innatō, innatāre — float on, swim in (poetic and post-Augustan prose, L&S); innatāns of the dishes floating round the edge of Pliny’s garden pool (Ep. 5.6.37).
  • ūrīnor, ūrīnārī — dive, go under water (Varro, L.L. 5.126; Pliny); ūrīnātor, ūrīnātōris m. — diver (M-O s.v. diver). For jumping in head first, see the Jump / dive in headfirst entry: praeceps dēsiliō.
  • bulla, bullae f. — bubble (Ov. Met. 10.734).
  • chlōrium, chlōriī n. — chlorine (M-O s.v. chlorine, a modern coinage; Traupman has none). aqua chlōrāta — chlorinated water; aqua sine chlōriō — water without chlorine. Both phrases are our formations.
  • Vīsne natāre? — Do you want to swim?
  • Ecce, bullae! — Look, bubbles!
  • Nōlō tē nimis diū in aquā chlōrātā manēre. — I don’t want you staying too long in the chlorinated water.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: piscina · Lewis & Short: nato · Lewis & Short: innato · Lewis & Short: urinor · Lewis & Short: bulla

Massage / rub down / masseur / oil / relax

fricō, fricāre · frictiō, frictiōnis f.

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsNeo-Latin
  • fricō, fricāre, fricuī, frictum — rub, rub down, massage (M-O s.v. massage); fricārī — have a massage, be rubbed down: numquam concessāmus lavārī aut fricārī aut tergērī aut ōrnārī — “we never stopped being bathed, rubbed down, dried and dressed” (Plaut. Poen. 219–220).
  • frictiō, frictiōnis f.; fricātiō, fricātiōnis f. — a rub-down, massage (Celsus, who gives it a chapter, 2.14). After a long walk: hunc reficit in ipsō quoque itinere frequēns frictiō, post iter prīmum sedīle, deinde ūnctiō — “he is restored by frequent rubbing on the way, and after the walk first a seat, then an oiling” (Cels. 1.3).
  • malaxō, malaxāre — knead, soften, massage (M-O s.v. massage, citing Seneca, Ep. 66.53, where it is scornful, of pampered luxury).
  • iātralīptēs, iātralīptae m. — massage therapist, a doctor who treats with oil and rubbing. Pliny asked Trajan for citizenship for his own: gravissimā valētūdine ūsque ad perīculum vītae vexātus iātralīptēn assūmpsī — “when a very serious illness put my life in danger, I took on a massage therapist” (Plin. Ep. 10.5.1).
  • tractātor, tractātōris m.; tractātrīx, tractātrīcis f. — masseur, masseuse (Sen. Ep. 66.53; Mart. 3.82.13), both in scornful passages; M-O s.v. masseur gives fricātor and, with a query, tractātor. alīptēs, alīptae m. — the trainer who oiled and rubbed down athletes (Cic. Fam. 1.9.15); ūnctor, ūnctōris m. — anointer (Cic., Mart.).
  • oleum, oleī n. — oil; ungō (unguō), ungere, ūnxī, ūnctum — rub with oil; ūnctiō, ūnctiōnis f. — oiling; unguentum, unguentī n. — ointment, scented oil.
  • animum relaxāre; sē ex labōre relaxāre — relax, unwind (M-O s.v. relax); quiēscere — rest.
  • Fricā mihi tergum, quaesō. — Rub my back, please.
  • Vīsne ut tibi umerōs fricem? — Shall I rub your shoulders?
  • Pedēs tibi oleō ungam. — I’ll rub your feet with oil.
  • Ah, quam bene est! — Ah, that feels good!

Quantities of the Greek loans follow the Greek: iātralīptēs (ἰᾱτραλείπτης), alīptēs (ἀλείπτης). ūnctor, ūnctiō, ūnxī and ūnctum have the long vowel before -nct-/-nx-.

Herbal remedies: herbal tea / infusion / decoction / poultice / compress / honey / chamomile / mint / thyme / sage / linden / nettle

īnfūsum, īnfūsī n. · dēcoctum, dēcoctī n. · fōmentum, fōmentī n.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations
  • īnfūsum, īnfūsī n. — herbal tea, infusion, with the genitive of the herb: īnfūsum chamaemēlī, īnfūsum mentae (M-O s.v. tea: herb tea, citing 19th-century pharmacy Latin, e.g. infūsum flōrum chamomillae; a Neo-Latin noun from īnfundō, īnfundere, īnfūdī, īnfūsum, pour in). M-O’s distinction: an infusion is boiling water poured over the herb and left to stand; a decoction is boiled with the herb in it. Traupman has no herb tea; he gives only thea (the tea entry).
  • dēcoquō, dēcoquere, dēcoxī, dēcoctum — boil down, boil (a herb) in water; dēcoctum, dēcoctī n. — decoction, the liquid so made (Pliny; M-O s.v. tea: herb tea, decoctum with the genitive). Pliny’s wild poppy melle dēcoctum ad faucium remedia, “boiled with honey, a remedy for the throat” (Plin. NH 18.229), and hyssop: hȳsōpī fasciculus cum quadrante mellis dēcoquitur ad tussim — “a bunch of hyssop is boiled with a quarter-pound of honey for a cough” (Plin. NH 26.31).
  • fōmentum, fōmentī n. — compress, warm application, fomentation (from foveō); fōmenta calida / frīgida. Celsus: fōmenta quoque calida sunt milium, sāl, harēna, quidlibet eōrum calfactum et in linteum conjectum — “warm compresses are millet, salt, sand, any of them heated and put in a cloth” (Cels. 2.17). Horace’s friend at the bedside assideat, fōmenta paret, medicum roget (Serm. 1.1.82). foveō, fovēre, fōvī, fōtum — bathe, soak a sore limb (Traupman 61–62: fovē illud genū in aquā frīgidā).
  • cataplasma, cataplasmatis n. — poultice (Celsus, Pliny; Greek κατάπλασμα); Celsus’s linseed poultice softens: praecipueque ad ēmolliendum potest cataplasma ex līnī vel fēnī Graecī sēmine (Cels. 2.33). malagma, malagmatis n. — softening poultice (Celsus).
  • mel, mellis n. — honey; mel cum aquā calidā — honey in hot water; hydromeli, hydromelitis n. — honey-water (Pliny). For a sore throat Celsus has you boil thyme or hyssop and gargle: hȳsōpum vel nepetam vel thumum … dēcoquere, eaque gargarīzāre (Cels. 4.7, on a swollen throat; the edition spells thumum). gargarīzō, gargarīzāre — gargle (Cels., Plin.; M-O s.v. gargle).
  • chamaemēlon, chamaemēlī n. — chamomile (Plin. NH 22.53, who explains the name: chamaemēlon, quoniam odōrem mālī habeat, “because it smells of apples”; M-O s.v. chamomile). Also anthemis, anthemidis f. (Pliny’s main headword) and the later chamomilla (Plin. Val.).
  • menta (mentha), mentae f. — mint (Ov., Plin.); menta piperāta — peppermint (M-O, pharmacy Latin); M-O’s own example is mentae īnfūsum, mint tea. Pliny: mentae ipsīus odor animum excitat — “the very smell of mint revives the spirit” (NH 20.147).
  • thymum, thymī n. — thyme (Verg., Hor., Plin.); serpyllum, serpyllī n. — wild thyme (Cato, Varro, Verg.), the kind on the hillsides above the village.
  • salvia, salviae f. — sage (Plin. NH 22.147, giving the Greek elelisphacum).
  • tilia, tiliae f. — linden, lime tree (see the forest trees entry); īnfūsum flōrum tiliae — linden-blossom tea, our formation on M-O’s pattern. Pliny knows linden bark for swellings and wounds (NH 24.49), not the blossom tea.
  • urtīca, urtīcae f. — nettle (Catull., Hor., Plin.); Pliny opens his chapter Urtīcā quid esse invīsius potest? at illa … vel plūrimīs scatet remediīs — “what could be more hateful than the nettle? yet it teems with remedies” (NH 22.31). For Catullus’s cold cured ōtiōque et urtīcā see the Common cold entry.
  • unguentum, unguentī n. — ointment, salve (see the massage entry); linīmentum, linīmentī n. — lotion, liniment (Traupman 64; M-O s.v. ointment, late: Palladius, Caelius Aurelianus); cērātum, cērātī n. — wax salve (Cels.). illinō, illinere, illēvī, illitum — smear on; M-O’s infricāre — rub in (Plin.).
  • remedium, remediī n. — remedy, with genitive or ad: remedium tussis / ad tussim (Traupman 370; Cic.); herbae medicae — medicinal herbs.
  • Īnfūsum tibi chamaemēlī parābō. — I’ll make you some chamomile tea.
  • Paulum mellis adde; sīc dulcius erit. — Add a little honey; it’ll be sweeter.
  • Exspectā dum refrīgēscat; nimis calidum est. — Wait for it to cool down; it’s too hot.
  • Fōmentum calidum tibi in pectus impōnam. — I’ll put a warm compress on your chest.
  • Paulum unguentī tibi illinam. — I’ll put a little ointment on it.
  • Hīc mentam et serpyllum legāmus, ut domī īnfūsum faciāmus. — Let’s pick mint and wild thyme here, to make tea at home.

Quantities follow L&S: chamaemēlon (Greek χαμαίμηλον), urtīca, serpyllum, hydromeli (short e, Greek ὑδρόμελι). īnfūsum is a Neo-Latin noun (M-O marks it * and writes infûsum); it is written with long ī as in L&S īnfundō, īnfūsus, since in- is long before f.

Doctor / medicine / pill / take medicine / prescription / pharmacy / hospital / nurse / dentist

medicus, medicī m. · medicāmentum, medicāmentī n. · pilula, pilulae f.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations
  • medicus, medicī m.; medica, medicae f. — doctor (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. doctor; Cic.). medicum arcessere — send for the doctor (Plaut. Men. 875; L&S). Traupman’s sick girl is told Vīse medicum quam prīmum — “see a doctor as soon as possible” (Traupman 55).
  • medicīna, medicīnae f. — the art of medicine; also a remedy, and the doctor’s surgery (Traupman 63, 166; M-O s.v. doctor’s office, citing Plautus).
  • medicāmentum, medicāmentī n.; medicāmen, medicāminis n. — medicine, a drug, a remedy (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. drug, medicine; Cic.). M-O gives ingerere for “take” medicine, from 19th-century medical Latin; the plain classical verb is sūmere, as in Seneca’s sopōre sūmptō — “having taken a sleeping draught” (Ep. 83.27).
  • pilula, pilulae f. — pill (Traupman 59, 65; Plin.); pastillus, pastillī m. — tablet, lozenge (Traupman 66; M-O s.v. pill, tablet, lozenge; Cels.); catapotium, catapotiī n. — pill, a Greek medical word in Celsus and Pliny. Traupman and M-O disagree on which to use for a pill; all three are ancient. pastillus tussiculāris — cough drop (Traupman 63, Neo-Latin); M-O’s cough syrup is syrūpus tussiculāris, with medieval syrūpus.
  • medicāmentum anōdynum — painkiller (M-O s.v. pain medicine, after Celsus 5.25); Traupman’s plainer phrase: pilula quae dolōrem levābit — “a pill that will ease the pain” (Traupman 57). dolōrem levāre / lēnīre — relieve pain.
  • praescrībō, praescrībere, praescrīpsī, praescrīptum — prescribe (M-O); medicī praescrīptum — the doctor’s orders (M-O, citing Plin. NH 14.143). Traupman’s prescription: praeceptum medicum (364). aegrum īnspicere — examine a patient (M-O; Plaut. Pers. 316 īnspicere morbum tuum lubet).
  • medicāmentārius, medicāmentāriī m. — chemist, druggist (Plin. NH 19.110); medicāmentāria, medicāmentāriae f. — pharmacy (Traupman 307, a coinage); pharmacopōlium, pharmacopōliī n. — pharmacy (M-O, modern). In Cicero and Horace a pharmacopōla is a quack, so we don’t use it for the chemist.
  • valētūdinārium, valētūdināriī n. — hospital (Traupman 64; M-O; Sen., Tac., Cels.); nosocomīum, nosocomīī n. — hospital (M-O; late Latin, Cod. Just.). nosocoma, nosocomae f.; nosocomus, nosocomī m. — nurse (Traupman 65; M-O; late Latin).
  • medicus dentārius — dentist (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. dentist, a modern phrase).
  • arcera, arcerae f. — ambulance (Traupman 271; M-O s.v. ambulance, adding automata); in the Twelve Tables and Gellius a covered cart for the sick. Traupman also has autoarcera.
  • Hodiē ad medicum īmus. — We’re going to the doctor today.
  • Medicus tē īnspiciet: ōs aperī, linguam exsere. — The doctor will look at you: open your mouth, stick out your tongue.
  • Hanc pilulam cum aquā sūme. — Take this pill with water.
  • Medicāmentum amārum est, sed prōderit. — The medicine is bitter, but it’ll do you good.

valētūdinārium: L&S has the adjective valētūdinārius; the neuter noun is in Celsus, Seneca and Tacitus. Lewis & Short gives nosocomīum with long ī (Greek νοσοκομεῖον).

Feeling ill: I don’t feel well / fever / sick / feel sick / throw up / tummy ache / headache / sore throat / sneeze

febris, febris f. · aeger, aegra, aegrum · vomō, vomere

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • aeger, aegra, aegrum; aegrōtus, aegrōta, aegrōtum — ill, sick (Traupman 65); aegrōtō, aegrōtāre — be ill. in morbum incidere — fall ill (Traupman 65); morbō corripī — come down with an illness (Traupman 95).
  • Mē male habeō. / Minus valeō. — I don’t feel well (Traupman 55, 98); Melius mē habeō. / Melius valeō. — I feel better (Traupman 56, 98).
  • febris, febris f. (acc. febrim or febrem) — fever (Traupman 64; M-O): febrim habēre (Cic. Fam. 7.26.1), in febrim incidere — get a fever (Cic. Fam. 14.8.1). febrīcula, febrīculae f. — a slight temperature (Cic. Att. 12.1.2, of his little daughter Attica: dē Atticae febrīculā … valdē doluī). febrīcitāre — run a fever (Traupman 64; Cels., post-Augustan).
  • Frōns calida est. — Your forehead is hot (after Traupman 55: frōns et genae sunt calidae).
  • Venter mihi dolet. / Caput mihi dolet. / Faucēs dolent. — My tummy / head / throat hurts (Traupman 55–56: stomachus dolet; caput dolet; faucēs dolent). Traupman also has dolor stomachī (385) and ā capite labōrāre, have a headache (268). M-O gives tormina, colic (Cic., Plin.), and capitis dolor. aurium dolor — earache (M-O); dentium dolor — toothache (Traupman 396; M-O, citing Cels. 6.9).
  • raucus, rauca, raucum — hoarse (Traupman 64; Cic.); faucēs asperae — sore throat (M-O); Traupman: exasperātae faucēs (382).
  • sternuō, sternuere, sternuī — sneeze; sternūmentum, sternūmentī n. — a sneeze (Traupman 65; Cic. Div. 2.84). After a sneeze: Salvē! or Salūtem! (Traupman 94); Pliny notes the custom: cūr sternuentēs salūtāmus? (NH 28.23). Catullus’s blessing: Amor … sternuit approbātiōnem (Catull. 45.8–9).
  • nausea, nauseae f.; nauseō, nauseāre — nausea; feel sick (M-O; Hor., Cels.); vehentium nausea — car sickness, motion sickness (M-O, a descriptive phrase).
  • vomō, vomere, vomuī, vomitum — throw up, be sick (Traupman 402; M-O); vomitus, vomitūs m. — vomiting (Plaut.).
  • alvus fūsa / cita — diarrhoea (Traupman 303); M-O: ventris fluctiō (Plin. NH 23.99). alvum suppressam habēre — be constipated (Traupman 296). crūditās, crūditātis f. — indigestion (Traupman 64; Cic.).
  • vertīgō, vertīginis f. — dizziness (Traupman 63; M-O; Liv., Plin.); animō linquī — faint (M-O, citing Suet. Caes. 45).
  • tremō, tremere, tremuī — shiver (Traupman 65); horror febrīlis — a feverish chill (Neo-Latin Lexicon, after Kirsch).
  • Quid tibi est? Ubi dolet? — What’s wrong? Where does it hurt?
  • Febrim habēs; hodiē domī manēbimus. — You’ve got a temperature; we’ll stay home today.
  • Nauseāsne? Dīc mihi, sī vomitūrus es. — Do you feel sick? Tell me if you’re going to throw up.

febris: L&S marks the e as common (fē^bris, “the ē predominating in poets”); the poets’ long scansion may only reflect the heavy syllable before -br-, and de Vaan (s.v. febris) does not discuss the quantity, so the e is left unmarked. febrīcula and febrīcitāre have long ī (L&S).

Bumps and scrapes: hurt yourself / bruise / bump / swelling / cut / scab / scar / plaster / bandage / sting / bite

contūsiō, contūsiōnis f. · vulnus, vulneris n. · fascia, fasciae f.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Nocuistīne tibi? — Did you hurt yourself? After Traupman 60: Ego mihi nocuī in gymnasiō. noceō, nocēre, nocuī + dative — hurt, harm.
  • contūsiō, contūsiōnis f. — bruise (Traupman 63; M-O s.v. sprain: bruise; rare, Scribonius); contundō, contundere, contudī, contūsum — bruise (Traupman 63, p. 60 cāsū cecidī et mē contudī); līvor, līvōris m. — a black-and-blue mark (Traupman 62; Plaut.), līvidus, līvida, līvidum — black and blue.
  • tūber, tūberis n.; tūberculum, tūberculī n. — bump, lump (M-O s.v. bump; Cels.); Traupman has only the verb offendō (see the Trip / slip entry).
  • tumidus, tumida, tumidum — swollen (Traupman 66; Cic.); tumēscō, tumēscere — swell up (Traupman 61: genū sinistrum tumēscit).
  • vulnus, vulneris n. — wound, cut (Ter., Cic.); neither source has a headword, Traupman only “bandage a wound”. sanguis, sanguinis m. — blood; cruor, cruōris m. — blood that has flowed from a wound (Traupman 57). Sanguis fluit. — It’s bleeding.
  • crusta, crustae f. — scab (M-O; Cels. 5.9 ulcerum crusta); cicātrīx, cicātrīcis f. — scar (Ter., Cic.; not in either source).
  • splēnium, splēniī n. — sticking plaster, a patch (Mart. 2.29.9; Plin. Ep. 6.2.2); emplastrum, emplastrī n. — medical plaster (Cato, Cels.). Comenius: Chīrūrgus cūrat vulnera et ulcera splēniīs (Orbis pictus 128). Traupman has only taenia adhaesīva, adhesive tape (268), and M-O gives no Latin for plaster, so “band-aid” is our application of splēnium.
  • fascia, fasciae f. — bandage (Traupman 62; Cels.); ligāre, dēligāre — bandage (Traupman 276); fascia gypsea — plaster cast (Neo-Latin Lexicon s.v. plaster cast, after Helfer).
  • luxō, luxāre — sprain, dislocate (Traupman 65; M-O; Sen., Plin.); Traupman’s noun is luxātūra (late, Marc. Emp.). fractūra, fractūrae f. — fracture (Traupman 64; Cato), os frangere — break a bone.
  • ambūstiō, ambūstiōnis f.; adūstiō, adūstiōnis f. — a burn (M-O s.v. burn; both Pliny).
  • acūleus, acūleī m. — sting (Traupman 385; Cic. Tusc. 2.52 apis aculeum); ictus, ictūs m. — bite or sting of an insect (Traupman 280); culex, culicis m. — mosquito, gnat (Traupman 347); pedīculus, pedīculī m. — louse (Traupman 342, printing pēdicul·us; L&S pĕdīculus; Cels.).
  • Ostende mihi ubi doleat. — Show me where it hurts.
  • Nihil est; līvor tantum. Fōmentum frīgidum impōnāmus. — It’s nothing, just a bruise. Let’s put a cold compress on it.
  • Vīsne splēnium? Ecce, jam melius est. — Do you want a plaster? There, that’s better already.

ambūstiō and adūstiō: L&S leaves the u unmarked; the long ū is assumed from ūstus by Lachmann’s rule and should be checked. L&S gives pĕdīculus, short e and long ī, for both the louse and the little foot; Traupman’s pēdiculus is not followed.

Little body things: freckle / dimple / mole / wrinkle / bald / curly / grey hair / left-handed

lentīgō, lentīginis f. · naevus, naevī m. · scaeva, scaevae m.

Ancient LatinSense distinctions
  • lentīgō, lentīginis f.; lenticula, lenticulae f. — freckle (M-O s.v. freckle; Cels., Plin.).
  • naevus, naevī m. — mole, birthmark (Cic. ND 1.79); nota genetīva — birthmark (M-O s.v. birthmark, after Suet. Aug. 80). The Neo-Latin Lexicon gives naevus (Lev.) and naevus māternus (Helfer).
  • gelasīnus, gelasīnī m. — dimple (M-O s.v. dimple; Mart. 7.25.6) (vōx rāra: Mart.).
  • rūga, rūgae f. — wrinkle (Traupman 66; Plaut., Hor.); rūgōsus, rūgōsa, rūgōsum — wrinkled.
  • calvus, calva, calvum — bald; calvitium, calvitiī n. — baldness (Traupman 62; Cic.); capillī mihi dēfluunt — I’m losing my hair (M-O, after Plin. 11.230).
  • crispus, crispa, crispum; cirrātus, cirrāta, cirrātum — curly (Traupman 58, M-O); cirrus, cirrī m.; cincinnus, cincinnī m. — curl, ringlet. cānus, cāna, cānum — grey-haired (M-O; Plaut., Hor.); flāvus, flāva, flāvum — fair, blond (M-O).
  • scaeva, scaevae m. — a left-handed person (M-O s.v. left-handed; Dig. 21.1.12); sinistrā manū agiliōre — left-handed (M-O; Suet. Tib. 68).
  • superiōris labrī barba — moustache (M-O, after Egger). Traupman 58 gives subium, which M-O notes occurs only in a word-list in the grammarian Charisius; M-O’s mystax is Greek, in Jerome.
  • Lentīginēs habēs, sīcut mamma. — You’ve got freckles, like Mum.

crispus: Traupman marks crīspāre with a long ī, but L&S leaves crispus and crispō unmarked, and no other evidence for a long vowel was found; the i is left unmarked.

Gestures and body actions: stretch / hold your breath / blush / wink / sigh / smile / frown / snap your fingers / shake hands

pandiculor, pandiculārī · ērubēscō, ērubēscere · subrīdeō, subrīdēre

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • pandiculor, pandiculārī — stretch oneself, as on waking (M-O s.v. stretch; Plaut. Men. 5.2.80 ut pandiculāns ōscitātur — “how he stretches and yawns!”). M-O adds Erasmus’s nervōs distendere.
  • animam comprimere — hold one’s breath (Ter. Ph. 5.6.28, in L&S: animam compressī, aurem admōvī); M-O’s animam continēre (Cic. de Or. 1.261). spīrāre; īnspīrāre; exspīrāre — breathe; breathe in; breathe out (Traupman 63).
  • ērubēscō, ērubēscere, ērubuī — blush, go red (Traupman 149; Cic.).
  • nictō, nictāre — wink, blink (Traupman 407; Plin.).
  • suspīrō, suspīrāre — sigh (Cic. Att. 2.21.2); Traupman 157 gives gemō, gemere, which is rather to groan.
  • subrīdeō, subrīdēre, subrīsī — smile (Traupman 158; M-O); M-O also gives arrīdēre, renīdēre.
  • frontem contrahere — frown, knit the brows (Cic. Clu. 72; Hor.); frontem exporrigere — smooth the brow, cheer up (M-O, citing Vives): Terence exporge frontem — “unknit that brow” (Ad. 839).
  • ōs dūcere — pull a face (Traupman 97); see also vultum dūcere in the body-parts entry.
  • digitīs concrepāre — snap one’s fingers (Traupman 98; M-O; Plaut. Mil. 206). dextram jungere cum aliquō — shake hands (Traupman 107; M-O dextrās jungere).
  • in digitōs ērigī — stand on tiptoe (M-O; Quint. 2.3.8). crūribus dēcussātīs sedēre — sit cross-legged (M-O, a modern phrase). nārēs fodere — pick one’s nose (M-O).
  • Pandiculāre, sīcut fēlēs! — Stretch, like a cat!
  • Animam comprime … jam ēmitte! — Hold your breath … now let it out!
  • Exporge frontem, mī fīlī. — Cheer up, my boy.

Waking up and bedtime: stretch / are you awake? / sleepy / dream / nightmare / snore / sleep in / make the bed

vigilō, vigilāre · somnium, somniī n. · stertō, stertere

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • vigilō, vigilāre — be awake (Traupman 35, 38): Etiam vigilās? — Vigilō. — Are you awake yet? — I am (Plaut. Most. 383, 373b). pervigilāre — stay awake all night (Traupman 56 noctem pervigilābam).
  • Tempus est surgere. — Time to get up (Traupman 35). bene māne — very early (Cic. Att. 4.9.2 bene māne haec scrīpsī; Traupman 35 Omnīnō ōdī surgere tam bene māne).
  • somniculōsus, somniculōsa, somniculōsum — sleepy (Traupman 380; Cordier: Cūr tū es adeō somniculōsus?); oculī somnō cōnīvent — my eyes are closing with sleep (M-O, after Cic. ND 1.82).
  • somnium, somniī n. — dream (Cic. Div.); somniō, somniāre — dream. Seneca: somnium narrāre vigilantis est — telling a dream is for someone awake (Ep. 53.8). vigilantis somnium — daydream (M-O, after Quint. 6.2.30).
  • somnium turbulentum — nightmare (Traupman 351); somnium terrificum (M-O, 16th century). Neither has an ancient citation; Ambrose’s hymn prays nec … pavor quiētōs suscitet — that no fright wake us at rest.
  • stertō, stertere, stertuī — snore (Traupman 381; Cic., Hor.). Erasmus: Nōn tē pudet … in multam lūcem stertere?
  • somnum in multum diem prōdūcere — sleep in, sleep late (M-O). Horace’s idlers in mediōs dormīre diēs (Ep. 1.2.30).
  • lectum sternere — make the bed (Traupman 38, 36 mementō sternere lectulum tuum).
  • ē lectulō extrahere — drag someone out of bed (Traupman 36).
  • Quid somniāvistī? — What did you dream?
  • Somnium malum erat; nunc vigilās, et ego hīc sum. — It was a bad dream; now you’re awake, and I’m here.
  • Audīn’? Avus stertit! — Hear that? Grandpa’s snoring!

Horace Ep. 1.2.30 is quoted from M-O and was not checked against a text.

Grooming: hairbrush / hairpin / hair band / curl / fringe / haircut / hairdresser / shave / tweezers / cut your nails

pēniculus comātōrius · tondeō, tondēre · rādō, rādere

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations
  • pēniculus comātōrius — hairbrush (Traupman 325; comātōrius, “for the hair”, is Petronius’s word). acus comātōria — hairpin (Traupman 325; Petr. 21.1). taenia, taeniae f.; vitta, vittae f. — hair band, ribbon (Traupman 117; L&S).
  • crispāre — curl the hair (Traupman 36, 38; M-O capillum crispāre, Plin.); calamister, calamistrī m. — curling iron (Traupman 38; Plaut.).
  • antiae, antiārum f. — fringe, bangs (Traupman 160; M-O; Apul.).
  • tondērī — get a haircut (M-O; Liv. 27.34.6); capillum alicui tondēre — cut someone’s hair (M-O; Cic.). Traupman: tōnsūra, facere ut capillus tondeātur (325).
  • tōnsor, tōnsōris m.; tōnstrīx, tōnstrīcis f. — barber, hairdresser (Traupman 276, 325; M-O); tōnstrīna, tōnstrīnae f. — barbershop (Traupman; Plaut.).
  • rādō, rādere, rāsī, rāsum — shave; barbam rādere (M-O); Traupman: faciem cotīdiē rāsitāre, shave every day (Suet. Oth. 12). novācula, novāculae f. — razor (Traupman 369; M-O).
  • volsella, volsellae f. — tweezers (M-O; Plaut., Mart.).
  • unguēs resecāre — cut one’s nails (Traupman 58); M-O: unguēs praesecāre (Hor. AP 294). Plautus’s miser who collects his barber’s nail clippings, praesegmina (Aul. 312), is a ready story.
  • lōmentum capillāre — shampoo (Traupman 377); classically lōmentum is a bean-meal face wash (Mart.), so this is a modern extension.
  • chartula hygiēnica — toilet paper (Traupman 395, modern). dentiscalpium, dentiscalpiī n. — toothpick (Traupman 396; M-O; Mart.).
  • gargarīzāre — gargle (M-O; Cels.); collūtōrium, collūtōriī n. — mouthwash (Traupman 64; M-O, modern).
  • Hodiē tondēberis. — You’re having a haircut today.
  • Dā mihi manum; unguēs tibi resecābō. — Give me your hand; I’ll cut your nails.

Existing entries already cover the comb, nail, toothbrush, soap, towel, hair dryer and mirror; this entry adds the rest of the barber’s and bathroom vocabulary.

Nātūra et alimenta

Nature & food

Wild fruit and nuts on a walk: cornelian cherries / sloes / blackberries

cornum, cornī n. · prūnum silvestre

Ancient wordsIdentification notes
  • cornum, cornī n. — cornelian cherry, the fruit of cornus (Ov. corna).
  • prūnum silvestre — wild plum, sloe; Vergil speaks of spīnōs jam prūna ferentēs (Georg. IV 145).
  • mōrum, mōrī n. — blackberry by application; see the existing bramble entry (mōrum rubī).
  • bāca / bacca, -ae f. — berry; both spellings are ancient; the libellī write bāca, the series spelling.
  • nucem frangere — crack a nut; acerbus, acerba, acerbum — sour, unripe; crūdus, crūda, crūdum — raw; ōs contrahere — pucker one’s mouth.
  • Prūna sunt, tata! Prūna invēnī! — Prūna quidem, sed spīnī — They’re plums, Dad! I found plums! — Plums indeed, but sloes (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Nucēs Octōbrī. Quaere sub jūglande; fortasse ūna manet. — Nuts are in October. Look under the walnut tree; maybe one is left. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Ubi sunt mōra, tata? — Where are the blackberries, Dad? (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Birds: raven / crow / woodpecker / magpie / blackbird / sparrow / seagull / pigeon / peacock / flap / fly away

corvus, corvī m. · cornīx, cornīcis f.

Ancient Latin
  • avis, avis f. — bird; volucris, volucris f. — winged creature, mainly poetic; rōstrum, rōstrī n. — beak; penna, pennae f.; plūma, plūmae f. — feather.
  • corvus, corvī m. — raven (Traupman 144); crōciō, crōcīre — croak (Plaut. Aul. 625; the verb of Libellus VII); crocitō, crocitāre — the frequentative (L&S); cornīx, cornīcis f. — crow (142).
  • pīcus, pīcī m. — woodpecker (Traupman 145); grāculus, grāculī m. — jackdaw; passer, passeris m. — sparrow; merula, merulae f. — blackbird; pīca, pīcae f. — magpie.
  • būteō, būteōnis m. — buzzard (Plin. NH X 21); noctua, noctuae f. — owl (Traupman 351).
  • pāvō, pāvōnis m. — peacock (Traupman 143); caudam explicāre — fan its tail. ānser, ānseris m. — goose.
  • corvōs, quī super agrōs crōciēbant, et cornīcēs, quārum ūna in fraxinō sedēns clāmābat — ravens croaking over the fields, and crows, one of which sat calling in an ash tree (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Habetne pīcus malleum, tata? — Nōn malleum, sed rōstrum, quod illī prō malleō est. — Does the woodpecker have a hammer, Dad? — Not a hammer but a beak, which serves it as a hammer. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Ave, ecce avēs! Cūr caudās tam brevēs habent? — Grandpa, look, birds! Why do they have such short tails? (moulting peacocks) (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • gāvia, gāviae f. — seagull (Traupman 375; Pliny, NH 10.91); columba, columbae f. — pigeon, dove (Traupman 144; Cic.).
  • ālīs plaudere — flap the wings (Traupman 141); āvolō, āvolāre — fly away (Traupman 141; Catull.).
  • Quācumque ībant, gāviae ē pinnīs āvolābant. — Wherever they went, seagulls flew off the battlements. (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • avēs magnae inter columbās gravī gradū ambulābant — big birds were walking with heavy steps among the pigeons (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Quae dum loquuntur, cornīx ālīs plaudēns āvolāvit. — While they were talking, the crow flapped its wings and flew away. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • cicōnia, cicōniae f. — stork; hirundō, hirundinis f. — swallow; cycnus, cycnī m. — swan; aquila, aquilae f. — eagle; būbō, būbōnis m. — eagle-owl (Traupman 142–145). nīdus, nīdī m. — nest; nīdificāre — build a nest (Traupman 141; Col.); ōva parere — lay eggs (Traupman 142).

piscis, piscis m. · sarda, sardae f.

Ancient wordsIdentification notes
  • piscis, piscis m. — fish; sarda, sardae f. — sardine (Traupman 73). Portuguese sarda is a mackerel.
  • lupus, lupī m. — sea bass, robalo (Hor., Mart.); aurāta, aurātae f. — gilthead bream, dourada (Col., Mart.); sargus, sargī m. — white bream, sargo (Ov., Plin.).
  • thynnus, thynnī m. — tuna (Traupman 145 prints thunnus); scomber, scombrī m. — mackerel (Plin.); trāchūrus, trāchūrī m. — horse mackerel (Plin.).
  • asellus, asellī m. — hake, cod (Plin. NH IX 61); asellus sale condītus et siccātus — salt cod, bacalhau; passer, passeris m. — flounder (Traupman 71).
  • squilla, squillae f. — shrimp (Traupman 73); ostrea, ostreae f. — oyster (72); locusta, locustae f. — lobster (71; L&S lŏcusta; de Vaan notes that lōc- and luc- are also found).
  • pōlypus, pōlypī m. — octopus, with long ō (Hor. Epod. 12, 5); lōlīgō, lōlīginis f. — squid; saepia, saepiae f. — cuttlefish (Plin. IX 83).
  • In mēnsīs piscātōriīs lupī jacēbant, aurātae, scombrī, pōlypī bracchiīs porrēctīs — On the fish stalls lay sea bass, gilthead bream, mackerel, octopuses with their arms spread out (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Quid est in ventre piscis, tata? — What’s in the fish’s belly, Dad? (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «In hōc pisce ānulus nōn est, tata.» — “There’s no ring in this fish, Dad.” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • salmō, salmōnis m. — salmon (Traupman 373; Plin. 9.68); myax, myacis m. — clam, a kind of mussel (Traupman 70; Plin. 32.95).

Ancient fish names do not always map onto one modern species. The identifications follow the Libellus IV glosses, matched to Portuguese market names.

Aquarium: shark / ray / moray eel / starfish / sea urchin / seahorse / jellyfish / seaweed

squalus, squalī m. · raja, rajae f.

Ancient wordsModern senses
  • squalus, squalī m. — shark (Plin. NH IX 78); raja, rajae f. — ray (IX 78); cartilāgō, cartilāginis f. — cartilage.
  • mola, molae f. — sunfish: a modern sense (Mola mola); the Latin word means millstone. mūrēna, mūrēnae f. — moray eel (Plin. IX 76).
  • urtīca marīna — sea anemone (Plin. IX 146); stēlla marīna — starfish (IX 183); echīnus, echīnī m. — sea urchin (IX 100).
  • hippocampus, hippocampī m. — seahorse (Plin. XXXII 58); dracō marīnus — sea dragon, here the animal Phycodurus. Pliny’s dracō marīnus (IX 82) is a different fish.
  • pulmō marīnus — jellyfish (Plin. NH IX 154); medūsa — the modern name.
  • alga, algae f. — seaweed; concha, conchae f. — shell.
  • Mamma ossa habet, tata! — Habet. Raja piscis nōn habet. — Mummy has bones, Dad! — She does. A ray hasn’t got any. (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • pulmōnēs marīnī pendēbant, vitreī, rotundī — jellyfish hung in the water, glassy and round (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • hippocampī stābant ērēctī, caudīs algās amplexī — seahorses stood upright, their tails wrapped round the seaweed (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • pinna dorsālis — dorsal fin (Traupman 144): a modern phrase; squāma, squāmae f. — scale (Traupman 142; Cic. N.D. 2.121).
  • Prīmus omnium squalus praeterlāpsus est, longus, cānus, lentus, pinnā dorsālī ērēctā — First of all a shark glided past, long, grey, slow, its dorsal fin upright (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Praenatābant et piscēs longī, squāmīs argenteīs, ōre acūtō — Long fish swam past too, with silver scales and pointed mouths (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Dolphin / whale / seal / otter / penguin / swim

delphīnus, delphīnī m. · sphēniscus, sphēniscī m.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin
  • delphīnus, delphīnī m. — dolphin (Traupman 142); also delphīn, delphīnis m., accusative delphīna in Ovid.
  • bālaena, bālaenae f. — whale (Traupman 145; L&S bālaena).
  • phōca, phōcae f.; vitulus marīnus — seal (Plin. NH IX 19).
  • lutra, lutrae f. — otter; short u with de Vaan (from *udrā-), where L&S prints lūtra; lutra marīna — sea otter.
  • sphēniscus, sphēniscī m. — penguin, after the genus Spheniscus: the word of Libellus V (Neo-Latin); pinguīnus, pinguīnī m. is another Neo-Latin form.
  • natō, natāre, natāvī, natātum — swim; in dorsō natāre — swim on one’s back.
  • Avēs natant! Cūr nōn volant, tata? — In āëre nōn volant; in aquā volant. Sphēniscī vocantur — Birds swimming! Why don’t they fly, Dad? — They don’t fly in the air; they fly in the water. They’re called penguins (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Estne delphīnus in caelō, tata? Vidēre volō! — Is there a dolphin in the sky, Dad? I want to see it! (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Olives / olive oil / pick / basket

olīva, olīvae f. · oleum, oleī n.

Ancient Latin
  • olīva, olīvae f. — olive, tree and fruit; olea, oleae f. (L&S).

  • Quōmodo ex olīvīs oleum fit? — Premuntur; oleum quod exit, eō coquō. — How is oil made from olives? — They are pressed; the oil that comes out is what I cook with. (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Olīvās avia in corbem lēgit — Grandma gathered the olives into a basket (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).

Fine weather and chilly days: it clears up / clear sky / chilly / drizzle / hoarfrost / breeze / the wind picks up / melt

disserēnat · pruīna, pruīnae f.

Ancient Latin
  • disserēnat — it clears up (Traupman 132, 135; Pliny, NH 18.356 disserēnābit); disserēnāscit (Liv. 39.46.4).
  • sūdum, sūdī n. — a clear, bright sky (sūdus, Verg. G. 4.77); serēnitās, serēnitātis f. — clear weather (Traupman 135; Cic. Div. 2.94).
  • frīgidulus, frīgidula, frīgidulum — chilly (Traupman 135; Catull. 64.131).
  • lēniter pluit — it is drizzling (Traupman 135).
  • pruīna, pruīnae f. — hoarfrost (Traupman 135; Cic. N.D. 2.26); the frost entry has gelū.
  • ventulus, ventulī m. — breeze (Traupman 135; Ter. Eun. 595 ventulum huic sīc facitō, said with a fan); perflō, perflāre — blow through, blow over (Verg. A. 1.83).
  • incrēbrēscō, incrēbrēscere, incrēbruī — of wind, pick up, get stronger (Traupman 137; Cic. Fam. 7.20.3 ventus).
  • liquēscō, liquēscere — melt (Traupman 136; Liv. 21.36 nivis liquēscentis); ningit, nīnxit — it snows, it snowed (Traupman 136), as in the snow entry.
  • mox disserēnābit. Exspectā. — it will soon clear up. Wait. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Nunc sūdum est,» inquit, «et invītat ad deambulandum. — The sky is clear now,” he said, “and it’s a day for a walk. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Puer Alpēs summā serēnitāte cōnspexit — The boy saw the Alps in perfectly clear weather (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • āēr tamen frīgidulus erat et ūmidus — but the air was chilly and damp (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Extrā fenestrās lēniter pluēbat — Outside the windows it was drizzling (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Cūr herba alba est?» «Pruīna est, quia nox frīgida fuit.» — “Why is the grass white?” “It’s frost, because the night was cold.” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Ex eā āreā, quam ventulus ā flūmine perflābat — From that square, where a breeze blew up from the river (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • In turre ventus incrēbrēscēbat. — On the tower the wind was picking up. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • «Liquēscetne illa nix, tata?» «In summīs montibus nē aestāte quidem liquēscit.» — “Will that snow melt, Dad?” “On the highest mountains it doesn’t melt even in summer.” (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Rime (fog frozen onto trees and fences) and hoarfrost are both pruīna; Latin doesn’t distinguish them. Comenius: rōs congelātus pruīna dīcitur (Orbis pictus 7). To be specific: pruīna ex nebulā; arborēs nebulā congelātā cānae — trees white with frozen fog (both ours). gelū is the freezing itself: Pruīna est, quia nocte gelū fuit.

Geography: westward / peninsula / border / estuary / riverbed / open plains / bend in the road / mountain range / slope down

paenīnsula, paenīnsulae f. · cōnfīnium, cōnfīniī n.

Ancient Latin
  • in occidentem versus — westward (Traupman 207); likewise in septentriōnēs / in orientem / in merīdiem versus.
  • paenīnsula, paenīnsulae f. — peninsula (Traupman 205; Liv. 26.42; Catull. 31.1).
  • cōnfīnium, cōnfīniī n. — border (Traupman 202; Caes.; Varro).
  • aestuārium, aestuāriī n. — estuary, tidal inlet (Traupman 203; Caes. BG 3.9).
  • alveus, alveī m. — riverbed (Traupman 206); classically any hollow, a trough or a channel.
  • campī patentēs — open plains (Traupman 205).
  • ānfrāctus, ānfrāctūs m. — bend, curve in a road (Traupman 203; Cic. N.D. 2.47, of curves).
  • perpetuīs jugīs tendere — stretch in an unbroken range (Traupman 201, 203); jugum is in the mountain entry.
  • vergō, vergere — slope, lie towards (Traupman 206).
  • America Merīdiāna — South America (Traupman 202).
  • Alterō in occidentem versus Lisbōnam volābimus — In the second we’ll fly west to Lisbon (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Hīc sumus, Lisbōnae, in extrēmā paenīnsulā; hīc domus nostra, prope Serdicam, in aliā paenīnsulā. — Here we are, in Lisbon, at the far end of a peninsula; here is our home, near Sofia, on another peninsula. (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Hīc Pȳrēnaeī montēs, in cōnfīniō Hispāniae et Galliae — Here are the Pyrenees, on the border between Spain and France (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Flūmen est, Tagus, quem ex trāmine vīdistī; hīc aestuārium efficit lātissimum. — It’s a river, the Tagus, which you saw from the train; here it forms a very wide estuary. (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Rīvus, quī vēre strepit, siccus erat, alveusque nūdīs lapidibus strātus. — The stream, which babbles in spring, was dry, and its bed was covered in bare stones. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Avia, quae campōs subjectōs patentēsque contemplābātur — Grandma, who was looking out over the open plains below (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • quā vehiculum per ānfrāctūs lentē serpēbat — where the bus wound slowly round the bends (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • nam Osoitsa ad rādīcēs Haemī jacet, quī perpetuīs jugīs per tōtam Bulgariam ad Pontum ūsque tendit — for Osoitsa lies at the foot of the Haemus, which stretches in an unbroken range across all Bulgaria to the Black Sea (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Prānsī in hortum botanicum intrāvērunt, quī ab aquaeductū ad flūmen vergit — After lunch they went into the botanical garden, which slopes from the aqueduct down to the river (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Sphēniscī vocantur, et ex ultimīs Americae Merīdiānae ōrīs veniunt — They’re called penguins, and they come from the farthest shores of South America (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).

Thunder / lightning / storm / hail / rainbow

tonitrus, tonitrūs m. · fulgur, fulguris n.

Ancient LatinComposed phrasesQuantity notes
  • tonitrus, tonitrūs m. — thunder (Traupman 136, 394); tonat, tonāre, tonuit — it thunders (Traupman 137, 394).
  • fulgur, fulguris n. — flash of lightning (Traupman 135); fulget, fulgēre, fulsit — there is lightning; also fulgurat (Traupman 136; L&S: less frequent than fulget). fulmen, fulminis n. — thunderbolt, lightning strike (Traupman 137); fulmine īcī — be struck by lightning (Traupman 340).
  • tempestās, tempestātis f. — storm, and also plain “weather”; procella, procellae f. — gale, squall (Traupman 136); tempestās coorta est — a storm blew up (Traupman 136); procellōsus, procellōsa, procellōsum — stormy (Traupman 136).
  • grandō, grandinis f. — hail (Traupman 135; Plaut.); grandinat — it is hailing (Traupman 135).
  • arcus caelestis; pluvius arcus — rainbow (Traupman 136, 368; M-O s.v. rainbow): aut flūmen Rhēnum aut pluvius dēscrībitur arcus (Hor. A.P. 18).
  • Fulget! Mox tonābit. — Lightning! It’ll thunder soon.
  • Nōlī timēre: tonitrus sonat tantum, nōn nocet. — Don’t be afraid: thunder only makes a noise, it doesn’t hurt.
  • Grandinat! Intrō currāmus. — It’s hailing! Let’s run inside.
  • Ecce arcus caelestis! Quot colōrēs vidēs? — Look, a rainbow! How many colours can you see?

Lewis & Short marks the second vowel of tonitrus as doubtful; it is left unmarked here. The fourth-declension genitive -ūs is certain.

Rain and sky: shower / it’s pouring / letting up / sunny / cloudy / foggy / windy

imber, imbris m. · aprīcus, aprīca, aprīcum

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • imber, imbris m. — shower, heavy rain (Traupman 136); magnī et adsiduī imbrēs — heavy, steady rain (Traupman 136). imber dētumēscit — the rain is letting up (Traupman 136, 368, printed dētūmēscit; L&S dētumēscō has a short u and is rare: Statius).
  • urceātim pluit — it’s pouring, raining buckets (Traupman 135, 368; Petr. 44.18); Morgan–Owens adds effunditur imber and catervātim pluit (M-O s.v. it’s pouring). Traupman prints ūrceātim on p. 135; Lewis & Short has a short u.
  • Vidētur quasi pluat. — It looks like rain (Traupman 136).
  • aprīcus, aprīca, aprīcum — sunny, warmed by the sun (Traupman 136): aprīcus campus (Hor. C. 1.8.3); aprīcī collēs (Liv. 21.37).
  • nūbilus, nūbila, nūbilum — cloudy, overcast (Traupman 136; L&S: poetic and post-Augustan); nūbilōsus (Traupman 135) is post-classical. nūbilāre — cloud over (Traupman 135; Varr.).
  • nebulōsus, nebulōsa, nebulōsum — foggy, misty (Traupman 135); ventōsus, ventōsa, ventōsum — windy (Traupman 137).
  • Urceātim pluit; domī manēbimus. — It’s pouring; we’ll stay at home.
  • Jam minus pluit; mox exībimus. — It’s raining less now; we’ll go out soon.
  • Caelum nūbilum est; pluet, opīnor. — The sky is cloudy; it’ll rain, I think.

Aquilō, Aquilōnis m. · aestus, aestūs m.

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsComposed phrases
  • Aquilō, Aquilōnis m. — north wind; Auster, Austrī m. — south wind; Eurus, Eurī m. — east wind; Zephyrus, Zephyrī m. — west wind (Traupman 135–137). For Favōnius see the fog and snow entry.
  • ventus cadit — the wind drops (L&S, citing Liv. 29.27.10: ventus premente nebulā cecidit); Traupman 137 gives ventus dētumēscit.
  • aestus, aestūs m. — heat, hot weather (Traupman 136). Calidum est. — It’s hot (Traupman 135); Morgan–Owens gives calor est (M-O s.v. cold: hot). aestuō, aestuāre — I’m hot (M-O, citing Cic. Tusc. 2.34: ēsuriendō, sitiendō, algendō, aestuandō).
  • aestuōsus, aestuōsa, aestuōsum — sultry, sweltering (Traupman 136): aestuōsa et pulverulenta via (Cic. Att. 5.14, cited by L&S). Morgan–Owens gives caelum crassum for humid air (M-O s.v. humidity, from Cic. Fat. 7); the Vatican lexicon gives āeris crassitūdō for muggy heat.
  • tepidus, tepida, tepidum — warm, mild; tepēscit — it is getting warm (Traupman 137).
  • frīgora, frīgorum n. pl. — cold spell (Traupman 135).

  • rōs, rōris m. — dew (Traupman 135).
  • gelārī; glaciārī — freeze, turn to ice (Traupman 135, 331); Morgan–Owens gives gelū concrēscere and conglaciāre (M-O s.v. freeze; Cic. N.D. 2.26). rigēns, rigentis — frozen stiff (Traupman 135).
  • Aquilō flat; pilleum indue. — The north wind is blowing; put your hat on.
  • Ecce, stīriae dē tēctō pendent! — Look, icicles hanging from the roof!
  • Herba rōre madet. — The grass is wet with dew.
  • Aestuō, tata! — I’m hot, Dad!

Temperature / thermometer / degrees / weather forecast / snowstorm

thermometrum, thermometrī n. · calor, calōris m.

Neo-LatinVariable terminology
  • temperātūra, temperātūrae f. — temperature (Traupman 136). Morgan–Owens gives calor, calōris m. instead (M-O s.v. temperature). In Lewis & Short temperātūra means due measure or temperament (ante-classical and post-Augustan), so calor is the safer word for heat. Traupman’s phrase: Quō gradū stat temperātūra? — What’s the temperature? (136).
  • thermometrum, thermometrī n. — thermometer (Traupman 136; M-O s.v. thermometer, a modern coinage); gradus, gradūs m. — degree; M-O: (calōris) gradus.
  • praenūntiātiō tempestātis — weather forecast (Traupman 405); Morgan–Owens gives nūntius meteōrologicus for the forecaster (M-O s.v. weatherman).
  • nivis cāsus — snowfall; ningor, ningōris m. — snowstorm (Traupman 136; L&S: Apuleius only); Morgan–Owens gives procella nivōsa for a blizzard (M-O s.v. snow: blizzard).
  • Quot gradūs thermometrum mōnstrat? Īnspiciāmus. — How many degrees does the thermometer show? Let’s look.
  • Nivem crās fore praenūntiant. — They’re forecasting snow tomorrow.

  • Sōl in occāsum vergit; mox advesperāscet. — The sun is going down; soon it’ll be getting dark.

Animal sounds: moo / bleat / neigh / oink / cluck / crow / bray / croak / chirp / buzz / yelp / purr / howl

mūgiō, mūgīre · bālō, bālāre · hinniō, hinnīre

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsComposed phrases
  • mūgiō, mūgīre, mūgīvī (mūgiī), mūgītum — moo, low (Traupman 142, 298): cum āctae bovēs mūgīssent (Liv. 1.7, as cited by L&S).
  • bālō, bālāre — bleat, of sheep, goats and lambs (Traupman 143–144; Plaut.; Ov.).
  • hinniō, hinnīre — neigh (Traupman 143; Quint. 7.3.3).
  • grunniō, grunnīre — grunt, oink (Traupman 143–144; Varr.).
  • glōciō, glōcīre — cluck (Traupman 141; Col. 8.5.4).
  • canō, canere, cecinī — of a cock, crow: quia gallī victī silēre solērent, canere victōrēs (Cic. Div. 2.56). Traupman 144 also gives cūcūriō, which is found only in the late Carmen dē Philomēlā.
  • rudō, rudere, rudīvī — bray (Traupman 142; Ov.).
  • coaxō, coaxāre — croak (Traupman 143; Suet. Aug. 94).
  • pīpō, pīpāre; pīpilō, pīpilāre — chirp, peep (Traupman 141, 144); gallīna pīpat (Varr. ap. Non. 156.25). Lesbia’s sparrow ad sōlam dominam ūsque pīpiābat (Catull. 3.10), from pīpiō, pīpiāre; L&S, on an older reading, cites the line as pīpilābat.
  • bombus, bombī m. — buzzing, humming: sī intus faciunt bombum, of bees (Varr. R.R. 3.16.32).
  • gannīre — yelp, whimper (Traupman 142, 144; Varr.); ringī — snarl (Traupman 142; Ter. Phorm. 341: ille ringitur, tū rīdeās); murmurāre — purr (Traupman 141); ululāre — howl (Traupman 145; Verg.); barrīre — trumpet, of an elephant (Traupman 142; Spartianus).
  • Quid dīcit vacca? — Mū! Vacca mūgit. — What does the cow say? — Moo! The cow is mooing.
  • Audīn' asinum rudentem? — Can you hear the donkey braying?
  • Rānae coaxant; fortasse pluet. — The frogs are croaking; maybe it’ll rain.

Not recommended: Traupman’s tetrinniō (quack), mintriō (squeak) and crocitāre are attested only in the late Carmen dē Philomēlā. His bombilāre (buzz), būbilāre (hoot) and gingrīre (cackle) are not Lewis & Short headwords (L&S has bombītāre, from the same late poem). For geese, owls and ducks, a plain verb such as clāmat or strīdet (Traupman 142) does the job.

At the zoo: tiger / panther / giraffe / camel / crocodile / hippopotamus / rhinoceros / ostrich / zebra / dinosaur

tigris, tigris (tigridis) m./f. · camēlopardalis, camēlopardalis f.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinQuantity notesComposed phrases
  • tigris, tigris or tigridis m./f. — tiger (Traupman 145; Verg.; Plin.); panthēra, panthērae f. — panther, leopard (Traupman 138, 143); pardus, pardī m. — leopard (Traupman 143).
  • camēlopardalis, camēlopardalis f. — giraffe (Traupman 143, 321; Plin.: the “camel-leopard”); camēlus, camēlī m. — camel (Traupman 141).
  • crocodīlus, crocodīlī m. — crocodile (Traupman 142); hippopotamus, hippopotamī m. — hippopotamus (Traupman 143; Plin.); rhīnocerōs, rhīnocerōtis m. — rhinoceros (Traupman 144; Plin.; Mart.).
  • strūthiocamēlus, strūthiocamēlī m. — ostrich (Traupman 143; Plin.).
  • zebra, zebrae f. — zebra (Traupman 138, in the zoo dialogue: tigrēs et zebrās); not in Lewis & Short, a modern word. dinosaurus, dinosaurī m. — dinosaur (Traupman 304, modern).
  • Ecce camēlopardalis! Quam longō collō est! — Look, a giraffe! What a long neck it has!
  • Hippopotamus in aquā dormit. — The hippo is asleep in the water.

Lewis & Short marks the first vowel of tigris as doubtful; it is left unmarked. zebra and dinosaurus have no ancient quantity.

Wild flowers and plants: daisy / poppy / dandelion / sunflower / violet / lily / nettle / acorn

bellis, bellidis f. · papāver, papāveris n.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinModern speciesComposed phrases
  • bellis, bellidis f. — daisy (Traupman 300; Plin. 26.26).
  • papāver, papāveris n. — poppy (Traupman 363; M-O s.v. poppy; Verg.; Plin.).
  • aphaca, aphacae f. — dandelion (M-O s.v. dandelion, citing Plin. 21.89 and André’s identification; L&S: “the common dandelion”).
  • hēlianthus, hēlianthī m. — sunflower (M-O s.v. sunflower; Linnaeus’s genus name, a modern coinage).
  • viola, violae f. — violet; līlium, līliī n. — lily; urtīca, urtīcae f. — nettle (Catull. 44.15); glāns, glandis f. — acorn. These are classical words from Lewis & Short; neither book has them in the sections swept.
  • Cavē urtīcās: urunt! — Mind the nettles: they sting!
  • Ecce, bellidēs in prātō! — Look, daisies in the meadow!
  • Glandēs sub quercū legāmus. — Let’s pick up acorns under the oak.

Travel & transport

Courier / delivery person

tabellārius, tabellāriī m.

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • tabellārius, tabellāriī m. — letter-carrier or courier; using it for a parcel delivery person is a modern application.
  • nūntius, nūntiī m. — messenger; cursor, cursōris m. — runner or courier; tabella, tabellae f. — writing tablet or letter.
  • nūntiō, nūntiāre, nūntiāvī, nūntiātum — announce or report.
  • Tabellārius adest. — The delivery person is here.
  • tabellārius is derived from tabella; cursor from currō. English nuncio, annunciation, cursor reflect these families.

Bus / coach

autoraeda longa

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • autoraeda longa — bus or coach; Morgan–Owens cites Albert, Helfer and Bacci. The noun is autoraeda, autoraedae f..
  • autocīnētum lāophoricum — a learned alternative; lāophorum, lāophorī n. — bus. The Greek-derived lāo- reflects “people,” and -cīnēt- “moving.”
  • autoraeda pūblica — public bus, also recorded in the modern lexicon.
  • Autoraedā longā īmus. — We’re going by bus.

Tram / streetcar

currus ēlectricus · currus trānsviārius

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • currus ēlectricus — tram (Traupman 218; Morgan–Owens): our preferred everyday term, used in Libellus V for the Lisbon eléctrico.
  • currus trānsviārius — tram; Morgan–Owens cites Palaestra Latina. currus, currūs m. — vehicle or carriage; trānsviārius, trānsviāria, trānsviārium — pertaining to a tramway.
  • pūblicus currus ēlectricus — another documented tram expression, cited there from the Lexicon Recentis Latinitatis.
  • currus tramviārius — a retained working alternative, with a borrowed tram- stem whose vowel length is not established here.
  • Currum trānsviārium exspectāmus. — We’re waiting for the tram.

Train / railway

trāmen, trāminis n.

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • trāmen, trāminis n. — train in modern Latin; trāmen ferriviārium — railway train.
  • ferrivia, ferriviae f. — railway; ferriviārius, ferriviāria, ferriviārium — pertaining to railways.
  • hamaxostichus, hamaxostichī m. — a competing learned Neo-Latin term for a train.
  • Morgan–Owens traces the lexical form trāmen to Charisius; the railway sense is modern. Related vocabulary: trahō, trahere, trāxī, tractum — draw or pull.

Bicycle / bicycle parts

  • birotārius, birotāria, birotārium — pertaining to bicycles; birotārius, birotāriī m. or birotāria, birotāriae f. — cyclist.
  • rota, rotae f. — wheel; radius, radiī m. — spoke; modiolus, modiolī m. — hub.

Helmet / knee pads / elbow pads

galea birotāria

Ancient wordsModern extension
  • galea, galeae f. — helmet; galea birotāria — bicycle helmet, a transparent modern description.
  • genuāle, genuālis n. (plural genuālia) — knee covering or band; extended here to a protective knee pad.
  • cubital, cubitālis n. (plural cubitālia) — an elbow cushion in ancient Latin; extended here to an elbow pad.
  • chīrothēca, chīrothēcae f. — glove, a post-Classical word; chīrothēcae birotāriae — cycling gloves.
  • lōrum galeae — helmet strap.
  • Galeam indue. Genuālia et cubitālia indue. — Put on your helmet, knee pads and elbow pads.
  • Nunc birotam conscende. — Now get on your bicycle.

The specific protective-sports senses are labelled as semantic extensions; the earlier blanket “attested” tag has been removed.

Adventure / venture

ausum, ausī n. · adventūra, adventūrae f.

Ancient LatinMedieval LatinModern semantic extension
  • ausum, ausī n. — a daring attempt, venture, undertaking or enterprise; our preferred word for modern adventure when the emphasis is on something voluntarily and boldly undertaken.
  • adventūra, adventūrae f. — a medieval Latin word connected with what happens, chance, fortune, risk or venture; retained here as a secondary word for modern adventure by later semantic extension, especially through the Romance development of the word.
  • Novum ausum suscipiāmus. — Let’s undertake a new adventure.
  • Hodiē novum ausum quaerāmus. — Let’s seek a new adventure today.
  • Nova adventūra nōs exspectat. — A new adventure awaits us; a modern-style use, not presented as an ancient idiom.

The English word adventure ultimately belongs to the adventūra family, but its cheerful modern sense is later than the core medieval Latin meanings. For ordinary family speech, prefer ausum when an ancient word is wanted; use adventūra when the later European word-family itself is useful.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short / Logeion: ausum · Mittellateinisches Glossar: adventura · Medieval legal glossary: adventura / adventurare / adventurarius

Airport / aeroplane / runway / fly / take off / land

āëroportus, āëroportūs m. · āëroplanum, āëroplanī n.

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • āëroportus, āëroportūs m. — airport (Traupman 215); āëroplanum, āëroplanī n. — aeroplane (215); āëroplanō vehī — travel by plane (218).
  • āërodromus, āërodromī m. — runway (Traupman 218); a modern formation, narrower here than English aerodrome.
  • volō, volāre, volāvī, volātum — fly; volātus, volātūs m. — flight (Traupman 216).
  • sūrsum in āëra ascendere — take off (Traupman 218); ad terram dēscendere, deorsum appellere — land (217).
  • gubernātor, gubernātōris m. — pilot (Traupman 217); in ancient Latin a helmsman.
  • via āëria — air route: a working description (locūtiō nostra), no longer used in the libellī.
  • Āëroplanō vehēmur. — We’ll go by plane. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Euax! Volāmus! Tata, volāmus! — Hooray! We’re flying! Dad, we’re flying! (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Postquam rotae cum sonitū terram tetigērunt, āëroplanum sēnsim tardius currēns tandem cōnstitit. — When the wheels had touched the ground with a thud, the plane, running ever more slowly, at last stopped. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

The airport vocabulary follows Traupman, chapter XXIV. These are modern lexicographic formations on Greek and Latin roots, not ancient words; the diaeresis in āë- marks two separate vowels.

Gate / waiting room / departure / delay / layover / connection

aditus, aditūs m. · commorātiō, commorātiōnis f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applications
  • aditus, aditūs m. — airport gate (Traupman 216); in ancient Latin an approach or entrance.
  • oecus praestōlātōrius — waiting room (Traupman 219); praestōlor, praestōlārī, praestōlātus sum — wait for (L&S).
  • abscēdō, abscēdere, abscessī, abscessum — depart; abscessus, abscessūs m. — departure (Traupman 216).
  • volātus dīlātus — delayed flight, from differō, differre, distulī, dīlātum (L&S); sērius — later; sērō — late.
  • commorātiō, commorātiōnis f. — layover, stopover (Traupman 217); conjūnctiō, conjūnctiōnis f. — connection (216).
  • āëroplana mūtāre — change planes (Traupman 215); ad āëroplanum sērius venīre — miss the plane, the phrase of Libellus I (literally, reach it too late).
  • trānsitus, trānsitūs m. — transfer, transit: the use of Libellus I (locūtiō nostra); L&S gives the general sense “a passing over”.
  • Ad aditum duodecimum oecus erat praestōlātōrius, sellīs multīs īnstrūctus — At gate twelve there was a waiting room with many seats (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Paulisper exspectandum est. — We’ll have to wait a little. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Ibi āëroplana mūtābimus — There we’ll change planes (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Conjūnctiō bona est, neque tam brevis ut ad alterum āëroplanum sērius veniāmus, neque nimis longa. — It’s a good connection, not so short that we reach the second plane too late, and not too long. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Security check / security officer / tray

scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f.

Ancient wordsWorking formation
  • scrūtātiō, scrūtātiōnis f. — security check: the descriptive term of Libellus I (locūtiō nostra), from scrūtor, scrūtārī, scrūtātus sum — search thoroughly (L&S). It is not a recorded Neo-Latin airport term.
  • custōs, custōdis m./f. — guard; here a security officer (Libellī I, VI).
  • cista, cistae f. — box or chest; applied in the libellī (I, VI) to the tray at the security check.
  • sarcinās excutere — search the bags (literally, shake them out; Libellus I); calceōs exuere — take off one’s shoes; see the existing shoe entry.
  • Ad scrūtātiōnem igitur ventum est, ubi custōdēs, nē quis rem perīculōsam in āëroplanum īnferat, omnium sarcinās excutiunt. — So they came to the security check, where the officers search everyone’s bags so that nobody takes anything dangerous onto the plane. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Pēram in cistam posuit, lapidem, cum rogārētur, prōmpsit — He put his bag in the tray and, when asked, took out the stone (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

Luggage / suitcase / backpack / luggage tag / luggage rack

sarcinae, sarcinārum f. pl. · vidulus, vidulī m.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applicationsWorking formation
  • sarcina, sarcinae f.; sarcinae, sarcinārum f. pl. — pack, bundle; luggage (Traupman 217). sarcina manuālis — hand luggage; Traupman 216 prints sarcinulae manuālēs.
  • vidulus, vidulī m. — suitcase (Traupman 218); in ancient Latin a travelling trunk (Plaut. Rud. 906 ff.). vidulus rotīs īnstrūctus — wheeled suitcase, the description in Libellus I.
  • pēra, pērae f. — shoulder bag (Traupman 218); pēra dorsuālis — backpack: working formation (dorsuālis, L&S).
  • pittacium, pittaciī n. — luggage tag (Traupman 217); bajulus, bajulī m. — porter (217, printed bajulus; L&S bājulus); no macron before consonantal i, as in major, ejus.
  • retināculum sarcināle; in retināculō repōnere — luggage rack; put in the rack (Traupman 217).
  • lībra, lībrae f. — scales; pēnsō, pēnsāre — weigh (L&S). vidulum trādere — check in a suitcase, the use of trādō in Libellus I.
  • Vidulus autem, quia rotīs īnstrūctus est, nōn portātur sed trahitur — The suitcase, though, having wheels, isn’t carried but pulled (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Quid,» inquit pater, «in pēram tuam condēs, Theodōre?» — “What,” said Dad, “will you put in your bag, Theo?” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • quī vidulōs magnōs acceptōs in lībrā pēnsant, pittaciō signant — (the check-in agents,) who weigh the big suitcases on the scales and tag them (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Nēmō umquam vidulum semel clausit. — Nobody ever closed a suitcase only once. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Passport / ticket / ticket agent / e-ticket

commeātūs diplōma, diplōmatis n. · tessera, tesserae f.

Ancient wordsNeo-Latin applications
  • commeātūs diplōma, diplōmatis n. — passport (Traupman 217); ancient diplōma is an official travel document, commeātus leave to come and go.
  • tessera, tesserae f.; tessera itinerāria, tessera ferriviāria — ticket; travel ticket; railway ticket (Traupman 218–219). Ancient tessera is a token or tally.
  • tesserārius, tesserāriī m. — ticket agent, check-in agent (Traupman 218).
  • tēlephōnum, tēlephōnī n. — telephone (Traupman); tessera in tēlephōnō — a ticket on the phone; chartāceus, chartācea, chartāceum — made of paper (L&S).
  • Hoc est commeātūs diplōma, in quō nōmen meum est et imāgō. — This is a passport, with my name and my picture in it. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Sine diplōmate nēmō in āëroplanum admittitur. — Nobody is let onto a plane without a passport. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • omnia nostra sarcinae manuālēs sunt, tesserae in tēlephōnō servantur. — all our things are hand luggage, and the tickets are kept on the phone. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Diplōmata? Tesserās? — Passports? Tickets? (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • tessera ūnīus cursūs / tessera itūs reditūsque — one-way / return ticket (Traupman 211, 218); scidula cōnscēnsiōnālis — boarding pass (M-O s.v. boarding pass, from Egger, a modern coinage).

Metro / underground / tunnel / tap the ticket

ferrivia subterrānea

Neo-LatinWorking formations
  • ferrivia subterrānea — underground, metro (Traupman 218); trāmen subterrāneum — metro train: the descriptive phrase of Libellus I.
  • tesseram māchinae appōnere — tap the ticket on the reader: the description in Libellus I (tesserae, quae māchinae appōnuntur ut porta aperiātur).
  • specus, specūs m. — tunnel; cave (Traupman 219, 203: Traupman prints only specus).
  • cunīculus, cunīculī m. — tunnel, underground passage: the ancient term. The same word means “rabbit” (see the animals entry).
  • columna, columnae f. — pillar; here the pole to hold on to.
  • Sub terrā currit trāmen, sub viīs, sub domibus — The train runs under the ground, under the streets, under the houses (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • ventus ē specū ērūpit, lūmina appāruērunt — a wind burst out of the tunnel, lights appeared (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Quot statiōnēs? — How many stops? (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Cum nūlla sēdēs vacua esset, stābant, Theodōrus columnam tenēns, ut virī solent. — As no seat was free, they stood, Theo holding the pole, as men do. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Journey / set out / arrive / return / traveller / abroad

Ancient Latin

In the car: get in / get out / car door / window / steering wheel / headlights / brake / park / car park / traffic light

autoraedam īnscendere · ōstiolum, ōstiolī n.

Neo-LatinAncient words, modern senses
  • autoraedam īnscendere — get into the car (Traupman 215; īnscendō, Plaut.); dē autoraedā ēgredī — get out of the car (Traupman 215).
  • ōstiolum, ōstiolī n. — car door (Traupman 215); classically a small door (Columella; Pliny).
  • fenestella, fenestellae f. — car window (Traupman 219); classically a small window (Columella).
  • receptāculum sarcinārum — boot, trunk (Traupman 219); see the car entry.
  • rota moderātrīx — steering wheel (Traupman 218).
  • lūmināria, lūminārium n. pl. — headlights (Traupman 216); in Late Latin “lamps” (sing. lūmināre).
  • rotās sufflāmināre — brake (Traupman 215), from sufflāmen, the drag on a wheel (Juv. 8.148 rotam adstringit sufflāmine); cursum reprimere — slow down (Traupman 218).
  • canthus, canthī m. — tyre: the iron tyre of a wheel (Quint. 1.5.8); canthus cummeus — rubber tyre (Traupman 218).
  • autoraedam statuere — park the car (Traupman 217); ārea statīva — car park (Traupman 217).
  • sēmaphorum, sēmaphorī n. — traffic light (Traupman 219: rubrum, flāvum, viride).
  • cum dē autoraedā ēgressī essent — when they had got out of the car (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Cūr cōnsistimus?» «Quia sēmaphorum rubrum est.» — “Why are we stopping?” “Because the light is red.” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Theodōrus manū quasi rotam moderātrīcem versāvit — Theo turned his hand as if on a steering wheel (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • ōstiolō apertō, avum cōnspicātus in complexum ejus cucurrit — the door opened, he saw Grandpa and ran into his arms (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Per fenestellam arborēs tam propinquae praeterībant ut eās paene tangere possēs. — Through the window the trees went by so close you could almost touch them. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Olīvās lūmināria autoraedae aliam post aliam ē tenebrīs ēdūcēbant. — The headlights brought the olive trees out of the dark one after another. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • quotiēns avus ad sēmaphorum rubrum rotās sufflāminābat — every time Grandpa braked at a red light (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Autoraedā in āreā statīvā relictā — When they had left the car in the car park (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
