Getting about: baggage trolley / ticket office / lift / ferry / fare / pack / check out

chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. · cellula scānsōria

Ancient words, modern sensesNeo-Latin
  • chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. — baggage trolley (Traupman 215: chīramaxium sarcinārum); in Petronius (28.4) a small hand-drawn carriage.
  • ōstiolum, ōstiolī n. — ticket window, ticket office (Traupman 218: ōstiolum tesserārum).
  • cellula scānsōria — lift, elevator (Traupman 309), after Vitruvius’s climbing machine, the scānsōrium (10.1.1).
  • nāvis trājectōria — ferry (Traupman 216).
  • vectūra, vectūrae f. — the fare, transport (Traupman 216); classical, as in prō vectūrā solvere (Cic. Att. 1.3.2).
  • sarcinās colligere — pack (Traupman 217); ā dēversōriō discēdere post ratiōnem compōnendam — check out of a hotel after settling the bill (Traupman 215).
  • ambulātiuncula, ambulātiunculae f. — aisle (Traupman 215); in Cicero a short walk or a small walk (Fam. 2.12; Att. 13.29).
  • hominēs autem cum chīramaxiīs stantēs exspectant suōsque quaerunt — and people stand waiting with their trolleys, looking for their own (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Tesserīs ad ōstiolum ēmptīs — When they had bought tickets at the ticket window (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Cum cellulā scānsōriā ūnā ascendissent — When they had gone up together in the lift (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • nāvēs trājectōriae lentē prōgredientēs — ferries slowly making their way (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Sub ipsīs moenibus, vectūrā solūtā, ē raedā dēscendērunt — Right under the walls they paid the fare and got out of the taxi (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Avus et avia, quī in cubiculō proximō dormīverant, sarcinīs collēctīs parātī in vestibulō exspectābant. Ratiōne putātā ā dēversōriō discessum est. — Grandpa and Grandma, who had slept in the next room, had packed and were waiting ready in the lobby. The bill was settled and they checked out. (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • quam pater et fīlius, per ambulātiunculam prōgressī, ūnā intrāvērunt — which father and son went into together, after walking down the aisle (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • chīramaxium īnfantile — pram, pushchair (M-O s.v. baby-carriage); Petronius’s chīramaxium is a little hand-drawn carriage (Petr. 28.4).

Dad’s bag: leather bag / wallet / notepad / pen / headphones

sacculus scorteus · crumēna, crumēnae f.

Ancient LatinWorking formation
  • sacculus scorteus — Dad’s leather hip bag, the word of the libellī (the Libellus I gloss: pēra parva quae ad latus geritur); scorteus “of leather” (Varro, LL 7.84). Traupman 117 has pēra scortea, leather bag; in the libellī a pēra is a backpack.
  • crumēna, crumēnae f. — purse, wallet (Traupman 367); classically a small money bag (Plaut.; Hor. Ep. 1.4.11).
  • pugillārēs, pugillārium m. pl. — notepad (Traupman 30); classically writing tablets (Sen. Ep. 108.6; Pliny).
  • stilus, stilī m. — pen; Traupman 28 has stilus sphaerātus, a ballpoint. Classically the writing stylus.
  • auscultābula, auscultābulōrum n. pl. — headphones: our formation (locūtiō nostra), after Traupman’s auscultābulum (p. 124), from auscultāre “listen”.
  • Praetereā pater sacculum scorteum ad latus gerit, in quō tēlephōnum, crumēnam, pugillārēs, stilum, auscultābula semper servat. — Dad also wears a leather bag at his side, in which he always keeps his phone, wallet, notepad, pen and headphones. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Tourism: tour / tourist / guided tour / tour guide / guidebook / souvenir / customs / customs officer / duty / duty-free

peregrīnātiō, peregrīnātiōnis f. · portitor, portitōris m.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinVariable terminology
  • peregrīnātiō, peregrīnātiōnis f. — tour, tourism, travel abroad; peregrīnātor, peregrīnātōris m. — tourist (Traupman 218–219; M-O s.v. tourism; tourist). Morgan–Owens specifies peregrīnātor fēriāticus or voluptārius; the Vatican lexicon gives periēgētēs for a tourist.

  • portitor, portitōris m. — customs officer; portōrium, portōriī n. — customs duty (M-O s.v. customs official; duty; Caes.; Cic.); telōnium, telōniī n. — customs house (M-O s.v. customs office; Vulg.). immūnis portōriōrum — duty-free (M-O s.v. duty-free; Liv. 38.14).
  • Hīc portitōrēs sarcinās īnspiciunt. — This is where the customs officers check the bags.
  • Memoriāle aviae emāmus. — Let’s buy Grandma a souvenir.

Picnic, beach and camping: picnic / picnic basket / tent / campsite / sunglasses / suntan / get a tan / beach chair

cēnula subdiālis · tentōrium, tentōriī n.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotationsVariable terminology
  • cēnula subdiālis — picnic (Traupman 53, 360; the Vatican lexicon writes cēnula subdīvālis); Morgan–Owens gives prandium subdiāle and cēna subdiālis (M-O s.v. picnic). subdiālis is post-Augustan (Plin.).
  • picnic basket: Traupman gives pānārium, pānāriī n., a bread basket (53, 360; Plin. Ep. 1.6.3; Suet.); Morgan–Owens gives sportula, sportulae f., a little basket (M-O s.v. picnic basket; Plaut.). Both are classical.
  • tentōrium, tentōriī n. — tent (M-O s.v. tent; Caes.). campsite: Traupman gives campus tentōrius (286), which the Vatican lexicon also uses; Morgan–Owens prefers castra fēriātica and rejects campus for ground that is not flat (M-O s.v. campground).
  • perspicilla sōlāria (īnfuscāta) — sunglasses (Traupman 388; Neo-Latin perspicillum, which the Vatican lexicon gives for spectacles).
  • colōrārī — get a tan: cum in sōle ambulem, nātūrā fit ut colōrer (Cic. de Or. 2.60, cited by M-O s.v. tan); adūstus color — suntan (Traupman 388, where Traupman’s active colōrāre should be the passive).
  • sella lītorālis — beach chair (Traupman 276).
  • Cēnulam subdiālem sub quercū sūmāmus! — Let’s have a picnic under the oak!
  • Tentōrium hīc pōnāmus. — Let’s pitch the tent here.

Roads and traffic: traffic / traffic jam / rush hour / motorway / crossroads / side street / dead end / avenue / pavement / pedestrian / zebra crossing / block

commeātus vehiculōrum · compitum, compitī n.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinVariable terminologyComposed phrases
  • commeātus vehiculōrum — traffic (Traupman 174, 397); celebritās viae — heavy traffic (Traupman 397); the Vatican lexicon gives viārum frequentia.
  • affluentia vehiculāria — traffic jam (Traupman 219); tempus maximae frequentiae — rush hour (Vatican lexicon; Morgan–Owens has no word for either).
  • motorway: Traupman gives strāta autocīnētica (216, 328), Morgan–Owens via autocīnētica (M-O s.v. freeway).
  • compitum, compitī n.; quadrivium, quadriviī n. — crossroads, junction (Traupman 173–174, 334; M-O s.v. intersection; classical). For a fork in the road, see the walk entry (trivium).
  • dēverticulum, dēverticulī n.; via laterālis — side street (Traupman 174, 379; M-O s.v. alley: side-street); fundula, fundulae f. — dead end (Traupman 174; M-O; Varro); platēa, platēae f. — avenue, wide street (Traupman 174; M-O s.v. avenue; Cic.); vīcus, vīcī m. — block, street (Traupman 173).
  • crepīdō viāria — pavement, sidewalk (Traupman 379); pedes, peditis m. — pedestrian (Traupman 358; M-O s.v. pedestrian); trānsitus peditum — zebra crossing (Traupman 358).
  • In crepīdine manē; hīc multa vehicula praetereunt. — Stay on the pavement; lots of cars go by here.
  • Hīc, in trānsitū peditum, viam trānsīmus. Dā mihi manum. — Here, at the zebra crossing, we cross the road. Give me your hand.

Directions: turn right / turn left / on the right / go straight on / opposite / where is …? / I’m lost / how far is it? / the quickest way / does this road lead to …?

dextrōrsum · sinistrōrsum · rēctā

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • dextrōrsum (sinistrōrsum) sē vertere — turn right (left) (Traupman 173, 206).
  • dextrā; ā sinistrā, ā laevā — on the right; on the left (Traupman 173, 339). For dexter and sinister see the climbing-directions entry.
  • Rēctā perge. — Go straight on (Traupman 173, 386).
  • exadversum + acc. — opposite, across the street from (Traupman 174).
  • Ubi est …, quaesō? — Where is …, please? Mihi videor deerrāvisse. — I seem to have lost my way (Traupman 172–173); aberrāre — get lost, stray from the way (Traupman 217).
  • Quantum abest? Quantum distat … ab …? — How far is it? How far is … from …? (Traupman 204).
  • Quae est via brevissima ad …? — What’s the quickest way to …? (Traupman 219); Dūcitne haec via ad …? — Does this road lead to …? (Traupman 217).
  • Ad compitum sinistrōrsum nōs vertēmus. — At the crossroads we’ll turn left.
  • Rēctā perge, Theodōre, ūsque ad portam. — Go straight on, Theo, as far as the gate.

Town, shops & places

Market / stalls / for sale / stallholder

mercātus, mercātūs m.

Ancient LatinModern application
  • mercātus, mercātūs m. — market (Traupman 131); macellum, macellī n. — provisions market (71).
  • mēnsa piscātōria, mēnsa holitōria, mēnsa pōmāria — fish, vegetable and fruit stall, with the ancient adjectives piscātōrius, holitōrius, pōmārius. Libellus IV uses the first two; its fruit stall is mēnsa pōmōrum.
  • vēnālis, vēnāle — for sale; vēneō, vēnīre — be for sale (Traupman 131); prōpōnō, prōpōnere — display.

superīnstitōrium, superīnstitōriī n. · pistrīna, pistrīnae f.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinWorking formation

  • taberna, tabernae f. — shop (Traupman 131); tabernāria, tabernāriae f. — shop assistant, cashier (131).

  • Carrulum Theodōrus trūdere voluit; sed cum carrulus ipsō major esset, in eō sēdit, patre impellente. — Theo wanted to push the trolley; but as it was bigger than he was, he sat in it while Dad pushed. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Go shopping / buy / pay / price / change / receipt / card

emō, emere, ēmī, ēmptum · Quantī cōnstat?

Ancient LatinNeo-Latin applications
  • obsōnō, obsōnāre; obsōnātum īre — buy food; go grocery shopping, with the supine (Traupman 38, 131).
  • emō, emere, ēmī, ēmptum — buy (Traupman 130); solvō, solvere, solvī, solūtum — pay (131).
  • Quantī cōnstat? — How much does it cost? (Traupman 131); pretium, pretiī n. — price.
  • nummī, nummōrum m. pl. — money, coins; nummulī, nummulōrum m. pl. — small change; dēnumerō, dēnumerāre — count out, pay (Traupman 131).
  • apocha, apochae f. — receipt (Traupman 131); syngrapha, syngraphae f. — cheque (130); chartula crēditōria — credit card: our description.
  • index, indicis m. — list (Traupman 72: index cibōrum); the measures entry already has index rērum emendārum for a shopping list.
  • chīliogramma, chīliogrammatis n. — kilogram (Neo-Latin); lībra, lībrae f. — scales; pound (Traupman 131).
  • Prīmum obsōnātum ībimus; deinde ego et tū crusta faciēmus — First we’ll go food shopping; then you and I will make the pies (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Tum pater eam interrogāvit: «Quantī cōnstant?» Pretiō audītō nummōs dēnumerāvit, vēnditrīx nummulōs reddidit. — Then Dad asked her, “How much are they?” When he heard the price he counted out the money, and the stallholder gave back the change. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Bene ēmistī — You got a good deal (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • vīlis, vīle — cheap (Traupman 130); bene emere — get a bargain (Traupman 130).
  • «Bene ēmistī,» inquit avus. «Hōc annī tempore vīlia sunt māla.» — “That’s a bargain,” said Grandpa. “Apples are cheap at this time of year.” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Place names: Portugal / Lisbon / Coimbra / Sintra / Portuguese

Lūsitānia, Lūsitāniae f. · Lisbōna, Lisbōnae f.

Ancient namesPost-classical namesQuantity notes
  • Lūsitānia, Lūsitāniae f. — Portugal; the ancient name of the province (L&S). Lūsitānus, Lūsitāna, Lūsitānum — Portuguese; Lūsitānicē — in Portuguese, our adverb, formed like Latīnē.
  • Lisbōna, Lisbōnae f. — Lisbon, the form used in the libellī (Braun & Hogenberg, Civitates orbis terrarum I, 1572, “vulgo Lisbona”); the ō follows Olisīpōn-. Olisīpō, Olisīpōnis m. — the ancient name (Pliny, NH 4.117; L&S Olisipo, with ī), for recognition.
  • Conimbrica, Conimbricae f. — Coimbra, a post-classical transfer of the name; Conimbriga, Conimbrigae f. — the Roman town nearby (Pliny 4.113 prints Conimbrica); Aeminium, Aeminiī n. — Roman Coimbra itself. Stem quantities are not established and are left unmarked.
  • Sintra, Sintrae f. — Sintra, the modern name declined in Latin (medieval Sintria; ancient Mōns Lūnae). Antanhol — the grandparents’ village, indeclinable.
  • Tagus, Tagī m. — the Tagus (L&S); Portus Cale — Porto; Alfama — indeclinable; statiō Orientālis — Gare do Oriente; Hortī Nātiōnum — Parque das Nações.
  • obrigado / obrigada — Portuguese “thank you”, from Latin obligātus, obligāta, “obliged”; the form agrees with the speaker.
  • Cities and small places take no preposition: Lisbōnam volābimus, Lisbōnae sumus, Sintrā (from Sintra); countries take one: in Lūsitāniam, in Lūsitāniā.
  • Ubi est Lūsitānia? Longēne abest? — Where is Portugal? Is it far away? (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Sintram īmus. — We’re going to Sintra. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Scīsne, Theodōre, quid sit obrigado? Lūsitānī ita grātiās agunt. — Do you know, Theo, what obrigado is? That’s how the Portuguese say thank you. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

The quantity of Lisbōna follows the libellī and lexicon-notes-01; Conimbrica, Conimbriga and Serdica are left unmarked because their quantities are not established in the checked sources.

Place names at home: Bulgaria / Sofia / Osoitsa / Balkan range / Rila / Bali

Serdica, Serdicae f. · Osoitsa, Osoitsae f.

Ancient namesModern names declined
  • Bulgaria, Bulgariae f. — Bulgaria; Bulgaricē — in Bulgarian.
  • Serdica, Serdicae f. — Sofia, the late-antique name, stem quantities left unmarked; Serdicae — in Sofia; Serdicēnsis — of Sofia.
  • Osoitsa, Osoitsae f. — Osoitsa, our village, first declension: Osoitsae (at), Osoitsam (to), Osoitsā (from); Osoitsēnsis — of Osoitsa.
  • Haemus, Haemī m. — the Balkan range, Stara planina (L&S); Rīla, Rīlae f. — Rila, declined in the libellī; Vitosha — Vitosha, stem quantities unmarked.
  • Balī — Bali, indeclinable; hiemō, hiemāre, hiemāvī, hiemātum — spend the winter.
  • Baba, Babae f. — from Bulgarian baba, grandmother; the household name, declined in the libellī (Babae, Babā).
  • Hīc sumus nōs: haec est Bulgaria; hīc Serdica, urbs magna; hīc, prope Serdicam, sub monte, Osoitsa, vīcus noster. — Here we are: this is Bulgaria; here is Sofia, a big city; here, near Sofia, below the mountain, Osoitsa, our village. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Spa / baths / sauna / steam room / hot tub / changing room

thermae, thermārum f. · sūdātōrium, sūdātōriī n.

Ancient LatinNeo-Latin
  • balneum (balineum), balneī n. — bath, bathroom; balneae, balneārum f. — public baths, a bath complex; thermae, thermārum f. — hot baths, a large bathing establishment, natural or artificial (Plin., Mart.). A modern spa is naturally thermae or balneae.
  • aquae, aquārum f. — mineral springs, a spa town: ad aquās venīre, go to the spa (Cic. Planc. 65; L&S); hence Aquae Sextiae (Aix) and Aquae Mattiacae (Wiesbaden).
  • sūdātōrium, sūdātōriī n. — sauna, sweating room (Traupman 374). Seneca defines it: sūdātōriīs, in quae siccus vapor corpora exhausūrus inclūditur — “sweating rooms, where dry heat is shut in to drain the body” (Ep. 51.6). Also assa, assōrum n. — dry sweating room (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.2), and Lacōnicum, Lacōnicī n. — dry-heat room (Cic. Att. 4.10.2; Vitruvius).
  • caldārium, tepidārium, frīgidārium — the hot, warm and cold rooms of a bath (Vitruvius, Seneca, Pliny’s letters). The lexicon also uses frīgidārium for refrigerator (Traupman); the bath sense is the ancient one.
  • apodytērium, apodytēriī n. — changing room (Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.2; Plin. Ep. 5.6.25); ūnctōrium, ūnctōriī n. — oiling room (Plin. Ep. 2.17.11); lābrum, lābrī n. — basin, tub: lābrum sī in balineō nōn est, ut sit (Cic. Fam. 14.20.1).
  • balneum verticōsum — whirlpool, hot tub, jacuzzi (M-O s.v. whirlpool).
  • Hodiē in thermās īmus. — We’re going to the spa today.

Selling and prices: sell / seller / expensive / cost a lot / set a price / discount / percent / bargain / sold out / goods / per pound

vēndō, vēndere, vēndidī, vēnditum · cārus, cāra, cārum

Ancient LatinClassical idioms
  • vēndō, vēndere, vēndidī, vēnditum — sell (Traupman 131; from vēnum dō); vēnditāre — keep offering for sale; vēnditor, vēnditōris m. — seller (Traupman 131; Cic.).
  • cārus, cāra, cārum — expensive (Traupman 130; M-O); percārus — very expensive (Ter. Phorm. 3.3.25, as cited by L&S); pretiōsus — costly, valuable.
  • magnī (parvī) cōnstāre — cost a lot (little) (Traupman 130, genitive of price); M-O magnō cōnstat, ablative. Both constructions are classical.
  • pretium facere or pretium statuere — set a price; mercis pretium inquīrere — ask the price (Traupman 130–131); M-O indicāre, name a price (Plaut.).
  • remissiō, remissiōnis f. — discount (Traupman 130); centēsima, centēsimae f. — one percent (Traupman 130; cf. classical centēsimae, one percent interest); pretium speciāle — a bargain, special price (Traupman 130).
  • omnia dīvēndita sunt — it’s all sold out (M-O; dīvendō, sell off piecemeal).
  • merx, mercis f. — an item, goods (Traupman 131); in lībrās — per pound (Traupman 131).
  • Hoc nimis cārum est. — This is too expensive.
  • Quantī hoc vēndis? — How much are you selling this for?
  • Haec māla parvī cōnstant. — These apples are cheap.

Money and paying: cash / cashier / till / bill / banknote / coin / currency / euro / cent / instalments / deposit / debt / bank / change money

argentum praesentārium · nummus, nummī m.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical idioms
  • argentum praesentārium — cash, ready money (Traupman 130; Plaut. Most. 2.1.14, as cited by L&S); pecūnia praesēns (Cic.).
  • arcārius, arcāriī m. — cashier (Traupman 287; classically a treasurer); arca, arcae f. — till, cash register (M-O, after Egger).
  • ratiō dēbitī — bill, what is owed (Traupman 279); M-O mēnstrua ratiō — monthly bill.
  • schedinummus, schedinummī m. — banknote (Traupman 279; Traupman also prints nummus chartāreus); M-O charta monētālis, monēta chartācea.
  • nummus, nummī m. — coin (Traupman 293); numisma, numismatis n. (M-O, after Egger; Hor. Ep. 2.1.234); monēta, monētae f. — currency (M-O).
  • nummus Eurōpaeus — euro (M-O; plain nummus when the context is clear); M-O also eurus. centēsima, centēsimae f. — cent (Traupman 130); M-O dēnārius.
  • pēnsiōnibus solvere — pay in instalments (Traupman 129, 131; pēnsiō, a payment, Cic. Att. 16.2.1: ex tertiā pēnsiōne).
  • arrabō, arrabōnis m. — deposit, down payment (Traupman 130; Plaut.; ante-classical per L&S, the classical form being arra); fidē suā emere — buy on credit (Traupman 130); aes aliēnum — debt (Traupman 130; Cic.).
  • argentāria, argentāriae f. — bank (Traupman 276); ratiō argentāria — bank account (Traupman 276).
  • permūtāre — change money (M-O); mēnsārius, mēnsāriī m. or nummulārius, nummulāriī m. — money-changer (classical, L&S); M-O permūtātor.
  • Habēsne nummōs, an chartulā crēditōriā solvēs? — Have you got cash, or will you pay by card?
  • Hunc nummum tū in arcam pōne. — You put this coin in the till.

Traupman’s nummus chartāreus (p. 279) is given as printed; it may be a misprint for chartāceus.

Traupman 131 gives cuppēdō for pastry shop, but L&S lists cuppēdō only as a form of cupīdō, so it is not used here.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinComposed phrases

  • Chartulam cursuālem aviae mittāmus. — Let’s send Grandma a postcard.

Ancient LatinComposed phrasesQuantity notes
  • tōnstrīx, tōnstrīcis f.; ōrnātrīx, ōrnātrīcis f. — hairdresser (Traupman 167, 325). Morgan–Owens gives tōnsor, tōnstrīx and capillōrum concinnātor (M-O s.v. barber, citing Col.). Classically tōnstrīx is a woman barber (Plaut.) and ōrnātrīx a lady’s maid who dressed her hair (Ov.).

  • tōnsūra, tōnsūrae f.; tōnsus, tōnsūs m. — haircut (Traupman 164, 325); facere ut capillus tondeātur — get a haircut (Traupman 325).
  • fullō, fullōnis m. — dry cleaner; fullōnica, fullōnicae f. — dry cleaner’s, laundry (Traupman 166, 174, 338; Plaut.: the ancient fuller).
  • sūtor, sūtōris m. — shoemaker, cobbler; sūtrīna, sūtrīnae f. — shoemaker’s shop (Traupman 169; Plaut.).
  • vestificus, vestificī m.; vestifica, vestificae f. — tailor, dressmaker (Traupman 169; the Vatican lexicon gives vestifica); sarcinātor, sarcinātōris m.; sarcinātrīx, sarcinātrīcis f. — someone who alters and mends clothes (Traupman 169; Plaut.).

Lewis & Short leaves the o of tōnsor and tōnstrīx unmarked. It is marked long here by the hidden-quantity rule before -ns-.

  • police officer: Traupman gives vigil, vigilis m. (168); classically a member of the night watch, Rome’s police and fire brigade. Morgan–Owens gives pūblicae sēcūritātis custōs, and circitor for a patrolman (M-O s.v. policeman; patrolman).
  • sīphōnārius, sīphōnāriī m. — firefighter (Traupman 167; M-O s.v. fireman, from Egger; the Vatican lexicon agrees).
  • sacerdōs, sacerdōtis m./f. — priest (Traupman 169); bibliothēcārius, bibliothēcāriī m. — librarian (Traupman 167; late, Fronto); phōtographus, phōtographī m. — photographer (Traupman 53, 168; M-O s.v. photographer).
  • cantor, cantōris m. — singer (Hor. S. 1.3.1); Traupman gives cantātor and cantātrīx (169; cantātor is in Gellius).
  • babysitter, nanny: Morgan–Owens gives gerula, gerulae f. (Tert.; Apul.) and medieval cūnābulāria (M-O s.v. babysitter; nanny); the Vatican lexicon gives īnfantāria.
  • lorry driver: Traupman gives autocīnētī onerāriī gubernātor (219), Morgan–Owens plaustrārius (M-O s.v. truck-driver).
  • itinerum prōcūrātor, itinerum prōcūrātrīx — travel agent (Traupman 169, 219; the Vatican lexicon agrees).
  • Sīphōnāriī ignem exstinguunt. — The firefighters are putting out the fire.
  • Vigil nōbīs viam mōnstrābit. — The police officer will show us the way.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: vigil · Lewis & Short: sacerdos · Lewis & Short: bibliothecarius · Lewis & Short: cantor · Lewis & Short: cantator · Lewis & Short: gerula · Lewis & Short: plaustrarius

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. policeman; patrolman; fireman, firefighter; photographer; babysitter; nanny; truck-driver. John C. Sermō cotīdiānus

Conversation, family & daily routines

Totoro

Totorō, Totorōnis m.

Working formation
  • Totorō, Totorōnis m. — our playful third-declension adaptation of the Japanese name, not an established Latin form.
  • Genitive Totorōnis; dative Totorōnī; accusative Totorōnem; ablative Totorōne; vocative Totorō.
  • Theodōrus Totorōnem videt. — Theo sees Totoro.
  • Cum Totorōne per silvam ambulat. — He walks through the forest with Totoro.
  • Domus Totorōnis in silvā est. — Totoro’s house is in the forest.

The long final -ō in the nominative and vocative is part of our chosen Latin declension. The remaining name vowels follow our local reading convention.

Meow / cat’s cry

miau

Working formation
  • miau — a conversational imitation of a cat’s cry; no canonical Latin vowel quantities are assigned to the sound.
  • miaulō, miaulāre — our working verb “meow”; Latin inflectional endings are marked, but it is not labelled as established Neo-Latin. The earlier unsupported stem mī- is removed.
  • fēlēs, fēlis f. — cat; fēlēs clāmat — the cat cries or calls, using attested ancient vocabulary.
  • Fēlēs miaulat: miau, miau. — The cat meows: meow, meow.
  • The previous claim for an ancient Greek μιαῦ parallel has been removed because no ancient passage was supplied or verified.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: feles · Lewis & Short: clamo

Stick / rod / pole / twig / branch

baculum, baculī n.

Ancient Latin
  • baculum, baculī n. — stick or staff, useful for a stick picked up on a walk.
  • bacillum, bacillī n. — small staff, wand; the diminutive of baculum (Lewis & Short, citing Juvenal 3.28). Our reader series uses it for Theo’s stick. baculum is the walking staff; fustis, fustis m. is a club or cudgel.
  • virga, virgae f. — slender rod, switch or twig; rāmus, rāmī m. — branch or bough.
  • rāmulus, rāmulī m. or sūrculus, sūrculī m. — small branch, twig or shoot.
  • Baculum cape. — Pick up the stick.
  • Hic rāmus frāctus est. — This branch is broken.
  • Accusative plural: rāmōs. Both vowels are long; the lemma is rāmus.
  • pertica, perticae f. — longer pole; Morgan–Owens records the surveyor’s-rod sense. virga is the shorter/slender rod or wand; baculum the stick or staff. See also curtain rods in the household section.
Sources & evidence

Ancient LatinBotanical extension

Magnetic tiles / shapes

tessella magnētica

Working formation
  • tessella magnētica — our descriptive term for a magnetic toy tile, not presented as a standardized toy name. tessella, tessellae f. originally means a small mosaic tile or cube.
  • magnēs, magnētis m. — magnet or lodestone; magnēticus, magnētica, magnēticum — magnetic, already attested in Claudian. Applying it to a toy is modern.
  • quadrātum, quadrātī n. — square; triangulum, triangulī n. — triangle.
  • pars, partis f. — part or piece; latus, lateris n. — side, distinct from lātus, “wide.”
  • ōra, ōrae f. — edge; angulus, angulī m. — corner or angle; basis, basis f. — base.
  • Quadrātum an triangulum vīs? — Do you want the square or the triangle?

Build / join / take apart

aedificō, aedificāre, aedificāvī, aedificātum

Ancient Latin
  • aedificō, aedificāre, aedificāvī, aedificātum — build; faciō, facere, fēcī, factum — make.
  • pōnō, pōnere, posuī, positum — put or place; jungō, jungere, jūnxī, jūnctum — join.
  • adjungō, adjungere, adjūnxī, adjūnctum — attach; disjungō, disjungere, disjūnxī, disjūnctum — separate.
  • dissolvō, dissolvere, dissolvī, dissolūtum — loosen or take apart; adhaereō, adhaerēre, adhaesī, adhaesum — adhere or stick.
  • sustineō, sustinēre, sustinuī, sustentum — support; dējiciō, dējicere, dējēcī, dējectum — knock or throw down; corruō, corruere, corruī — collapse.
  • Aedificēmus turrim. — Let’s build a tower.
  • Castellum faciāmus. — Let’s make a castle.
  • Hanc tessellam hīc pōne. — Put this tile here.
  • Duās tessellās junge. — Join two tiles.
  • Adhaeret. — It sticks.
  • Nōn tenet. — It won’t hold.
  • Cavē: cadit. — Careful: it’s falling.
  • Turris corruit. — The tower has collapsed / is collapsing.
  • Theodōre, quid aedificās? — Theo, what are you building?
  • Useful spatial words: suprā, sub, jūxtā, inter, intrā, extrā, ante, post.

Family / parents / small child / great-grandmother / cousin / spouse / mother-in-law / age

pater, patris m.

Ancient Latin
  • pater, patris m. — father; māter, mātris f. — mother; fīlius, fīliī m. — son; fīlia, fīliae f. — daughter.
  • avus, avī m. — grandfather; avia, aviae f. — grandmother; frāter, frātris m. — brother; soror, sorōris f. — sister.
  • tata, tatae m. — daddy, an ancient nursery word; mamma, mammae f. — mummy in nursery language, also “breast” in other contexts.
  • puer parvulus — a little boy; puer, puerī m. has no universally fixed minimum age of seven in every Latin context.
  • Tata, venī. — Daddy, come.
  • Ubi mamma est? — Where is mummy?
  • proavia, proaviae f. — great-grandmother (Traupman 24): Baba is Theo’s proavia and Raja’s avia.
  • cōnsobrīnus, cōnsobrīnī m.; cōnsobrīna, cōnsobrīnae f. — cousin; uxor, uxōris f. — wife (Traupman 24); conjūnx, conjugis m./f. — spouse.
  • senex, senis m. — old man; anus, anūs f. — old woman.
  • bīmus, trīmus — two, three years old (Plaut., Hor.); trēs annōs nātus; puer trium annōrum — a three-year-old; Quot annōrum es? — How old are you?
  • Rajae avia, Theodōrī proavia, quae Osoitsae cum eīs habitat — Raja’s grandmother, Theo’s great-grandmother, who lives with them in Osoitsa (Libellus IV, gloss on Baba).
  • Baba ferē nōnāgintā annōs nāta est, lenta quidem, sed suīs pedibus ambulat. — Baba is nearly ninety, slow indeed, but she walks on her own feet. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Theodōrus contrā eum nōn agnōvit, nec mīrum, cum tum bīmus fuisset. — Theo, for his part, didn’t recognise him, and no wonder, since he had been two at the time. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • socrus, socrūs f. — mother-in-law (Traupman 24; Ter. Hec.).
  • fīliolus, fīliolī m. — little son, an endearment (Traupman 24; Cic. Att. 1.2.1).
  • Deinde māter socrum quoque, quae prope stābat, salūtāvit. — Then Mum said hello to her mother-in-law too, who was standing nearby. (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Dormī, fīliole. — Sleep, my little son. (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).

Wake up / get out of bed

surgō, surgere, surrēxī, surrēctum

Ancient Latin
  • surgō, surgere, surrēxī, surrēctum — get up or rise; ēvigilō, ēvigilāre, ēvigilāvī, ēvigilātum — wake up.
  • expergīscor, expergīscī, experrēctus sum — wake up; expergēfaciō, expergēfacere, expergēfēcī, expergēfactum — wake someone up.
  • māne — in the morning; lectus, lectī m. — bed.
  • Surge, Theodōre. — Get up, Theo.
  • Jam māne est. — It’s morning now.
  • Satisne dormīvistī? — Did you sleep enough?
  • Ē lectō surgāmus. — Let’s get out of bed.
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: surgo · Lewis & Short: evigilo · Lewis & Short: mane · Lewis & Short: lectus · Dickinson: Latin Core Vocabulary

Lewis & Short: expergiscor · Lewis & Short: expergefacio

Sleep / bedtime / go to bed / nap / doze / fast asleep

dormiō, dormīre, dormīvī, dormītum

Ancient Latin
  • dormiō, dormīre, dormīvī, dormītum — sleep; somnus, somnī m. — sleep.
  • Tempus est dormīre. — It’s time to sleep.
  • Nunc dormiāmus. — Let’s sleep now.
  • Oculōs claude. — Close your eyes.
  • Dormī bene. — Sleep well.
  • Somnus mē premit. — I’m sleepy; literally, sleep weighs on me.
  • cubitum īre — go to bed (Traupman 122; Cic.); in somnum dēlābī — drift off to sleep (Traupman 306); artē dormīre — be fast asleep (Traupman 313).
  • merīdiō, merīdiāre — have an afternoon nap (Catull. 32.3; Suet.).
  • dormītō, dormītāre — be drowsy, doze (Plaut.; Cic.); nūtō, nūtāre — nod off (Suet. Calig. 38); sēmisomnus, sēmisomna, sēmisomnum — half asleep (Cic. Fam. 7.1.1).
  • Theodōrō veste nocturnā indūtō cubitum itum est. — When Theo had his pyjamas on, they went to bed. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Theodōrus, statim in somnum dēlāpsus, per tōtum iter dormīvit — Theo dropped off at once and slept the whole way (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • deinde in cubiculō albō, trānsennā dēmissā, merīdiāvit — then he had a nap in the white bedroom with the shutter down (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • «Ut sīc sedēs,» inquit avia, «nūtantī capite?» «Dormītō.» — “Why are you sitting like that,” said Grandma, “with your head nodding?” “I’m dozing.” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • «Modo,» inquit pater sēmisomnus, «ecce modo … sine paululum.» — “In a minute,” said Dad, half asleep, “just a minute … let me be a little.” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • Pater, cīnctūrā laxātā, puerum artē dormientem ex autoraedā tollēns — Dad, undoing the seat belt and lifting the sound-asleep boy out of the car (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

Happy / sad / angry / frightened / eager / curious / laugh out loud

laetus, laeta, laetum

Ancient Latin
  • laetus, laeta, laetum — happy; trīstis, trīste — sad; īrātus, īrāta, īrātum — angry.
  • timeō, timēre, timuī — be afraid; rīdeō, rīdēre, rīsī, rīsum — laugh.
  • Trīstis es? — Are you sad?
  • Quid timēs? — What are you afraid of?
  • Mihi dīc quid acciderit. — Tell me what happened.
  • Tēcum sum. — I’m with you.
  • alacer, alacris, alacre — eager, lively (Traupman 149); cūriōsus, cūriōsa, cūriōsum — inquisitive (Traupman 154); bellulus, bellula, bellulum — cute (Traupman 151; Plaut.).
  • rīsum effundere — burst out laughing (Traupman 94); cachinnō, cachinnāre — laugh out loud, cackle (Cic. Verr. 2.3.62).
  • Theodōrus alacer ad arborem cucurrit — Theo ran eagerly to the tree (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Puer tamen cūriōsus in lupum apertum iterum īnspexit — But the boy, curious, looked into the opened bass again (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • avia plaudēns «Ō sīmium bellulum!» inquit — Grandma clapped and said, “What a cute monkey!” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Quō audītō puer rīsum effūdit — When he heard that, the boy burst out laughing (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Cry / hurt / comfort

plōrō, plōrāre, plōrāvī, plōrātum

Ancient Latin

Hug / lap / carry a child

amplector, amplectī

Ancient Latin
  • amplector, amplectī — embrace or hug; gremium, gremiī n. — lap or bosom.
  • complector, complectī, complexus sum — embrace, hug (Traupman 330).
  • in ulnīs tenēre — hold in one’s arms; ulna, ulnae f. — forearm.

Some older dictionaries print ūlna. The plain u here follows the short-vowel analysis explained in Michelson’s correction to Bennett; this hidden quantity is disputed.

Colours / choose a colour

ruber, rubra, rubrum

Ancient Latin
  • ruber, rubra, rubrum — red; caeruleus, caerulea, caeruleum — blue; viridis, viride — green.
  • flāvus, flāva, flāvum — yellow or golden; albus, alba, album — white; niger, nigra, nigrum — black.
  • ēligō, ēligere, ēlēgī, ēlēctum — choose.
  • Quō colōre est? — What colour is it?
  • Pila rubra est. — The ball is red.
  • Colōrem ēlige. — Choose a colour.
  • grey: Traupman gives cinereus (ash-grey), pullus (dark grey) and cānus (light grey, of hair) (251); Morgan–Owens gives cinereus, rāvus, and the medieval griseus (M-O s.v. gray). brown: Traupman gives fulvus, fuscus (dark brown) and spādīx (251; he notes brunneus is Germanic); Morgan–Owens gives castaneus (Vives) and the medieval brūnus (M-O s.v. brown).
  • pink: roseus; pūniceus (Traupman 251; M-O s.v. pink: roseus, subruber). purple, violet: purpureus; violāceus (Traupman 251–252). orange: Traupman gives aurantius and lūteus (251), Morgan–Owens aureus, flammeus and croceus (M-O s.v. orange). golden, silver: aureus; argenteus (Traupman 251–252).
  • āter / niger — dull black / shiny black; albus / candidus — dull white / shining white (Traupman 251–252). saturātus / dīlūtus — dark / light, of a shade (M-O s.v. dark, deep; light, pale; Plin.). The prefix sub- makes “-ish”: subalbus (Varr.), subruber, subflāvus (Traupman 252); Morgan–Owens gives nigricāns — blackish (M-O s.v. blackish).

Trampoline / jumping / hopping on one foot

petaurum, petaurī n.

Ancient wordModern extensionComposed phrases

petaurum, petaurī n. — a trampoline in our family vocabulary. The ancient word names an acrobatic apparatus; its precise ancient construction is debated. Leo Latinus uses it for the modern trampoline. This modern sense is not a claim that Romans had modern trampolines.

  • saliō, salīre — jump or leap.
  • saltus, saltūs m. — a jump or leap.
  • dēsultōrium, dēsultōriī n. — trampoline (Traupman 397); a secondary term beside petaurum.
  • pēs, pedis m. — foot; the ablative is pede, with short e.
  • In petaurō salī. — Jump on the trampoline.
  • Altius salī. — Jump higher.
  • Ūnō pede salī. — Jump on one foot. Ūnō agrees with masculine pede; this is an ablative of means.
  • Ambōbus pedibus salī. — Jump with both feet.
  • Iterum salī. — Jump again.
  • Dēsilī. — Jump down.
Sources & evidence

Monkey Tree Game / arm / branch / hanging / swinging

Sīmius et arbor

Ancient wordsFamily gameComposed phrases

Our Monkey Tree Game: Dad holds an arm horizontally, supports his fist with the other arm, and Theo jumps to grab the arm and swing from it. Sīmius et arbor means “The Monkey and the Tree” and works as a title without adding “game.” Lūdus sīmiī is the shorter explicit alternative, “The Monkey Game.” These are our game names, not attested ancient game titles.

  • sīmius, sīmiī m. — monkey or ape.
  • arbor, arboris f. — tree.
  • rāmus, rāmī m. — branch; in this game, Dad’s arm is the branch.
  • bracchium, bracchiī n. — arm.
  • pugnus, pugnī m. — fist. Short u: vowels before gn are short unless the stem is long (Bennett and Buck; Allen, Vox Latina). Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary and de Vaan (s.v. pungō) print pūgnus, after Priscian’s rule.
  • lūdus, lūdī m. — game or play.
  • lūsus, lūsūs m. — playing, play or a game; its meanings overlap with lūdus.
  • prehendō, prehendere — grab or take hold of.
  • teneō, tenēre — hold.
  • pendeō, pendēre — hang; intransitive.
  • Ego arbor erō; tū sīmius eris. — I’ll be the tree; you’ll be the monkey.
  • Bracchium meum prehende. — Grab my arm.
  • Salī et bracchium meum prehende. — Jump and grab my arm.
  • Firmē tenē. — Hold tight.
  • Ē rāmō pendē. — Hang from the branch.
  • Tē hūc illūc movē. — Move yourself back and forth; a simple prompt for swinging.
Sources & evidence

Sailor and Waves / duvet sea game / bedtime / balance / falling / tumbling

Nauta et undae

Ancient wordsFamily gameComposed phrases

Our bedtime sea game: Theo stands on the duvet while Dad holds a corner or side and moves it to make waves; Theo jumps, falls and tumbles. Nauta et undae means “The Sailor and the Waves.” The title is our own. Strāgulum is a broad bed-covering word, used here for the duvet without specifying its filling.

  • strāgulum, strāgulī n. — bed covering; our practical word for the duvet in this game.
  • angulus, angulī m. — corner.
  • latus, lateris n. — side, with short a; distinguish lātus, “broad.”
  • mare, maris n. — sea.
  • unda, undae f. — wave.
  • nauta, nautae m. — sailor.
  • nāvis, nāvis f. — ship or boat.
  • aequilībrium, aequilībriī n. — balance or equilibrium; applied here to keeping one’s balance.
  • genū, genūs n.; plural genua — knee; knees. The u in the plural genua is short: no macron.
  • moveō, movēre — move.
  • tollō, tollere — lift.
  • dēmittō, dēmittere — lower or let down.
  • agitō, agitāre — move about, shake.
  • undō, undāre — billow, undulate; intransitive in our phrases. Ancient usage includes a billowing cloak.
  • flectō, flectere — bend.
  • jactō, jactāre — toss about.
  • cadō, cadere — fall.
  • volūtō, volūtāre — roll or tumble about; use tē for “roll yourself.”
  • stō, stāre — stand.
  • dēsinō, dēsinere — stop or cease.
  • Tū nauta es; hoc est mare. — You’re the sailor; this is the sea.
  • In strāgulō stā. — Stand on the duvet.
  • Strāgulī angulum teneō. — I’m holding a corner of the duvet.
  • Strāgulī latus teneō. — I’m holding a side of the duvet.
  • Strāgulum tollō et dēmittō. — I lift and lower the duvet.
  • Strāgulum moveō ut undet. — I move the duvet so that it billows.
  • Strāgulum undat. — The duvet is billowing.
  • Ecce unda magna. — Here comes a big wave.
  • Vīs undās magnās an parvās? — Do you want big waves or little waves?
  • Undās fac. — Make waves.
  • Genua flecte. — Bend your knees. All three vowels in genua are short in the ordinary three-syllable form.
  • Aequilībrium servā. — Keep your balance.
  • Undīs jactāris. — You’re being tossed by the waves.
  • Cecidistī. — You fell.
  • Cecidī. — I fell.
  • Tē volūtā. — Roll around.
  • Iterum stā. — Stand up again.
  • Dēsine. — Stop.
  • Iterum. — Again.

The game’s imagery and example sentences are composed for Theo. Undāre describes the duvet billowing; to make it billow, we move it (moveō, agitō). We do not use transitive strāgulum undō, which would suggest flooding the duvet.

Mission / assigned task / quest / search

mūnus, mūneris n.; expedītiō, expedītiōnis f.

Ancient sensesPlaytime applications
  • mūnus, mūneris n. — task, duty or function; our choice for a playtime “mission.” mandātum, mandātī n. — commission, instruction or something entrusted to someone.
  • opus, operis n. — a work or job, including one a child sets himself; better than mūnus, which is a duty laid on someone. Opus perfēcistī! — You’ve finished the job!
  • expedītiō, expedītiōnis f. — expedition or campaign in ancient usage; our contextual application to an adventurous playtime quest. It is not presented as a verified fixed translation of a modern fantasy-game quest.
  • investīgātiō, investīgātiōnis f. — search or investigation; use for the searching activity itself. For an adventure as a daring undertaking, the existing adventure entry prefers ausum, ausī n..
  • Hoc est mūnus tuum: uncum reperī. — Here’s your mission: find the hook. Eāmus thēsaurum quaesītum! — Let’s go look for treasure! The latter uses the supine of purpose after a verb of motion.
  • These are contextual choices for conversation with Theo. The adventure and search senses need not be expressed by the same noun.

Praise: well done! / good job / you carried that well

Macte virtūte!

Classical idiomsQuotations
  • Macte virtūte! — Well done! (Traupman 322; Liv. II 12, 14; Cic. Att. XII 6, 3); macte novā virtūte, puer (Verg. Aen. IX 641). The final e of macte is short.
  • Bene factum! — Well done! (Traupman 99; said by Dad in Libellus V).
  • Pulchrē, bene, rēctē! — praise for a finished result (Hor. Ars 428; Dad over the pies in Libellus IV).
  • Bene portāvistī. — You carried that well (composed).
  • Tū decus omne tuīs. — You are the pride of your family (Verg. Ecl. 5, 34); said to the cook.
  • Pater puerum Rōmānōrum illud «Macte virtūte!» docuerat; quod igitur Baba Bulgaricē dīcit, puer ipse sibi Latīnē. — Dad had taught the boy the Roman “Macte virtūte!”; so what Baba says in Bulgarian, the boy says to himself in Latin. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Rēctē factum! — well done! (Traupman 101).
  • Cui pater «Rēctē factum!» inquit. — Dad said to him, “Well done!” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Walk / fork in the road / which way? / this way, that way / pocket full of stones

ambulātiō, ambulātiōnis f. · trivium, triviī n.

Ancient Latin
  • ambulātiō, ambulātiōnis f. — walk; trivium, triviī n. — fork in the road; hāc — this way; illāc — that way.
  • sinus, sinūs m. — the fold of a coat, used for a pocket.
  • In prīmō triviō, ut semper, dēlīberātum est. «Nōlō illāc īre, tata. Hāc eāmus!» «Fīat.» — At the first fork, as always, there was a debate. “I don’t want to go that way, Dad. Let’s go this way!” “All right.” (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • omnis enim ambulātiō lapidem aliquem reddit, quō fit ut pater sinūs lapidibus plēnōs domum referat — for every walk yields some stone, and so Dad brings home pockets full of stones (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Greetings: goodbye / have a good flight / welcome / I’m glad you’re back

Valē! · Salvum tē advēnisse gaudeō.

Classical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Valē! Valēte! — Goodbye!; Bene volāte! — Have a good flight!
  • Ī, bene ambulā. — Off you go, safe journey (Plaut. Asin. 108, where the manuscripts spell the imperative ei; also Traupman 212).
  • Redī cito. — Jam ego hīc erō. — Come back soon. — I’ll be back in no time. The first is said by the one who stays, the second by the one who leaves (Plaut. Men. 225).
  • Salvum tē advēnisse gaudeō. — I’m glad you’ve arrived safely, said by the one who waits (Ter. Phorm. 286); to a woman salvam, to several salvōs vōs.
  • Mea māter, salvē. — Gaudeō vēnisse salvum. — the son arriving, the mother waiting (Ter. Hec. 353).
  • Ō pater, pater mī, salvē. — Salvē multum, gnāte mī. (Plaut. Trin. 1180); Vēnistī! Ō mihi nūntiī beātī! (Catull. 9, 5).
  • «Valēte,» inquit, «bene volāte! Theodōre, patrī pārē, et aviae meīs verbīs salūtem dīc.» — “Goodbye,” she said, “have a good flight! Theo, do what Dad says, and give Grandma my love.” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • bene ambulā et redambulā — safe journey there and back (Plaut. Capt. 900; quoted in Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

On the way: where are we going? / why? / not yet / too early / it’s getting dark / not far now

Quō īmus? — Ad avum īmus.

Family phrasesClassical quotations
  • Quō īmus? — Cūr? — Where are we going? — Why? Theo’s own travel questions in the libellī. Jam advēnimus? — Nōndum. — Are we there yet? — Not yet (composed; Theo never asks it).
  • Nimis paene māne est. — It’s far too early (Plaut. Persa 114); Māne quod tū occēperis negōtium agere, id tōtum prōcēdit diem. — what you start in the morning goes well all day (114–115).
  • Quid stās? quid cessās? — Why are you standing there? Why the delay? (Ter. And. 979).
  • Brevis est via. — It won’t be long (Verg. Ecl. 9, 23, via Ranieri).
  • Jam advesperāscit. — It’s getting dark already (Ter. And. 581); vesperāscit — evening is coming.
  • Fīat lūx. — Let there be light (Gen. 1:3), when the light goes on.
  • Quō īmus, tata? — Ad avum īmus. — Where are we going, Dad? — We’re going to Grandpa’s. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Quandō rūrsus volābimus? — Mox. Nōndum dīmidium itineris cōnfēcimus. — When will we fly again? — Soon. We haven’t done half the journey yet. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Nimis paene māne est. — It’s almost too early. (Plaut. Persa 114; quoted in Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • surge et ambulā — get up and walk: Dad, lifting the sleeping boy out of bed (Mt 9, 5, in jest; quoted in Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Safety and instructions: careful, don’t fall / don’t touch / mind your fingers / come here

Cavē nē cadās; astā.

Family phrasesClassical quotations
  • Cavē nē cadās; astā. — Careful you don’t fall; stand still (Plaut. Most. 324). In Libellus VII Theo sings it to himself as he climbs.
  • Nōlī tangere.; Nē tangās. — Don’t touch. Prohibitions take nōlī + infinitive, nē + perfect subjunctive, or in everyday speech nē + present subjunctive (Traupman 33, as cited).
  • Cavē digitōs. — Mind your fingers; Manum alteram procul. — Keep your other hand away.
  • Ad pinnās, nōn ad marginem. — Stay by the wall, not by the edge.
  • Hoc facitō; hoc fugitō. — Do this; avoid that (Ter. Ad. 417).
  • Ōcius hūc ades! — Come here, quickly! (Verg. Ecl. 7, 8–9, via Ranieri).
  • Tacē. — Be quiet; Tacē, occultēmus lūmen et vōcem. — Licet. — Hush, let’s hide the light and our voices. — All right (Plaut. Curc. 95), for a game in the dark.
  • Ostende hūc manūs. — Em tibi, ostendī, eccās. — Show me your hands. — There you are, look (Plaut. Aul. 640–641); Satis est; terge. — That’s enough; dry them.
  • Nōlī tangere, Theodōre; calidissima sunt. — Don’t touch, Theo; they’re very hot. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Digitōs laevae ā cultellō procul habē; cavē nē digitum secēs. — Keep the fingers of your left hand away from the knife; mind you don’t cut a finger. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Pater «Cavē nē cadās,» inquit; quod puer, dum scandit, ipse sibi cantat. — Dad said “Careful you don’t fall”; and the boy sings it to himself as he climbs. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • Cavē nē cadās, astā. — Careful you don’t fall; stand still. (Plaut. Most. 324; also in Libellus II).

Quid hodiē fēcistī?

Family phrasesClassical quotations
  • Quid hodiē fēcistī?; Hodiē quid ēgistī? (Plin. Epist. I 9, 2); Herī quid ēgistī? — What did you do today / yesterday?

  • Quid tibi vīsa Lūsitānia? — How did you find Portugal? (Hor. Epist. I 11, 1, with Chios replaced).

  • Tē dēsīderō. — I miss you.
  • garriō, garrīre — chatter; garrīmus quicquid in buccam — we chatter about whatever comes to mind (Cic. Att. XII 1, 2).
  • Avia «Quid autem,» inquit, «tibi maximē placuit, Theodōre?» — Grandma said, “And what did you like best, Theo?” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • tēlephōnum sonuit, et in quadrō appāruit māter — the phone rang, and Mum appeared on the screen (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Theodōre, quid hodiē fēcistī? — Theo, what did you do today? (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Quid ēgistī? — Per tabulam deciēs dēlāpsus sum, tata! — What did you do? — I went down the slide ten times, Dad! (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Bedtime story / stroke your hair / rub your back / fall asleep / good night

Narrā mihi fābulam!

Ancient LatinFamily phrases
  • Narrā mihi fābulam, pater! — Tell me a story, Dad!
  • cāra mihi subolēs — my dear child: Ranieri’s adaptation of Verg. Ecl. 4, 49 (cāra deum subolēs).
  • permulceō, permulcēre, permulsī, permulsum — stroke (Traupman 142); capillōs permulcēre — stroke someone’s hair.
  • tergum, tergī n. — back; tergum fricāre — rub the back. The body-parts entry gives tergum alongside dorsum.
  • obdormiō, obdormīre, obdormīvī, obdormītum — fall asleep; in sinū — in someone’s arms.
  • Bene valeās et quiēscās. — Good night (Traupman 351); lūmine exstīnctō — with the light off.
  • Narrā mihi fābulam, tata. — Tell me a story, Dad. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Narrābō, cāra mihi subolēs — I will, my dear child (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Dum narrat, pater capillōs puerī manū lentē permulcēbat — As he told it, Dad slowly stroked the boy’s hair (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • trānsennā dēmissā, lūmine exstīnctō — with the shutter down and the light out (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • lallō, lallāre — sing a lullaby (M-O s.v. lullaby): īrātus mammae, lallāre recūsās — “cross with your nurse, you won’t let her sing you to sleep” (Pers. 3.18); lallum, lallī n. — lullaby (M-O; Ausonius, post-classical).

Days of the week

diēs Lūnae · diēs Sōlis

Neo-LatinLexicographic evidence
  • diēs Lūnae — Monday; diēs Mārtis — Tuesday; diēs Mercuriī — Wednesday (not in the libellī; added to complete the week).
  • diēs Jovis — Thursday; diēs Veneris — Friday; diēs Sāturnī — Saturday.
  • diēs Sōlis — Sunday; also diēs Dominicus (Traupman IX for the whole series).
  • hebdomas, hebdomadis f. — week.
  • Postrīdiē, quī diēs Lūnae erat — The next day, which was Monday (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Diēs Jovis erat, quem Americānī Diem Grātulātiōnis vocant. — It was Thursday, which Americans call Thanksgiving Day. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Postrīdiē quam rediērunt diēs Sōlis illūxit — The day after they came back, Sunday dawned (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • diēs profēstus — weekday, working day (Traupman 54, 77; M-O s.v. weekday; Liv.; Hor.). Weekend: Traupman gives fīnis hebdomadis and hebdomade exeunte — at the weekend (54); Morgan–Owens gives exiēns hebdomada, fīniēns hebdomada and fēriātum bīduum (M-O s.v. weekend); the Vatican lexicon gives exiēns hebdomada. septimāna, septimānae f. — week (Traupman 54, 77), a late word (L&S under septimānus).

Telling the time: quarter past / half past / afternoon / later / ago

hōra, hōrae f. · quadrāns, quadrantis m.

Ancient wordsModern application
  • hōrā decimā et quadrante — at 10:15 (Traupman X); hōrā nōnā et dīmidiā — at 9:30.
  • post merīdiem — in the afternoon, p.m.; ante merīdiem — a.m.
  • dōdrāns hōrae — three quarters of an hour (dōdrāns, dōdrantis m.; Cic., Plin.).
  • vesperī — in the evening; sērō — late; sērius — later.
  • abhinc — ago; post quīnque diēs — in five days’ time.
  • Nōbīs enim multō māne surgendum: āëroplanum hōrā decimā et quadrante abscēdet — For we must get up very early: the plane leaves at a quarter past ten (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • abhinc plūs mīlle annōs in summō monte castellum aedificāvērunt — more than a thousand years ago they built a castle on the top of the mountain (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Mīlle annōs, tata? Quam multōs! — Multōs vērō, immō plūrimōs. — A thousand years, Dad? So many! — Many indeed; very many. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

For minutes the lexicon uses neuter minūtum, minūtī n. (measures entry); feminine minūta, minūtae f. (Traupman 87) is also current.

Counting / once, twice, ten times / countless

numerō, numerāre · semel, bis, ter

Ancient Latin
  • numerō, numerāre, numerāvī, numerātum — count.
  • ūnus, duo, trēs, quattuor, quīnque, sex — the first numbers, as Theo counts the apples.
  • semel, bis, ter, quater, quīnquiēs, sexiēs, septiēs, octiēs, noviēs, deciēs, centiēs — once, twice … ten times, a hundred times.
  • bīnī, ternī, … octōnī — distributives, “two each … eight each”.
  • sescentī, sescentae, sescenta — six hundred, and colloquially “countless” (Plaut., Cic.).
  • Jussus numerāre, sex numerāvit. — Told to count, he counted six. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Deciēsne? — Deciēs dēlāpsus sum, et Baba mē spectābat. — Ten times? — Ten times I slid down, and Baba was watching me. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • zero: use nihil or nūllus when talking to a child. Traupman gives zērum (137) and Morgan–Owens the medieval cifra (M-O s.v. numeral: zero); neither is classical. deciēs centēna mīlia — a million, the classical expression (M-O s.v. million); mīlle, duo mīlia (Traupman 253).

Castle walls / battlements / guard / enemy / edge

moenia, moenium n. pl. · pinnae, pinnārum f. pl.

Ancient Latin
  • moenia, moenium n. pl. — fortifications, city walls (Traupman 174); castle, tower and gate are in the existing building-pieces entry.
  • pinnae, pinnārum f. pl. — battlements (L&S pinna II.B; Caes. BG V 40, 6).
  • custōs, custōdis m. — guard; vigilō, vigilāre — keep watch; hostis, hostis m. — enemy (Traupman XXI).

  • Quis venit? Vidēsne aliquem, tata? — Nēminem videō. — Who’s coming? Can you see anyone, Dad? — I can’t see anyone. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Hostēs veniunt? — Nōn veniunt. — Are enemies coming? — They aren’t. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Dragon / giant / echo / darkness / is there a dragon in here?

dracō, dracōnis m. · gigās, gigantis m.

Ancient LatinFamily game
  • dracō, dracōnis m. — dragon (L&S); gigās, gigantis m. — giant (L&S).
  • Ēchō, Ēchūs f. — echo, with Greek declension; nympha, nymphae f. — nymph.

  • Gigās ea posuit! — Nōn gigās. — A giant put them there! — Not a giant. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Saying grace / giving thanks / Thanksgiving Day / fold your hands

grātiās agere · Diēs Grātulātiōnis

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinFamily phrases
  • grātiās agere (+ dative of the person; prō + ablative of the thing) — give thanks, say grace (Traupman 393).
  • Diēs Grātulātiōnis — Thanksgiving Day (Traupman 393; Vicipaedia); Fēlīcem Diem Grātulātiōnis! (393). Classical grātulātiō is a public thanksgiving (Cic.). This is preferred to the periphrastic diēs grātiārum āctiōnis (Morgan–Owens).
  • manūs jungere — fold one’s hands; oculōs claudere — close one’s eyes; caput inclīnāre — bow one’s head.
  • Ōrātiō Dominica — the Lord’s Prayer; Āmēn.
  • Cōnfitēminī Dominō, quoniam bonus: quoniam in aeternum misericordia ejus. (Ps. 135 [136], 1) — said responsively, Dad the first half-verse and Theo the second.
  • grātiās agere is thanking in words; grātiam referre is repaying in deed (Cic. Off. I 47).
  • Pater caelestis, ā quō omne dōnum perfectum dēscendit, grātiās tibi agimus prō hōc cibō … et prō hāc domō — Heavenly Father, from whom every perfect gift comes down, we thank you for this food … and for this home (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Ego grātiās agō. — I say thank you. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Deō; haec enim omnia dōna ejus sunt. — To God; for all these things are his gifts. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Time: in good time / every so often / the day after tomorrow / look at the time / pass the time / at dusk

temperī · perendiē

Ancient Latin
  • temperī — in good time, early enough (Traupman 89; Plaut.; Cic.).
  • subinde — every so often, repeatedly (Traupman 88; Liv.).
  • perendiē — the day after tomorrow (Traupman 86; Plaut. Merc. 2.3.41 crās agitō, perendiē agitō; Cic. Att. 12.44.3); crās — tomorrow.
  • hōrās īnspicere — check the time (Traupman 89); hōrologium īnspicere — look at the clock or watch (Traupman 122).
  • tempus fallere — pass the time (Traupman 89).
  • crepusculum, crepusculī n. — twilight, dusk (Traupman 89; Plaut. Cas. prol. 40); crepusculō — at dusk.
  • Tum temperī profectī sunt. — Then they set off in good time. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Diū exspectātum est, patre subinde hōrās in tēlephōnō īnspiciente — There was a long wait, Dad checking the time on his phone every so often (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Haec quoque,» inquit avia, «perendiē cum patre tuō vidēbis, sed vēra et magna.» — “You’ll see these too,” said Grandma, “the day after tomorrow with your dad, but real and big.” (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • dōnec avia, hōrologiō īnspectō, eum revocāvit: «Domum! Prandium parandum est.» — until Grandma looked at her watch and called him back: “Home! Lunch has to be made.” (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Ad aditum dēnique, ut tempus fallerent, per lūsum latitāvērunt et quaeritāvērunt — Finally, at the gate, to pass the time, they played hide and seek (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Trāmine commūnī per crepusculum Lisbōnam rediērunt — They went back to Lisbon on the slow train at dusk (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Exclamations: oh no! / hey! / wow! / hooray! / here, take it! / truly

Atat! · Heus! · Papae! · Iō!

Ancient LatinClassical idioms
  • Atat! — oh no!, of a sudden realisation (Plaut.; Ter.).
  • Heus! — hey!, to get attention; Heus tū! — hey, you! (Plaut.; Ter.; Cic.).
  • Papae! — wow! (Plaut.; Ter.).
  • Iō! — hooray!, in two syllables (Hor. C. 4.2.49 iō triumphe); Euax! — hooray!, as in the airport entry.
  • Em! — here!, handing something over; Accipe, em. — here, take it; Em manum! — here’s my hand (see the safety entry).
  • nae — truly, indeed, with a pronoun: Nae tū bene meministī. — You remember well, you do.
  • Atat, lapis deest! Lapis mēcum dormit! — Oh no, the stone’s missing! The stone sleeps with me! (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Pater, «Heus, dā mihi manum!» identidem clāmitāns — Dad, calling out again and again, “Hey, give me your hand!” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Heus tū!» inquit pater, custōdem agēns. «Quis es?» — “Hey, you!” said Dad, playing the guard. “Who are you?” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • «Papae,» inquit puer, «etiam autoraedā longā vehimur!» — “Wow,” said the boy, “we’re going on a bus too!” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Iō, septem! Septem vehiculīs vectus sum!» — “Hooray, seven! I’ve been on seven vehicles!” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Accipe, em. Ita tenē: laeva ministeriō, dextra est intenta labōrī.» — “Here, take it. Hold it like this: the left hand helps, the right does the work.” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Nae tū bene meministī — You remember well, you do (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.

Coming! / wait a moment / hurry / do you get it? / I get it / you’re right / really? / what now?

Jam aderō. · Manē dum! · Jam teneō!

Classical idiomsFamily phrases
  • Jam aderō. — I’ll be right there, coming! (Traupman 101).
  • Manē dum! — wait a moment! (Traupman 90, 110).
  • Mātūrā! Mātūrāte! — hurry up! (Traupman 101); āctūtum — at once (Plaut.; Ter.).
  • Jam tenēs? — do you get it now?; Jam teneō! — now I get it! (Traupman 99).
  • Bene dīxistī. — you’re right, well said (Traupman 107).
  • Ain' vērō? — do you really mean it?; the answer is Ajō. (Traupman 103; Plaut.; Ter.).
  • Quid nunc? — what now? (Traupman 104); Satin' est? — is that enough?, will this do? (Traupman 97).
  • animī pendēre — be in suspense (Traupman 108); gestiō, gestīre + infinitive — be itching to (Traupman 101; Cic.).
  • Tum dēmum pater fīliō respondit: «Jam aderō.» — Only then did Dad answer his son: “Coming.” (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • «Mātūrā,» inquit pater. «Raeda mox aderit.» «Jam aderō, tata!» — “Hurry up,” said Dad. “The taxi will be here soon.” “Coming, Dad!” (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Pater «Manē dum!» clāmābat — Dad kept calling, “Wait a moment!” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Agedum,» inquit pater, «onerā palliolō umerōs tuōs, et āctūtum sequere mē.» — “Come on,” said Dad, “put your little coat on your shoulders and follow me at once.” (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Mendum est sīcut lapillus quī in calceō tuō latet: nōn bene ambulās, dōnec lapillum invēneris et ējēceris. Jam tenēs? — A bug is like a pebble hiding in your shoe: you can’t walk properly until you find the pebble and throw it out. Do you get it now? (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • «Tū obrigado, quia puer es.» «Jam teneō!» — “You say obrigado, because you’re a boy.” “Now I get it!” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «Nōn attulit! Mīnōtaurus Conimbrigae manet!» «Bene dīxistī.» — “He didn’t bring it! The Minotaur stays at Conimbriga!” “You’re right.” (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Pater subjēcit: «Theodōrus mēcum fēcit.» «Ain' vērō?» inquit avus. — Dad added, “Theo made it with me.” “Did he really?” said Grandpa. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «Quid nunc faciēmus, tata?» — “What shall we do now, Dad?” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «Satin' est, tata?» «Satis est; rēctē factum.» — “Is that enough, Dad?” “That’s enough; well done.” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Theodōrus, animī pendēns, quaesīvit: «Ut tē jūvit crustum, ave?» — Theo, in suspense, asked, “How did you like the pie, Grandpa?” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «Gestiō gustāre!» «Post cēnam gustābimus.» — “I’m itching to taste it!” “We’ll taste it after dinner.” (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Theodōrus et pater · Ad Larem avītum, Libellī I–VII, as they stood on 7 November 2026, with their glosses. Examples marked “Libellus” quote those texts word for word; classical passages are cited by author.

We’re fine / so far so good / I’m having fun / take care / let me catch my breath / let me go / stop right there / that’s enough / why so sad?

Bene habēmus. · Cūrā ut valeās.

Classical idiomsFamily phrases
  • Bene habēmus. — we’re fine (Traupman 105); Bellē adhūc. — so far so good (Traupman 108); Mihi bene est. — I’m having a lovely time (Traupman 109).
  • Cūrā ut valeās. — take care of yourself, the close of Cicero’s letters (Traupman 94).
  • Sine respīrem, quaesō. — let me catch my breath, please (Traupman 95); to several, Sinite respīrem.
  • Mitte mē! — let me go!; Mitte mē, sīs! — let go of me, please! (Traupman 99, 102; Plaut.).
  • Stā īlicō! — stop right there! (Traupman 108; īlicō “on the spot”, Ter.).
  • Parce! — that’s enough!, take it easy! (Traupman 102, 108).
  • Quid tū es tam trīstis? — why so sad? (Traupman 99); Quid tibi est? — what’s the matter? (Traupman 92).
  • Amō tē. — thank you, for a kindness done (Traupman 109; Plaut.); amābō — please, with an imperative (Plaut.; Ter.).
  • «Rēctēne advēnistis?» inquit avia. «Bene habēmus,» inquit pater. — “Did you have a good journey?” said Grandma. “We’re fine,” said Dad. (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Mediō itinere «Bellē adhūc,» inquit. — Halfway along he said, “So far so good.” (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • «Mihi bene est, tata!» — “I’m having a lovely time, Dad!” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • «Cūrā ut valeās, mī fīlī,» inquit avia. — “Take care of yourself, my son,” said Grandma. (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • «Sinite respīrem, quaesō,» inquit. «Vōs mūrōs ascendite; ego hīc vōs exspectābō.» — “Let me catch my breath, please,” he said. “You go up on the walls; I’ll wait for you here.” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • In scālīs mōbilibus cum Theodōrus, «Mitte mē, tata!» clāmitāns, manū patris dīmissā sōlus stāre vellet — When Theo, on the escalator, kept shouting “Let me go, Dad!” and wanted to let go of his hand and stand by himself (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • Theodōrum ad orbitās properantem pater inclāmāvit: «Stā īlicō! Dā mihi manum.» — As Theo hurried towards the tracks, Dad called out to him, “Stop right there! Give me your hand.” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • nunc per lectum in latus sē volūtat, quoad pater «Parce!» inquit — now rolls sideways across the bed, until Dad says, “That’s enough!” (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • «Quid tū es tam trīstis, pāvō?» inquit. «Nōlī trīstis esse! Etiam sine caudā pulcher es!» — “Why are you so sad, peacock?” he said. “Don’t be sad! You’re handsome even without a tail!” (Libellus V, Lisbōna: castellum et ōceanārium).
  • «Quid tibi est? Aurēs dolent?» — “What’s the matter? Do your ears hurt?” (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).
  • «Bene factum,» inquit avia. «Amō tē.» — “Well done,” said Grandma. “Thank you.” (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • «Id, amābō,» inquit, «adjuvā mē, tata!» — “Help me with it, please, Dad!” he said (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Bonō animō es! — Cheer up! (Cic. Att. 5.18); see the Feelings II entry for more.

Quiet and gestures: in a low voice / finger to the lips / point / on tiptoe / slip away / creep out

summissā vōce · suspēnsō pede

Ancient LatinClassical idioms
  • summissā vōce; vōce summissā — in a low voice.
  • digitō silentium suādēre — put a finger to the lips for silence (cf. Ov. Met. 9.692 digitōque silentia suādet).
  • digitum ad aliquem intendere — point at someone (Traupman 98); digitō intentō — pointing.
  • suspēnsō pede — on tiptoe; sē subdūcere — slip away quietly.
  • prōrēpō, prōrēpere, prōrēpsī — creep out, crawl out (Hor. S. 1.1.37).
  • Pater digitō silentium suāsit. Theodōrus, quī alibī clāmāre solet, hīc vōce summissā «Pluteī sunt, tata,» inquit, «sīcut avī, sed aurātī.» — Dad put a finger to his lips. Theo, who shouts everywhere else, said here in a low voice, “They’re bookshelves, Dad, like Grandpa’s, but golden.” (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • Theodōrus pittam cum cucurbitulīs, melongēnīs, piperītidibus rubrīs poposcit, nōn per patrem sed ipse, digitō in imāginem intentō. — Theo asked for the pitta with courgettes, aubergines and red peppers, not through Dad but himself, pointing at the picture. (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).
  • Tum, cum puer artē dormīret, suspēnsō pede, ut cotīdiē, sē subdūxit — Then, when the boy was fast asleep, he slipped away on tiptoe, as he does every day (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).
  • ē lectō prōrēpsit et ad fenestram accessit — crept out of bed and went to the window (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).

Climb up / climb down / reach the top / jump down

scandō, scandere · dēscendō, dēscendere

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • scandō, scandere — climb or clamber. L&S gives no perfect or supine for this verb; none is invented here. See also playground movement verbs.
  • ascendō, ascendere, ascendī, ascēnsum — go or climb up.
  • dēscendō, dēscendere, dēscendī, dēscēnsum — go or climb down.
  • dēsiliō, dēsilīre, dēsiluī — jump down; the infinitive has long ī.
  • perveniō, pervenīre, pervēnī, perventum — reach, arrive at.
  • Vīsne scandere? — Do you want to climb?
  • Scandāmus. — Let’s climb.
  • Scande, Theodōre. — Climb, Theo.
  • Dēscende lentē. — Climb down slowly.
  • Nōlī dēsilīre. — Don’t jump down.
  • Ad summum pervēnistī. — You’ve reached the top.

Grasp / hold on / let go / reach / lift / pull / push with the feet

prehendō, prehendere · nītor, nītī

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • prehendō, prehendere, prehendī, prehēnsum — grasp, take hold of.
  • teneō, tenēre, tenuī, tentum — hold, keep holding; contrasts with taking hold in the first place.
  • dīmittō, dīmittere, dīmīsī, dīmissum — let go of, release.
  • tangō, tangere, tetigī, tāctum — touch; useful for reaching far enough to touch a hold.
  • attollō, attollere — lift or raise. L&S gives no perfect or supine.
  • trahō, trahere, trāxī, tractum — pull, draw.
  • nītor, nītī, nīsus sum / nīxus sum — lean or bear upon, support oneself, push upward; deponent. The supporting limb or object may be in the ablative.
  • Ansam firmiter tenē. — Hold the hold firmly.
  • Potesne illam ansam tangere? — Can you touch that hold?
  • Pedem dextrum attolle. — Lift your right foot.
  • Tē sūrsum trahe. — Pull yourself upward.
  • Pedibus nītere. — Push with your feet / support yourself on your feet.
  • Hanc ansam dīmitte. — Let go of this hold: use only when releasing that particular hold is intended.

Climbing directions / hand and foot placement / coloured holds

hīc · hūc · altius · dexter · sinister

Ancient LatinComposed phrasesModern application
  • hīc; hūc; illīc; illūc — here (location); to here; there (location); to there.
  • sūrsum; deorsum; altius; paulō altius — upward; downward; higher; a little higher.
  • dexter, dextra, dextrum; sinister, sinistra, sinistrum — right; left.
  • ad dextram; ad sinistram — to the right; to the left, with partem understood.
  • lentē; lentius; firmiter — slowly; more slowly; firmly.
  • manus, manūs f.; pēs, pedis m.; bracchium, bracchiī n.; genū, genūs n. — hand; foot; arm; knee. The nominative genū has long ū. See the body-parts entry in Corpus et mōtus.
  • Pōne pedem hīc. — Put your foot here, specifying where it should be placed.
  • Manum sinistram hūc pōne. — Put your left hand here, indicating movement toward this spot.
  • Paulō altius. — A little higher.
  • Prehende rubram / caeruleam / viridem / flāvam. — Grab the red / blue / green / yellow one, with feminine accusative ansam understood.
  • ansa alba; ansa nigra — a white hold; a black hold. See also the colours entry under Cum Theodōrō.

Climbing encouragement / help / fear / tiredness / rest / try again

euge · auxilium · quiēscō · cōnor

Ancient LatinComposed phrases
  • euge — well done; an interjection of approval.
  • auxilium, auxiliī n.; adjuvō, adjuvāre, adjūvī, adjūtum — help; help someone.
  • timeō, timēre, timuī — be afraid, fear.
  • fessus, fessa, fessum — tired.
  • quiēscō, quiēscere, quiēvī, quiētum — rest, take a break. See also the trip / slip / fall / rest entry under Cum Theodōrō.

  • Euge, Theodōre. — Well done, Theo.
  • Ego hīc sum. — I’m here.

  • Vīsne ut tē adjuvem? — Do you want me to help you?
  • Timēsne? Vīsne dēscendere? — Are you afraid? Do you want to climb down?
  • Fessus es? — Are you tired? Said to a boy; Fessa es? to a girl.
  • Quiēscāmus paulisper. — Let’s rest a little.
  • Vīsne iterum cōnārī? — Do you want to try again?

Splash / sprinkle / drench / slap the water / don’t splash / that’s enough

spargō, spargere · plangō, plangere

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • spargō, spargere, sparsī, sparsum — scatter, splash water (on someone); perfundō, perfundere, perfūdī, perfūsum — drench, pour all over. Diana splashing Actaeon: sīc hausit aquās vultumque virīlem perfūdit, spargēnsque comās ultrīcibus undīs — “she scooped up water, drenched the man’s face, and splashing his hair with the avenging water…” (Ov. Met. 3.189–190).
  • aspergō, aspergere, aspersī, aspersum — sprinkle, spatter; frequent in ritual, but everyday too: adspersistī aquam, “you’ve splashed water on me” (Plaut. Truc., quoted by L&S).
  • plangō, plangere, plānxī, plānctum — strike with a smack; aquam palmīs plangit — he slaps the water with his palms, modelled on plangēbant aliae prōcērīs tympana palmīs (Catull. 64.261). plangor, plangōris m. — the slap of water, of waves (Catull. 64.273). Avoid plānctus, which nearly always means beating the breast in mourning.
  • Nōlī aquam spargere! — Don’t splash!
  • Nōlī aquam plangere! — Don’t slap the water!
  • Nimis spargis! — You’re splashing too much!
  • Modo tantum aquae spargēbās! — You were splashing so much earlier!
  • Hoc nimium est! Satis est! — That’s too much! That’s enough!
  • Ōhē, jam satis est! — Whoa, that’s enough now! (Hor. Serm. 1.5.12–13; Mart. 4.89.1)

Feelings II: sorry / ashamed / bored / fed up / cross / grumpy / cheer up / don’t worry / calm down / surprised / shy

mē paenitet · mē pudet · taedet · stomachor, stomachārī

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • mē paenitet (+ gen. or infinitive) — I’m sorry, I regret it (Traupman 157, 383). An apology for a child: Sī quid perperam fēcī, mē paenitet. — If I’ve done anything wrong, I’m sorry (Traupman 112).
  • mē pudet (+ gen.) — I’m ashamed (Traupman 93); Ecquid pudet? — Aren’t you ashamed? (Cordier).
  • taedet; pertaedet — I’m bored, fed up (Traupman 96, 107): taedet jam audīre eadem mīliēns — “I’m sick of hearing the same thing a thousand times” (Ter. Ph. 487). Taedetne tē? — Are you bored?
  • mōrōsus, mōrōsa, mōrōsum — grumpy, peevish (Traupman 151; Cic. Sen. 65). stomachor, stomachārī — be cross, in a huff (Cic.); stomachōsus, stomachōsa, stomachōsum — touchy, irritable (Traupman 158; Hor.). īrācundus, īrācunda, īrācundum — hot-tempered (Traupman 154); īrācundiā efferrī — lose one’s temper; īrācundiam cohibēre — keep one’s temper (Traupman 392).
  • suscēnseō, suscēnsēre + dat. — be cross with: nihil fēcit quod suscēnseās — he did nothing for you to be cross about (Traupman 93; Ter., Cic.).
  • Bonō animō es! — Cheer up! (Cic. Att. 5.18; Plaut. Merc. 3.1.33, in L&S); Traupman’s Habē animum bonum! (150). hilarus / hilaris — cheerful; maestus — gloomy (Traupman 150, 153).
  • Nōlī sollicitārī! — Don’t worry! (Traupman 409); Nōlī perturbārī. — Don’t be upset (Traupman 110).
  • Tē continē. — Control yourself (Traupman 96); Compēsce mentem! — Keep your cool! (Traupman 101); aequō animō — calmly.
  • Gaudeō tuā causā. — I’m glad for you (Traupman 18).
  • exanimātus metū — scared to death (Traupman 107); mīror, mīrārī — be surprised, amazed (Traupman 388).
  • verēcundus, verēcunda, verēcundum — shy, bashful (L&S; Plaut. Am. 3.2.22); Traupman 157 gives timidus, which is rather “fearful”.
  • mē dēsīderium tenet (+ gen.) — I’m homesick for (Traupman 154); patriae dēsīderium — homesickness (M-O s.v. nostalgia).
  • bonum animum habēre; bonō animō esse — be in a good mood (Traupman 104, 153).
  • Quid stomachāris, mī fīlī? — What are you cross about, my boy?
  • Nōlī lacrimāre; nihil malī factum est. — Don’t cry; nothing bad has happened.

Character for a little boy: naughty / cheeky / good boy / behave / obedient / silly / lazy / stubborn / greedy / clever / darling

improbus, improba, improbum · frūgī (indecl.) · animulus, animulī m.

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • improbus, improba, improbum — naughty; petulāns, petulantis — cheeky (Traupman 350); nēquam (indecl.) — good-for-nothing, rascal (Traupman 99) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.).
  • lascīvus, lascīva, lascīvum — playful, frisky, up to tricks (Traupman 110); of young animals in Horace and Vergil.
  • frūgī (indecl.) — good, well-behaved: Frūgī homō es — “you’re a good lad” (Ter. Ad. 959); sum bonus et frūgī (Hor. Ep. 1.16.49). Traupman 99: frūgī es.
  • sē probē gerere — behave oneself (Traupman 278); bene / male mōrātus — well / badly behaved (Traupman 154, 159).
  • oboediēns, oboedientis + dat. — obedient (Traupman 352); the classical idiom is dictō audiēns — doing as one is told (Cato Agr. 142; Cic. Phil. 7.2).
  • ineptus, inepta, ineptum — silly; Nōlī ineptīre! — Don’t be silly (Traupman 107; Ter. Ad. 934; Catull. 8.1 dēsinās ineptīre).
  • piger, pigra, pigrum; ignāvus, ignāva, ignāvum — lazy (Traupman 35, 155).
  • obstinātus, obstināta, obstinātum; pertināx, pertinācis — stubborn (Traupman 158; L&S).
  • edāx, edācis — greedy with food (Traupman 153; Plaut., Ter.).
  • callidus, ingeniōsus — clever (Traupman 158); jocōsus, festīvus — funny (Traupman 153, spelling it with i); benignus, mītis, cōmis — kind, gentle, polite (Traupman 153–156); patiēns — patient.
  • animulus, animulī m. — darling, only in the vocative: mī animule (Traupman 151; Plaut. Cas. 1.46, in L&S; Cordier). dēliciae, dēliciārum f. — darling: Tulliola, dēliciae nostrae (Cic. Att. 1.5.8). Plautus’s string meus ocellus, meum labellum … meum mel, meum cor (Poen. 366–367).
  • Improbe! Quid fēcistī? — You rascal! What have you done?
  • Frūgī es: omnia tua reposuistī. — Good boy: you’ve put all your things away.
  • Venī hūc, mī animule. — Come here, my darling.

Terence, Horace, Catullus, Cicero (Att.) and Cordier from the Latinitas loci collections; Plautus (Poen.) checked against the Perseus Latin texts. The example sentences are composed.

Give it here! / really? / why so? / what happened? / ouch! / nonsense! / never mind / excuse me / of course / no way

Cedo! (pl. cette) · Itane? · Quid ita? · Au!

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Cedo! (plural cette) — give it here! hand it over! tell me! An old imperative from -ce + the root of dō, with short e and short final o (L&S cĕdo; de Vaan s.v. cedo); it takes an object: Cedo manum. — give me your hand (Plaut. Capt. 859, Most. 332). Not cēdō, cēdere “go, give way”. Terence: Nōlō, volō; volō, nōlō rūrsum; cedo, cape (Ph. 950); Plautus: Vigilō, cedo bibam (Most. 373b) (Traupman 99, 104).
  • Itane? — Really? Is that so? (Traupman 101; Plaut., Ter.); see also Ain’ vērō? in the Coming! entry.
  • Quid ita? Quīdum? — Why so? How so? (Traupman 101) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.). Quidnī? / Quippinī? — Why not? Of course (Traupman 111; Ter. And. 315).
  • Quid factum est? — What happened? (Traupman 100).
  • Au! — Ouch! Oh! (L&S s.v. hau, “an exclamation of pain or grief”, often in Plautus and Terence: Au, obsecrō, Ter. Ph. 803). Oiei! — Oh dear! (Traupman 105, for “ouch”; L&S, citing Ter. Eun. 4.4.47 and Ph. 4.3.58 in its numbering). Vae miserō mihi! — Oh dear me! (Traupman 104).
  • Nūgās! / Nūgae! — Nonsense! (Traupman 104); Aufer nūgās (Plaut. Truc. 861); Nūgās agis (Plaut. Men. 621).
  • Sine! — Never mind! Let it be (Traupman 104). Omitte mē! — Leave me alone! (Traupman 102). Dēsine! / Dēsiste! — Stop it! (Traupman 96).
  • Nōlī mihi obloquī! — Don’t interrupt me! (Traupman 101); Nōlī interpellāre (Traupman 33). Dēsinite rīxārī. — Stop bickering (Traupman 36).
  • Aspicedum contrā mē. — Look me in the eye (Traupman 97; Plaut.).
  • Ignōsce mihi. — Excuse me, sorry (Traupman 97); Mē tibi excūsō. — I apologise (Traupman 93). libenter — with pleasure (Traupman 105).
  • Amō tē. / Multum tē amō. — Thank you (so much) for what you’ve done (Traupman 109), the idiom of Cicero’s letters.
  • scīlicet, profectō — of course (Traupman 105); Minimē! / Nūllō modō! — No way! (Traupman 104); Sīc est. / Ita est. — That’s right (Traupman 107, 109); Sīc opīnor. / Ego nōn putō. — I think so / I don’t think so (Traupman 109).
  • Nīl interest. — It makes no difference (Traupman 96); Patī nequeō amplius. — I can’t take any more (Traupman 109).
  • Periī! / Interiī! — I’m done for! (Traupman 96) (vōx cōmica); Īlicet. — It’s no use (Traupman 110) (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.).
  • Fēlīciter! — Good luck! (Traupman 103); Quis homō est? — Ego sum. — Who is it? — It’s me (Traupman 111); Fac silentium! — Quiet! (Traupman 367; Plaut. Pers. 4.3.50).
  • Cedo istum lapidem! — Give me that stone!
  • Cette manūs, ambō; viam trānsīmus. — Give me your hands, both of you; we’re crossing the road.

cĕdo (short e, short final o) is a different word from cēdō, cēdere (“go, give way”); L&S lists them separately. The lexicon writes it without macrons: Cedo, cette.

Why oiei, not ojei: we keep the spelling of L&S, since it is unclear whether its i’s are vowels or consonants. The form also depends on the edition: the Perseus text of Terence does not print oiei at the places L&S cites.
