Family II: husband / children / uncle / aunt / nephew / niece / grandson / in-laws / step-family / little brother / little sister / eldest, youngest

marītus, marītī m. · patruus, patruī m. · amita, amitae f.

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsSense distinctions
  • marītus, marītī m. — husband (Traupman 24); caelebs, caelibis — single (Traupman 20). in mātrimōnium dūcere — marry (of the man) (Traupman 21); nūbō, nūbere, nūpsī + dat. — marry (of the woman).
  • parentēs, parentum m. — parents; līberī, līberōrum m. — children (Traupman 24). Cicero: nātūrā fierī ut līberī ā parentibus amentur (Fin. 3.62).
  • patruus, patruī m. — uncle, father’s brother; avunculus, avunculī m. — uncle, mother’s brother (Traupman 24).
  • amita, amitae f. — aunt, father’s sister; mātertera, māterterae f. — aunt, mother’s sister (Traupman 24).
  • fīlius frātris / sorōris; fīlia frātris / sorōris — nephew; niece (Traupman 24; Traupman 351).
  • nepōs, nepōtis m.; neptis, neptis f. — grandson; granddaughter (Traupman 24); pronepōs, pronepōtis m. — great-grandson (Comenius 119); proavus, proavī m. — great-grandfather (Traupman 24).
  • socer, socerī m. — father-in-law; gener, generī m. — son-in-law; nurus, nurūs f. — daughter-in-law (Traupman 24; Erasmus: Socer uxōris meae pater est mihi. Gener fīliae meae marītus … Nurus fīliī meī uxor). affīnis, affīnis m./f. — an in-law (Traupman 24).
  • lēvir, lēvirī m. — husband’s brother; glōs, glōris f. — husband’s sister (Traupman 24; both rare, Dig.). Traupman’s plainer phrases: marītus sorōris, uxor frātris (283, 379).
  • vitricus, vitricī m.; noverca, novercae f.; prīvignus, prīvignī m.; prīvigna, prīvignae f. — stepfather, stepmother, stepson, stepdaughter (Traupman 24; Cic.).
  • cognātus, cognātī m.; cognāta, cognātae f. — relative (Traupman 24).
  • stirps, stirpis f. — family tree, lineage (Traupman 24, 313 adds stemma); majōrēs, majōrum m. — ancestors. Traupman 24 gives atavī for forefathers, but strictly atavus is a great-great-great-grandfather (L&S).
  • frāterculus, frāterculī m.; sorōrcula, sorōrculae f. — little brother; little sister (Traupman 24; Juv. 4.98; Plaut. fr.); fīliola, fīliolae f. — little daughter (Traupman 24).
  • major / minor / maximus / minimus nātū — older, younger, eldest, youngest (Traupman 21, 23): Quis frāter est maximus nātū?
  • Jack’s rule: familia is the household, not “wife and children” (use suī, domus); Traupman 24 lists it as “family”.
  • Hic est patruus tuus, frāter patris. — This is your uncle, Dad’s brother.
  • Uter est major nātū, tū an cōnsōbrīnus tuus? — Who’s older, you or your cousin?

Babies and little children: newborn / baby carriage / nanny / lullaby / twins / swaddling / teething / kindergarten / when you’re big

īnfāns, īnfantis m./f. · chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. · lallō, lallāre

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations
  • īnfāns, īnfantis m./f. — baby (Traupman 24); recēns nātus — newborn (M-O, 17th century). Neo-Latin Lexicon s.v. baby: īnfantulus (Apul., post-classical), neonātus (Helfer), recēns nātus, modo nātus.
  • pūsiō, pūsiōnis m. — little boy (Cic. Tusc. 1.57); Traupman 410 gives puerculus, which is late (Arnobius). frustum puerī — “you scrap of a boy!” (Traupman 336; Plaut. Pers. 5.2.68, in L&S) (vōx cōmica).
  • chīramaxium, chīramaxiī n. — pram, baby carriage (Traupman 275; M-O chīramaxium īnfantile, warning against the spelling chīromaxium); in Petronius a small hand-drawn carriage. Neo-Latin Lexicon adds vehiculum puerīle (Bauer, Helfer). See the trolley entry for chīramaxium sarcinārum.
  • laguncula īnfantilis — baby bottle (M-O); M-O’s titina is late medical Latin. subligāculum īnfantile — nappy (M-O, modern; classically subligāculum is a loin-cloth).
  • gerula, gerulae f. — nanny, child-carrier (M-O; Tert., post-classical); nūtrīx, nūtrīcis f.; nūtrīcula, nūtrīculae f. — nurse, nanny (Cic.; Hor. Ep. 1.4.8 quid voveat dulcī nūtrīcula majus alumnō).
  • lallō, lallāre — sing a lullaby; lallum, lallī n. — lullaby (M-O; Pers. 3.18 īrātus mammae lallāre recūsās; Aus.).
  • geminī, geminōrum m.; gemellī, gemellōrum m. — twins (L&S; Erasmus et quidem gemellōs); trigeminī — triplets (M-O; Liv. 1.24).
  • fasciae, fasciārum f.; incūnābula, incūnābulōrum n. — swaddling clothes (Plaut. Truc. 5.13, in L&S: fasciīs opus est, pulvīnīs, cūnīs, incūnābulīs). Comenius: Īnfāns involvitur fasciīs, repōnitur in cūnās (Orbis pictus 120).
  • dentītiō, dentītiōnis f. — teething (M-O; Plin.); dēns īnfantilis / dēciduus — baby tooth (M-O); dēns mōbilis — loose tooth (M-O; Plin.).
  • paedotrophēum, paedotrophēī n. — kindergarten (Traupman 336, modern coinage); conclāve īnfantium — nursery (Traupman 352).
  • nāscor, nāscī, nātus sum — be born (Traupman 282); obstetrīx, obstetrīcis f. — midwife (Plaut., Ter.); gravida; praegnāns — pregnant (L&S, classical; not in either source); parturīre — be in labour (M-O).
  • cum magnus eris; cum adolēveris — when you’re big, when you’ve grown up. Traupman 324 gives juvenēscō, but that means “reach youth, grow young again” (Hor., Ov.), not a child’s growing up.
  • Cum magnus eris, ipse birotā vehēris. — When you’re big, you’ll ride a bike yourself.
  • Tū quoque in cūnīs vāgiēbās, cum īnfāns erās. — You too used to cry in your cradle when you were a baby.

Birthday / happy birthday / birthday party / birthday present / birthday cake

diēs nātālis · nātālīcia, nātālīciae f. · nātālīcium, nātālīciī n.

Ancient LatinClassical quotationsFamily phrases
  • diēs nātālis; nātālis, nātālis m. — birthday (Traupman 280; M-O s.v. birthday; Cic., Hor.). Cicero’s little girl met him nātālī suō ipsō diē — “on her very birthday” (Att. 4.1.4).
  • Fēlīcem nātālem (tibi exoptō)! — Happy birthday! (Traupman 280).
  • nātālīcia, nātālīciae f. — birthday party: dat nātālīciam in hortīs — “he’s giving a birthday party in his gardens” (Cic. Phil. 2.15, as cited in L&S); nātālīciam dare / agitāre — throw a birthday party (Traupman 280).
  • nātālīcium, nātālīciī n. — birthday present (Traupman 280; Censorinus, in L&S).
  • lībum nātālīcium — birthday cake (Traupman 280); lībum, a cheese cake, was the Roman birthday offering. Cato’s recipe: lībum hōc modō facitō (Agr. 75). Ovid’s birthday shared with his brother: ūna celebrāta est per duo lība diēs — “one day was celebrated with two birthday cakes” (Tr. 4.10.12).
  • Horace’s birthday questions: nātālīs grātē numerās? — “do you count your birthdays gladly?” (Ep. 2.2.210).
  • Crās est diēs nātālis tuus! Quot annōs nātus eris? — Tomorrow’s your birthday! How old will you be?
  • Hoc tibi nātālīcium est. — This is your birthday present.

What time is it? / at what time? / half an hour / an hour and a half / wall clock / wristwatch / hourglass / clock hand / stopwatch

Quota hōra est? · sēmihōra, sēmihōrae f.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotationsComposed phrases
  • Quota hōra est? — What time is it? (Traupman 81, 89; M-O s.v. time: what time is it?; Hor. S. 2.6.44 hōra quota est?). Also Quot hōrae sunt? (Traupman 89). hōrās quaerere — ask the time (M-O, citing Plin. 7.182).
  • Quotā hōrā …? — At what time …? (Traupman 81). Est prīma ferē hōra. — It’s about one o’clock (Traupman 81).
  • sēmihōra, sēmihōrae f. — half an hour (Traupman 87, 330; M-O s.v. hour: 30 minutes; Cic.); also dīmidium hōrae (Traupman 87). sesquihōra, sesquihōrae f. — an hour and a half (Traupman 87, printed sēsqui-; Plin. Ep. 4.9.9). Lewis & Short leaves the e unmarked, so it is unmarked here.
  • ūncia / sextāns / triēns / bēs hōrae — five / ten / twenty / forty minutes (M-O s.v. hour), the classical twelfths applied to the hour. For the quarter and three quarters (quadrāns, dōdrāns) see the telling-the-time entry.
  • hōrologium parietārium — wall clock (Traupman 403); hōrologium manuāle / bracchiāle — wristwatch (M-O s.v. watch, which prints brachiāle); index, indicis m.; digitus, digitī m. — clock hand (M-O s.v. hand, from Vives).
  • hōrologium arēnārium; clepsammidium, clepsammidiī n. — hourglass, sand timer (M-O s.v. hourglass); classical clepsydra is a water-clock. chronoscōpium (Traupman 386) / chronometrum (M-O s.v. stop-watch) — stopwatch.
  • Quota hōra est, tata? — Septima ferē. — What time is it, Dad? — About seven.
  • Sēmihōram exspectā; deinde lūdēmus. — Wait half an hour; then we’ll play.
  • Spectā: ubi est index parvus? — Look: where’s the little hand?

Ancient LatinClassical idiomsComposed phrases

  • dīlūculum, dīlūculī n. — daybreak; prīmā lūce, dīlūculō — at daybreak (Traupman 86, 300; M-O s.v. day: dawn; Cic. Att. 16.13.1).

  • interdiū — by day (Traupman 84, 86); diem noctemque — day and night (Traupman 351).

Time phrases: a little while ago / shortly after / just now / lately / any day now / how long? / how soon? / sooner or later / in a moment / waste time / once upon a time

paulō ante · paulō post · propediem

Ancient LatinClassical idiomsComposed phrases
  • paulō ante — a little while ago; paulō post — a little later; posteā aliquantō — some time later (Traupman 87, 89).
  • modo — just now, a moment ago; nūper — lately, recently (Traupman 87–88).
  • propediem — any day now, very soon (Traupman 86; Plaut.; Cic.).
  • Quam diū? Quam prīdem? Quam mox? — How long? How long ago? How soon? (Traupman 87).
  • sērius ōcius — sooner or later (Traupman 88; Hor. C. 2.3.26).
  • in diēs — from day to day; Variat in diēs. — It varies from day to day (Traupman 82, 86).
  • mōmentō temporis — in a moment (Traupman 87).
  • tempus perdere — waste time; Tempus nōn est mihi. — I haven’t got time; Tempus maximē est ut … — it’s high time to … (Traupman 89).
  • (alicui) in morā esse — keep someone waiting, be late for someone (M-O s.v. late).
  • ōlim — once upon a time (Traupman 88).
  • Quam mox veniet avia? — Propediem. — How soon will Grandma come? — Any day now.
  • Nōlī tempus perdere: calceōs indue. — Don’t waste time: put your shoes on.
  • Ōlim erat rēx quīdam, cui trēs fīliae erant. — Once upon a time there was a king who had three daughters.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinVariable terminologyComposed phrases
  • fēriae, fēriārum f. pl. — holidays, vacation; vacātiō, vacātiōnis f. (Traupman 52–54, 401; M-O s.v. tourist: vacation); fēriae aestīvae — summer holidays (Traupman 53). diēs fēriātus — a day off (Traupman 29; M-O s.v. holiday). fēriātus esse — be on holiday (Traupman 32, 401).

  • Pascha, Paschae f.; Pascha, Paschatis n. — Easter (Traupman 308; M-O s.v. Easter; Tert.); Paschālis, Paschāle — Easter (adj.). Traupman prints the genitive Paschātis; Lewis & Short has a short a.

Classroom commands: sit down / sit up straight / listen / pay attention / look at me / put your hand up / speak up / lower your voice / stop talking / stop squabbling / not so fast / never mind / may I go to the toilet?

Cōnsīde. · Attende. · Eho, nōn tam cito!

Ancient LatinClassical idiomsFamily phrases
  • Cōnsīde (cōnsīdite). — Sit down. Rēctē sedē. — Sit up straight (Traupman 34).
  • Audī dīligenter. Attende (attendite). — Listen carefully. Pay attention (Traupman 33–34). Converte oculōs in mē. — Look at me (Traupman 33).
  • Attolle manum. — Put your hand up (Traupman 34).
  • Ēloquere. — Speak up. Remitte vōcem. — Lower your voice (Traupman 33–34).
  • Dēsine loquī. — Stop talking. Dēsine rīxārī. — Stop squabbling (Traupman 34; rīxor is classical).
  • Eho, nōn tam cito! — Whoa, not so fast! (Traupman 34); eho is the interjection of comedy (Plaut.; Ter.).
  • Sine. — Never mind (Traupman 33). Paucīs tē volō. — I want a word with you (Traupman 33; Ter. Andr. 29).
  • Licetne mihi in lātrīnam īre? — Licet. — May I go to the toilet? — Yes (Traupman 28, 32).
  • Cōnsīde, quaesō, et attende: fābulam narrābō. — Sit down, please, and listen: I’m going to tell a story.
  • Vōs ambō, dēsinite rīxārī! — You two, stop squabbling!

Left out: Traupman 33’s nōlī eum taxāre for “don’t tease him”. In Lewis & Short taxō means “touch sharply; censure” (post-Augustan), not “tease”.

Kitchen, meals & drinks

Soup / broth / stock / sauce / gravy boat

jūs, jūris n.

Ancient LatinWorking descriptions
  • jūs, jūris n. — soup, broth (Traupman 73); a homonym of jūs, “right, law”.
  • jūs viride — Portuguese caldo verde, the rendering in Libellus III; jūs ex holeribus — vegetable soup; jūs gallīnāceum — chicken stock; ōlla, ōllae f. — pot (the series spelling).
  • jūsculum, jūsculī n. — sauce, broth (Traupman 73); vāsculum jūris — gravy boat (323).
  • in crāstinum servāre — keep for tomorrow.
  • Domum reversa avia jūs coxit, quod Lūsitānī caldo verde vocant, id est jūs viride — Back home, Grandma made the soup the Portuguese call caldo verde, that is, green soup (Libellus III, Apud avum et aviam).
  • In culīnā jūs ex holeribus in ōllā foculō impositā calēbat, quod in crāstinum servātum est. — In the kitchen a vegetable soup was keeping warm in a pot on the stove; it was kept for the next day. (Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum).

Meat / turkey / stuffing / truss / baste / bacon

carō, carnis f. · gallopāvō, gallopāvōnis m.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinQuantity notes
  • carō, carnis f. — meat (Traupman 72).
  • gallopāvō, gallopāvōnis m. — turkey (Traupman 399, 145).
  • fartum, fartī n. — stuffing, from farciō, farcīre (cf. Traupman 73, pastillum fartum); īnfarciō, īnfarcīre — stuff into.
  • adstringere — truss, tie up; perungō, perungere — rub with oil; perfundō, perfundere — baste. Latin needs no special basting verb.
  • lārdum, lārdī n. — bacon, lard: the preferred form (L&S, contracted from lāridum); Traupman 70 prints lardum; the libellī write lārdum (III, IV).
  • crūs, crūris n.; pectus, pectoris n. — leg, drumstick; breast.
  • Estne avis, tata? Cūr tanta est? — Avis est, gallopāvō, avis Americāna, quae tanta crēscit. — Is it a bird, Dad? Why is it so big? — It’s a bird, a turkey, an American bird that grows this big. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • avia gallopāvōnem in furnum mīsit, quem jam fartō complēverat — Grandma put the turkey in the oven; she had already filled it with stuffing (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • avem deinde fīlō adstrīnxerat, oleō perūnxerat, sale pipereque asperserat — then she had trussed the bird with string, rubbed it with oil and sprinkled it with salt and pepper (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Dough / knead / rolling pin / roll out / pie dish

massa, massae f. · depsō, depsere, depsuī, depstum

Ancient LatinWorking formation
  • massa, massae f. — dough (Vulgate).
  • depsō, depsere, depsuī, depstum — knead (Cato, Agr. 74: pānis depstīcius); subigō, subigere — work, knead, Cato’s own verb for working the dough.
  • cylindrus, cylindrī m. — rolling pin: our use of “cylinder”, a working formation; in orbēs tenuēs extendere — roll out thin, as in Libellus IV.
  • patina, patinae f. — pie dish (Traupman 124); forāmen, forāminis n. — hole, the vent in a pie crust.
  • frustātim — in pieces; paulātim — little by little; spargō, spargere — scatter.
  • «Massa nunc dormiet,» inquit pater; et eam in frīgidārium condidit. — “The dough will sleep now,” said Dad, and put it in the fridge. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Cūr massa dormit? — Ut requiēscat; tum melius extenditur. — Why is the dough sleeping? — To rest; then it rolls out better. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Massa ē frīgidāriō relāta cylindrō in orbēs tenuēs extenta est — Brought back from the fridge, the dough was rolled out thin with the rolling pin (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Manūs mortāriumque bene lavātō. — Wash your hands and the bowl well. (Cato, Agr. 74; quoted in Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • fistula, fistulae f. — rolling pin (Traupman 124, 372), alongside our cylindrus; classically fistula is a pipe or tube.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinWorking formations
  • mortārium, mortāriī n.; pistillum, pistillī n. — mortar, mixing bowl; pestle (Cato).
  • trulla, trullae f. — ladle (Traupman 71); also a builder’s trowel (168).

  • scabellum, scabellī n. — stool (Traupman 125).
  • fūsōrium, fūsōriī n. — kitchen sink (Traupman 125); epitonium, epitoniī n. — tap (123). epitonium vertere — turn the tap on (Varro’s verb, RR III 5, 16: epitoniīs versīs); epitonium claudere or aquam sistere — turn it off. Not Traupman’s versāre / reversāre (reversāre is Late Latin): Jack’s ruling, 29 October 2026.
  • fistula, fistulae f. — water pipe (Traupman 124); aqua ē fistulā — tap water.
  • ad mēnsam pater et Theodōrus, hic quidem in scabellō, stābant — Dad and Theo stood at the table, Theo on a stool (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Tandem tinnīvit hōrologium culīnārium. — At last the kitchen timer rang. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • «Satis est,» inquit. «Siste aquam.» Puer epitonium ipse clausit. — “That’s enough,” he said. “Turn the water off.” The boy turned the tap off himself. (Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae).

Set the table: tablecloth / napkin / plate / platter / candle / silverware / salt cellar / tray

mēnsam pōnere · mantēle, mantēlis n.

Ancient Latin
  • mēnsam pōnere — set the table (Traupman 125).
  • mantēle, mantēlis n. — hand towel, napkin: the classical sense (Varr. LL VI 85; Verg. A. I 702) and the house word for a hand towel (Jack’s ruling, 29 October 2026). Later also a tablecloth, a post-classical sense (Lewis & Short: Isidore, Orig. 19.26.6; Trebellius Pollio), which Traupman (p. 125) gives; the libellī use linteum for the tablecloth (Mart. XIV 138).
  • mappa, mappae f. — napkin (Traupman 72).
  • patella, patellae f. — plate (Traupman 72); lānx, lancis f. — platter (123).
  • candēla, candēlae f. — candle; dispōnō, dispōnere — set out.
  • Spoons, forks, knives and cups are in the existing table entry; the cochleāria, furcillās, cultrōs, pōcula of Libellus IV belong there.
  • Avia linteum candidum strāvit; Theodōrus mappās quattuor et patellās quattuor et cochleāria disposuit; pater, argenteīs ēscāriīs ē māchinā ēlūtōriā prōmptīs, furcillās, cultrōs, pōcula, urceum aquae, salīnum, piperīnum; duae candēlae accēnsae sunt — Grandma spread a white tablecloth; Theo set out four napkins, four plates and the spoons; Dad took the silver cutlery out of the dishwasher and set out the forks, knives, glasses, a jug of water, the salt and the pepper; two candles were lit (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • argentea ēscāria — the silver cutlery, silverware (Traupman 125; ēscāria, Juv. 12.46); in mēnsam appōnere — put on the table.
  • salīnum, salīnī n. — salt cellar (Traupman 124; Hor. C. 2.16.14); piperīnum, piperīnī n. — pepper pot (Traupman 72); urceus aquae — a jug of water.
  • ferculum, ferculī n. — tray (Traupman 125); classically a carrying frame, and a course of a meal.
  • Pater intereā catillōs, cochleāria, salīnum in mēnsam apposuit. — Dad meanwhile put the plates, spoons and salt cellar on the table. (Libellus II, Sintra: castellum et puteus).
  • Mēnsa deinde secunda in ferculō allāta est — Then dessert was brought in on a tray (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).

Classical phrases at the table: I’m hungry / have some more / no, thank you / it’s in the oven

Ēsuriō hercle! · Benignē.

Classical quotationsFamily phrases
  • Ēsuriō hercle. — I’m starving, really! (Plaut. Cas. 801). Said before breakfast.
  • Vēscere, sōdēs. — Jam satis est. — At tū, quantum vīs, tolle. — Benignē. — Eat, please. — I’ve had enough. — Take as much as you like. — No, thank you (Hor. Epist. I 7, 15–16). Here benignē is a polite refusal.
  • Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs. — My mind has been on the dishes for ages (Ter. Eun. 816); said while waiting at the oven.
  • Bonum sit! — May it turn out well! (Verg. Ecl. 8, 106, via Ranieri); said as the dish goes into the oven.
  • Ēn erit umquam ille diēs? — Will that day ever come? (Ecl. 8, 7–8); for waiting at the oven.
  • Īte domum saturae, venit Hesperus. — Go home full, the evening star is coming (Ecl. 10, 77); said after the meal.
  • Utramque in furnum mīsērunt. «Bonum sit!» inquit pater. — They put both in the oven. “May it turn out well!” said Dad. (Libellus IV, Diēs Grātulātiōnis).
  • Jamdūdum ēsuriō, tata! — I’ve been hungry for ages, Dad! (Libellus I, Iter in Lūsitāniam).

These are quotations, and their sources are given. Libellī II and IV and the back-matter lists of “locī memoriā tenendī” suggest when to use them with Theo.

Cooking words from the Culīna: sieve / tin / pastry brush / kitchen paper / bubble / season / soak / skim / lumps

crībrum, crībrī n. · fōrma, fōrmae f.

Ancient LatinModern descriptions
  • crībrum, crībrī n. — sieve (Cato, Agr. 76.3; Cic. Div. 2.59); per crībrum trānsmittere — sieve.
  • fōrma, fōrmae f. — baking tin, mould: classically a mould or form for shaping things.
  • pēniculus, pēniculī m. — brush; in the kitchen a pastry brush (classically a brush or sponge for cleaning, Plaut.).
  • charta bibula — kitchen paper: Pliny’s blotting paper (charta bibula, Ep. 8.15.2), here for the paper that drains fried food.
  • bulliō, bullīre — bubble (Vitr. 8.3; Celsus); condiō, condīre — season, flavour (Cato; Cic.).
  • mācerō, mācerāre — soak, steep (Cato, Agr. 156.5; Ter.); dēspūmō, dēspūmāre — skim (Verg. G. 1.296).
  • glomerō, glomerāre — form into a ball; glomerārī — of flour in a sauce, go lumpy.
  • flābellum, flābellī n. — fan (Ter. Eun. 595); in an oven, the fan.
  • Farīnam, pulverem fermentārium, nitrum, salem per crībrum in catīnum trānsmittitō — Sieve the flour, baking powder, soda and salt into a bowl (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • Fōrmās būtȳrō unguitō. — Grease the tins with butter. (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • chartā bibulā siccātōs calidōs aut tepidōs appōnitō — drain them on kitchen paper and serve them hot or warm (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • dōnec crustum flāvēscat et sūcus per forāmina bulliat — until the crust turns golden and the juice bubbles through the holes (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • reliquum adipem cochleārī dēspūmātō et abjicitō — skim off the rest of the fat with a spoon and throw it away (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • semper agitāns, nē farīna glomerētur — stirring all the time so that the flour doesn’t go lumpy (Culīna Theodōrī).
  • Sī furnus tuus flābellō āëra calidum circumagit, vīgintī gradūs dētrahitō. — If your oven has a fan that circulates hot air, take off twenty degrees. (Culīna Theodōrī).

Mineral water / sparkling water / still / whisky / ice in drinks

aqua medicāta · aqua spūmāns

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinVariable terminology
  • aqua medicāta — mineral water; classical: Seneca, N.Q. 3.25.9, and Pliny, N.H. 2.222 (medicātās aquās); M-O s.v. mineral water. aqua minerālis — the modern term (Traupman 72).
  • aqua acidula — acidulous mineral water (L&S: “mineral water”). Pliny names such springs: Lyncēstis aqua quae vocātur acidula vīnī modō temulentōs facit — “the Lyncestian water called acidula makes people drunk like wine” (N.H. 2.230; cf. 31.9). He does not describe it as fizzy.
  • aqua spūmāns (or spūmōsa) — sparkling, fizzy water (M-O s.v. fizzy, carbonated); aqua Selterāna — soda water, seltzer (Traupman 382).
  • vischium, vischiī n. — whisky (Traupman 406; M-O s.v. whisky); spīritus frūmentī — grain spirit (M-O, from 19th-century scientific Latin). aqua vītae is the medieval name for distilled spirits in general; the Gaelic uisce beatha, source of English “whisky”, translates it.
  • glaciēs, glaciēī f. — ice.
  • Vīsne aquam spūmantem an sine bullīs? — Do you want sparkling water or still?
  • Nōn opus est glaciē in aquā. — You don’t need ice in the water.
  • Haec glaciēs vischiō meō servātur. — This ice is for my whisky.

At table: finish your fish / bite it / slow down / oily hands / rinse your mouth / dessert / pastry / chocolate / cream

bellāria, bellāriōrum n. · crustulum, crustulī n.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinFamily phrases
  • bellāria, bellāriōrum n. — dessert, sweets (Traupman 71); Varro’s quip via Gellius: bellāria … ea maximē sunt mellīta, quae mellīta nōn sunt — the sweetest desserts are the ones without honey (Gell. 13.11.6).
  • crustulum, crustulī n. — small pastry, biscuit; serviceable for an éclair and the like. Horace’s teachers coax boys with them: ut puerīs ōlim dant crustula blandī doctōrēs, elementa velint ut discere prīma (Serm. 1.1.25–26).
  • socolāta, socolātae f. — chocolate (Traupman 70; M-O). crēmum, crēmī n. — cream (Traupman 71, post-classical); flōs lactis — cream (Traupman 71; M-O, from pharmacopoeia Latin). Not cremor, which in L&S is a thick broth.
  • Comēde tōtum piscem! — Finish all your fish! (perēdō is poetic.)
  • Sī omnem piscem et omnia holera comēderis, tū quoque accipiēs. — If you eat all your fish and vegetables, you’ll get some too.
  • Paene cōnfēcistī! Paulum tantum superest. — You’re almost done! There’s only a little left.
  • Ūnum morsum etiam, deinde bellāria. — One more bite, then dessert. (morsus, morsūs m.: L&S leaves the o unmarked; nothing supports a long vowel.)
  • Mordē! Nimis magnum est. — Bite it! It’s too big. (mordeō is second conjugation, so mordē.)
  • Nōlī tantum cibī simul in ōs inserere! Lentius mandūcā! — Don’t put so much food in your mouth at once! Chew more slowly!
  • Lentē! Festīnāre tē nōlō. — Slowly! I don’t want you to rush (festīnāre tē nōlō, Cic. Fam. 16.11.1). Augustus’ “make haste slowly” was Greek, σπεῦδε βραδέως (Suet. Aug. 25; Gell. 10.11.5); festīnā lentē is the later Latin form.
  • Vīsne sūcum citreī in pisce? — Do you want lemon juice on your fish? (citreum: see the lemon entry.)
  • Manūs tuae oleō oblitae sunt! — Your hands are covered in oil! (oblitus, short i, from oblinō; not oblītus from oblīvīscor.)
  • Prīmum aquam bibe, ut ōs colluās. — Drink some water first, to rinse your mouth (colluō, Pliny).
  • Utrum māvīs, socolātam an crēmum? — Which do you prefer, chocolate or cream?
  • Bonum est, nōnne? — It’s good, isn’t it? Hoc nōn vīs? — Don’t you want this?

Eggs: fried / hard-boiled / soft-boiled / scrambled / omelette / yolk / egg white

ōva frīcta · vitellus, vitellī m.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinComposed phrases
  • ōvum frīctum, ōva frīcta — fried egg(s) (Traupman 67, 308). M-O gives ōvum frīxum (s.v. egg); frīctus is the classical participle of frīgō, frīxus late (Sidonius; L&S).
  • ōvum dūrum — hard-boiled egg (Traupman 71); M-O ōvum dūrātum or ōvum excoctum.
  • ōvum hapalum — soft-boiled egg: L&S hapalus “soft, only with ova” (Apicius). Traupman 67 prints apalum without the h; M-O also gives ōvum tremulum.
  • ōva permixta — scrambled eggs (Traupman 67, 71; M-O s.v. egg); M-O also cites Helfer’s ōva agitāta.
  • laganum ex ōvīs — omelette (Traupman 72); M-O gives Apicius’ ōva spongia and placenta ōvōrum. Classically laganum is a flour-and-oil cake (Hor. S. 1.6.115), so Apicius’ dish is the nearer ancient one.
  • vitellus, vitellī m. — yolk (Cels.; Cic. Div. 2.134; Hor.; Mart. 13.40.1); neither book gives it (M-O has lūtea ōvōrum). albūmen, albūminis n. — egg white (Traupman 308; Plin. 28.66).
  • Comenius: Ōvum tegitur testā, sub quā est albūmen, in hōc vitellus. — “The egg is covered by a shell; under it is the white, and in that the yolk” (Comen. OP 18; post-classical).
  • Vīsne ōvum frīctum an dūrum? — Do you want a fried egg or a boiled one?
  • Pānem in vitellum intinge. — Dip your bread in the yolk.
  • Cavē testam! Nōlī eam mandūcāre. — Watch out for the shell! Don’t eat it.

Traupman marks permīxta with a long ī; we write permixta, for the reasons given under the mixer (māchina mixtōria).

Meat at the butcher’s: beef / pork / lamb / veal / chicken / duck / ham / chop / steak / roast / rare / well done / mince

būbula, būbulae f. · porcīna, porcīnae f.

Ancient LatinModern applicationsClassical quotations
  • būbula, būbulae f. — beef (Traupman 70; M-O carō būbula); būbulus “of cattle” is classical (Plaut.). porcīna, porcīnae f. — pork (Traupman 72; Plaut.); M-O also suilla, suillae f. (Cels., Plin.).
  • agnīna, agnīnae f. — lamb (Traupman 71; M-O carō agnīna); vitulīna, vitulīnae f. — veal (Traupman 73; Plaut.); carō ovilla — mutton (M-O; ovillus, Cato).
  • gallīnācea, gallīnāceae f. — chicken as food (Traupman 70); M-O pullus gallīnāceus (Vives). anatīna, anatīnae f. — duck as food (Traupman 71), substantive of anatīnus (Plaut.).
  • perna, pernae f. — ham (Traupman 71; M-O; Cato, Agr. 162); perna fūmōsa — smoked ham (Traupman 325): holus fūmōsae cum pede pernae (Hor. S. 2.2.117).
  • offa porcīna — pork chop (Traupman 72); classically offa is a morsel, ofella a chop (Juv., Mart.). frustum būbulae — steak (Traupman 73, who prints frūstum; the series spelling is frustum).
  • assum, assī n. — a roast (Traupman 72; assum vitulīnum, roast veal, Cic. Fam. 9.20.1); būbula assa — roast beef (Traupman 68, 72); M-O assum būbulum.
  • sēmicoctus, -a, -um — rare, half-done (Traupman 68; Col., Plin.); percoctus, -a, -um — well done (Traupman 68; percoquō); M-O parum percoctus — undercooked.
  • minūtal, minūtālis n. — a dish of minced meat, hash (M-O s.v. hash; Juv. 14.129; Mart.).
  • Quid est hoc? — Būbula. — What’s this? — Beef. (cf. Corderius, Coll. II 10: Carō est, sed quaenam? — Būbula.)
  • Dā mihi, quaesō, lībram pernae. — A pound of ham, please.
  • Utrum sēmicoctam an percoctam māvīs? — Do you want it rare or well done?

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations

Sandwich / salad / dressing / mayonnaise / ketchup / pickle / chips / crisps

pastillum fartum · acētāria, acētāriōrum n.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinVariable terminology
  • pastillum fartum — sandwich (Traupman 73); pastillum pernā fartum — ham sandwich (325). M-O prefers pānis fartus (or replētus), noting that pastillum, a little loaf, is found only in two grammarians (Varro ap. Charis.; Paul. ex Fest.).
  • acētāria, acētāriōrum n. — salad (Traupman 72; M-O; Plin. 19.58); commīxta acētāria — mixed salad (Traupman 72).
  • embamma, embammatis n. — dressing, a sauce to dip in (Traupman 71; M-O s.v. sauce; Col.; Plin.).
  • liquāmen Magōnicum — mayonnaise (Traupman 72, after Mahón); M-O liquāmen majonēnse, following the vernacular (the o is unmarked there).
  • ketsupum, ketsupī n. — ketchup (Traupman 71); M-O lycopersicātum, lycopersicātī n., formed like Apicius’ piperātum. Both are modern.
  • cucumis muriāticus or cucumis muriā conditus — pickled cucumber, pickle (M-O s.v. cucumber: pickle); muria is brine (Cato). Traupman 72 gives salgamum, but L&S has salgamum only as “food, sustenance” (Cod. Just.), so it is not used here.
  • pōma terrestria frīcta — chips, French fries (Traupman 71); M-O māla terrestria frīcta, batātae frīctae. lāminae pōmōrum terrestrium — crisps (Traupman 363); M-O orbiculī batātae.
  • Vīsne pastillum pernā fartum? — Do you want a ham sandwich?
  • Acētāria sine embammate mālō. — I prefer the salad without dressing.

Cooking methods: boiled / stew / grill / gridiron / bake / smoked / breaded / whip / mince / dice

ēlixus, ēlixa, ēlixum · crāticula, crāticulae f.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinClassical quotations
  • ēlixus, ēlixa, ēlixum — boiled (Traupman 70; Hor. S. 2.2.74). Plautus contrasts it with assus, roast: ēlixus esse quam assus soleō suāvior (Most. 5.1.66, as cited by L&S). ēlixāre, boil, is late (Apicius; M-O s.v. stew).
  • lentō igne coquere — stew, cook slowly (Traupman 385); jūrulentum, jūrulentī n. — stew (Traupman 73), from the post-Augustan adjective jūrulentus, “in its juice” (L&S). M-O gives Vives’ jussulenta.
  • crāticula, crāticulae f. — grill, gridiron (Traupman 71, 276): rāra tibi curvā crāticula sūdet ofellā — “let the gridiron sizzle with a few chops” (Mart. 14.221.1). super crāticulam assāre — grill, barbecue (Traupman 71, 276).
  • in furnō coquere — bake (Traupman 276; M-O s.v. boil: bake); coquō alone also means bake.
  • fūmōsus, -a, -um — smoked (Traupman 71, perna fūmōsa; Cato).
  • farīnā circumlitus — breaded, coated in flour (M-O s.v. breaded, after Mattioli). Traupman 70 gives saligneus, but L&S has salignus, saligneus only as “of willow”; probably a slip for silīgineus, of fine wheat. Not used here.
  • peragitāre — beat, whip (eggs, cream): rudiculā ligneā peragitāre (Col. 12.46.3; M-O s.v. beat, whip).
  • minūtim concīdere — chop finely, mince (M-O); tessellātim concīdere — dice (Apic. 4.3; late, L&S).
  • Ōvum ēlixum mihi placet, nōn frīctum. — I like a boiled egg, not a fried one.
  • Caepam minūtim concīde. — Chop the onion finely.

Sweets and baked treats: sweets / cheesecake / birthday cake / bun / doughnut / croissant / pretzel / jam / popcorn / chewing gum / sugar cube

dulcia, dulcium n. · lībum, lībī n.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinVariable terminology
  • dulcia, dulcium n. — sweets (M-O s.v. sweets; L&S under dulcis); cuppēdia, cuppēdiōrum n. — dainties, treats (L&S; Plaut.). Traupman 70 makes it feminine, cuppēdiae; L&S has the feminine singular only as “daintiness” (Cic. Tusc. 4.26). dulciolum, dulciolī n. — a sweet (Traupman 286; not in L&S). M-O adds tragēmata (Plin.) and cuppēdia saccharīna.
  • lībum, lībī n. — cake of meal, cheese and honey (Cato, Agr. 75); lībum nātāle — birthday cake (Traupman 70).
  • savillum, savillī n. — cheesecake (Traupman 70; Cato, Agr. 84: savillum hōc modō facitō); M-O placenta cāseāta (cāseātus, Apul.).
  • collȳris, collȳridis f. — bun, roll (Traupman 70; L&S: Vulgate, Augustine). lucunculus, lucunculī m. — a kind of pastry (Afranius; Statius; L&S); M-O uses it for doughnut, printed lucunulus. pānis corniculātus — croissant (M-O).
  • pretiola, pretiolae f. — pretzel (Traupman 72, 364, modern); M-O nōdus pānis; LRL crustulum sale conditum (cited in M-O s.v. pretzel). Traupman’s “muffin”, scriblīta (72), is classically a tart (Cato, Agr. 78; Plaut.); M-O uses it for pizza.
  • bācārum conditūra — jam (Traupman 335, printed baccārum condītūra; series spelling bāca; L&S has conditūra, from condō, preserve). M-O pōma conditīva (cf. conditīvus, Cato). quilon, quilī n. — jelly (Traupman 71; L&S post-classical, Vegetius).
  • maizium īnflātum — popcorn (Traupman 363; M-O, after Helfer); LRL maizae grāna tosta (cited in M-O s.v. popcorn).
  • cummis masticābilis — chewing gum (Traupman 290; cummis, gum, is classical; masticābilis is modern); M-O mastichē, mastichēs f., mastic gum (Plin.; M-O prints masticha).
  • saccharum cubicum — sugar cube (Traupman 73); M-O sacchari tessella. saccharum pulvereum — icing sugar (Traupman 72); saccharō conditus — candied (M-O).
  • Ūnum tantum dulciolum, deinde dentēs pūrgābimus. — Just one sweet, then we’ll brush your teeth.
  • Avia lībum nātāle tibi coquit. — Grandma is baking you a birthday cake.
  • Hoc lībum ad avum afferāmus. — Let’s take this cake to Grandpa.

Quantity: L&S leaves the a of savillum unmarked; loci-cato prints sāvillum, from suāvis. Unmarked here until settled.

Ancient LatinNeo-LatinVariable terminology

extrāculum, extrāculī n. · fidēlia, fidēliae f.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinModern applications
  • extrāculum, extrāculī n. — corkscrew (Traupman 71, 297; M-O, citing LRL and Helfer); M-O also cochlea extractōria.
  • cortex, corticis m. — cork (M-O; Cato, Agr. 120; Hor. C. 3.8.10); obtūrāmentum, obtūrāmentī n. — stopper (Plin.); obtūrāculum (M-O, citing LRL; post-classical).
  • aperculum, aperculī n. — can opener (M-O, modern; also in the Calepinus Neo-Latin list).
  • vāsculum stanneum — a tin, a can (Traupman 286; stanneus, Plaut., Plin.); M-O pyxis ferrea (pyxis, a small box, Cic.).
  • fidēlia, fidēliae f. — jar, earthenware pot (M-O; Col.; Pers.): M-O finds it especially apt for a preserving jar; pyxis vitrea — glass jar (M-O).
  • capsella, capsellae f. — small box (M-O; Petr.); cistula, cistulae f. — little box (Plaut.). fasciculus, fasciculī m. — parcel, package (M-O, after Egger; classically a bundle of letters, Cic.).
  • cūpa, cūpae f. — barrel, cask (M-O; Caes.); dōlium, dōliī n. — a large storage jar (Traupman 122 gives it for barrel; M-O for vat).
  • gutus, gutī m. — cruet, narrow-necked oil flask (M-O; Juv.; L&S); acētābulum, acētābulī n. — vinegar vessel, later any small cup (Traupman 402; L&S).
  • Ubi est extrāculum? Lagoenam aperīre volō. — Where’s the corkscrew? I want to open the bottle.
  • Mel in fidēliā est; eam operculō claude. — The honey is in the jar; put the lid on it.

gutus: M-O prints gûtus; L&S leaves the u unmarked. Left unmarked. aperculum has no attested quantity; its vowels are short as in aperiō.

patera, paterae f. · vāsa ēscāria

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinModern applications
  • patera, paterae f. — saucer (Traupman 124); classically a broad flat dish for libations. M-O has only doubtful proposals (suppositōrium?).
  • magida, magidae f. — soup bowl (Traupman 383); in Varro a kind of dish (L&S under magis).
  • vāsa ēscāria — dishes, tableware (M-O); Traupman 125 īnstrūmenta ēscāria.
  • synthesis, synthesis f. — a set of dishes, a service (M-O; Mart. 4.46.15); synthesis caffeāria — coffee set (Traupman 70).
  • pōculum chartāceum — paper cup (M-O; chartāceus, Dig.).
  • paxillī ēscāriī — chopsticks (M-O s.v. cutlery: chopstick, which prints esacrius); paxillus is a small peg (Varro; Col.).
  • Pōculum in pateram pōne, nē mēnsa madefīat. — Put the cup on the saucer, so the table doesn’t get wet.
  • Paxillīs ēsse potes? — Can you eat with chopsticks?
Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: patera · Lewis & Short: magis · Lewis & Short: escarius · Lewis & Short: synthesis · Lewis & Short: chartaceus · Lewis & Short: paxillus

Small appliances: mixer / food processor / juicer / coffee maker / grinder / toaster oven / hob / hotplate / camping stove / slow cooker / rice cooker / bread maker

māchina mīxtōria · authepsa, authepsae f.

Neo-LatinModern applicationsVariable terminology
  • māchina mixtōria — mixer (Traupman 346, mīxtōria); M-O māchina agitātōria, keeping mixtōria for the blender.
  • māchina coquīnāria — food processor (Traupman 123; Helfer, cited in M-O).
  • māchina expressōria — juicer (M-O).
  • māchina caffeāria — coffee maker (Traupman 293; M-O spells it cafeāria); the lexicon follows caffēa.
  • māchina carnāria — meat grinder (Traupman 344); mola caffeāria — coffee grinder (M-O, spelled cafeāria).
  • clībanus tostōrius — toaster oven (M-O; clībanus, a small baking oven, Plin.).
  • discus coctōrius — hob, burner (Traupman 284; M-O); foculus mēnsārius — hotplate (M-O, after Vives); foculus campester — camping stove (M-O, citing LRL, Helfer and Egger).
  • authepsa, authepsae f. — self-heating cooker, “somewhat like our tea-urns” (L&S): authepsa illa, quam tantō pretiō nūper mercātus est (Cic. Rosc. Am. 133). M-O builds on it: authepsa lenta or coctōrium lentum — slow cooker; coctōrium oryzae — rice cooker; authepsa theāria — samovar.
  • māchina pānifica — bread maker (M-O).
  • Ōva et farīnam in māchinā mixtōriā misceāmus. — Let’s mix the eggs and flour in the mixer.
  • Nōlī discum tangere; ārdet! — Don’t touch the hob; it’s hot!

Why mixtōria, not mīxtōria: Traupman marks the i long, but L&S leaves it unmarked in mixtum, and de Vaan (2008: 382–383) prints mixtum, mixtūra with a short i, explaining mixtum as syncopated from *mixitum. Spanish mestizo and French métis, from Late Latin mixtīcius, also continue a short i. Bennett’s list of hidden quantities has not been checked yet.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: machina · Lewis & Short: clibanus · Lewis & Short: foculus · Lewis & Short: authepsa · Lewis & Short: mola

ignītābulum, ignītābulī n. · sīphō, sīphōnis m.

Ancient wordsNeo-LatinModern applications
  • ignītābulum, ignītābulī n. — lighter (Traupman 340; M-O; anciently a fire-lighting implement, Solinus); rāmentum flammiferum — match (Traupman 343; rāmentum, a shaving).
  • sīphō, sīphōnis m. — drinking straw (Traupman 73, 386; M-O; Cels.).
  • dentiscalpium, dentiscalpiī n. — toothpick (Traupman 396; Mart. 14.22).

  • vāsculum sacchari — sugar bowl (Traupman 73, 387).
  • pānārium, pānāriī n. — bread basket, picnic basket (Traupman 360; Varro); M-O sportula, sportulae f. (Plaut.).
  • refrīgerātōrium portātile — cool box (M-O, after Vives’ wine-cooler); fōrmula glaciēī — ice tray (M-O).
  • artopta, artoptae f. — loaf tin, bread pan (M-O; Plaut. Aul. 2.9.4, as cited by L&S).
  • armārium culīnārium — kitchen cupboard (M-O); īnstrūmenta coquīnātōria — kitchen utensils (Traupman 124; coquīnātōrius is not in L&S).
  • lōmentum catillīs aptum — washing-up liquid (M-O); see the cleaning entry for lōmentum.
  • Ignītābulum nōn est lūdibrium. — The lighter isn’t a toy.
  • Vīsne sīphōnem? — Do you want a straw?

smoothie noun draft

  • pōtiō, pōtiōnis f. — drinknoun, third declension · our formationOur short contextual word for a smoothie. The noun is pōtiō with long ō (L&S pōtio; cf. pōtus, pōtāre); the earlier short-o spelling was corrected on 23 October 2026.

Other words

  • pōtiō ex pōmīs holeribusque contrītīs — a drink made from blended fruit and vegetablesalso used · our formationOur explicit description, not a claimed standard Neo-Latin headword. The drink label and complete smoothie phrase are our working descriptions. Crassus/tenuis describe consistency; dulcis, acidus and amārus describe sweetness, sourness and bitterness.

  • Cucumerem mihi porrige, quaesō.Pass me the cucumber, please. composed

See also blender, blend, juice, thick, thin.

curtain rod noun draft

  • virga aulaeīour formationOur preferred transparent formation for a slender cylindrical rod, such as the metal rod used with curtain rings; for the photographed slender metal rod it is preferred. The individual nouns are ancient; virga aulaeī, pertica aulaeī and canālis aulaeī are transparent modern formations, and no strong lexicographic evidence was found that any one of them is an established traditional term.

Other words

  • pertica aulaeī — curtain polealso used · our formationUseful especially when the support is longer, thicker or more pole-like.
  • virga extensilis aulaeī — extendable or telescoping curtain rodalso used · our formation

Examples

  • Aulaeum ex virgā pendet.The curtain hangs from the rod. composed

See also curtain, curtain ring, curtain bracket, curtain track.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: virga · Lewis & Short: pertica · Morgan–Owens: rod

Tools, fasteners & household repair

adze noun draft

  • ascia, asciae f. — adze, the carpenter’s axe for dressing timbernoun, first declension · classical · Plin. NH 7.198: fabricam māteriāriam Daedalus et in eā serram, asciam, perpendiculum, terebram; Plin. NH 16.207: mollissima tilia … quod citissimē asciās retundat; Vitr. 7.2.2: sūmātur ascia et, quemadmodum māteria dolātur, sīc calx in lacū mācerāta asciētur; Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae, gloss: secūris fabrī quā trabēs dolanturLewis & Short: “an axe for hewing wood, a carpenter’s axe”; secūris is the ordinary axe. Pliny, NH 7.198 makes Daedalus the inventor of carpentry and of its first tools; the square and the level go to Theodorus of Samos. In NH 16.207 lime wood blunts adzes fastest. In Vitruvius 7.2.2 the adze also tests slaked lime: if the lime clings to the iron like glue, it is ready for plastering.

Examples

  • Asciam mihi dā.Give me the adze. composed
  • «Asciam nōvī!» inquit Theodōrus. «Asciam volō!»I know the adze! I want the adze! Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae
  • malleus, serra, ascia, quam Bulgarī teslam vocant, secūris, terebra, scalprum, rēgula, norma, forceps, runcīna, trulla, quā tēctōrēs tēctōrium indūcunt, līnea cum perpendiculō, capsa clāvōrumhammer, saw, the adze the Bulgarians call tesla, axe, drill, chisel, ruler, square, pincers, plane, the trowel plasterers spread plaster with, a plumb line, a box of nails Libellus VII, Diēs ūnus Osoitsae

See also hew, axe, square, plane, trowel, plumb bob, hammer, saw, nail, chisel.

hook onto verb draft

  • uncō affīgere — fasten with a hookour formationOur descriptive phrase. uncō can also be the dative “to a hook”; the construction and context determine the relation. The two English verb senses (hook onto, catch with a hook) are expressed compositionally; neither phrase is presented as a separately verified technical headword.

Other words

  • affīgō, affīgere, affīxī, affīxum — fasten or attachverb, third conjugation · also used · classicalaffīgere emphasizes attachment or fastening; it is not a universal equivalent of English “hook.” Choose the verb according to the action and result.
  • suspendō, suspendere — hang up, suspendverb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Verg. G. 2.389: oscilla ex altā suspendunt mollia pīnūFor hooking something over a bar and leaving it hanging, as in the composed example of the stick on the scaffolding; compare Vergil for suspendere ex + ablative. trānsversārium is Vitruvius’s crosspiece; a scaffold tube is not a vectis (lever, crowbar).

Examples

  • Hoc huic uncō affīge.Hook this onto this hook / attach this to this hook. composed
  • Theodōrus bacillum aduncum ex trānsversāriō māchinae suspendit.Theo hung the hooked stick from the scaffold’s crossbar. composed

See also hook, catch with a hook, upright.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: affigo · Lewis & Short: suspendo · Lewis & Short: transversarius

The example sentences marked “composed” are ours.

screw noun draft

  • cōchlea / cochlea, -ae f.noun, first declension · modern · M-O s.v. screwAncient cochlea already denotes spiral and screw mechanisms; later technical Latin applies it directly to the modern threaded fastener. Lewis & Short marks the first vowel of cochlea as variable (cō̆-), so this lexicon does not pretend that one quantity is uniquely correct. The modern English distinction between screw and bolt is not mapped consistently onto one fixed pair of Latin nouns in the sources checked; cochlea is therefore kept broad here rather than creating a false precision. Modern Latin sources do not maintain a single universally standardized terminology for every modern screwdriver, screw and wrench subtype; specific types should therefore be formed or selected case by case.

Examples

  • Cochleam vertitōriō intorque.Screw the screw in with the screwdriver. composed

See also screwdriver, nut, screw thread, screw in, unscrew.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: coclea / cochlea · Morgan–Owens: screw

The example sentence marked “composed” is ours.

Draft of 9 November 2026, not yet reviewed.

scaffold noun draft

  • māchina, māchinae f.noun, first declension · classical · Digest 13.6.5.7 (Ulpian): a plasterer lent out falls dē māchinā; the risk differs if he was lent to work dē plānō, on the ground, or if the scaffold was minus dīligenter … ligāta or failed through fūnium perticārumque vetustāte; Vitruvius 7.2.2: māchinīs comparātīs (scaffolds set up for vaulting rooms); Vitruvius 10.1.1: scānsōriae māchinae, built tignīs statūtīs et trānsversāriīs conligātīs; M-O s.v. scaffoldingScaffold or scaffolding for building, the Roman word. Lewis & Short I.B.3 also cites Pliny 19.2.8 §30 (NH 19.30), but there māchinīs aedificātiōnum means building machinery such as hoists, which is weak evidence for scaffolding. The noun is broader than modern English “machine.”

Other words

  • māchina ex fistulīs ferreīs — scaffolding made of iron tubesalso used · our formationOur descriptive phrase for the modern construction-site object.
  • compāgēs, compāgis f. — frameworknoun, third declension · also used · modern · M-O s.v. scaffoldingClassically it never names a builder’s scaffold; the scaffolding sense is modern lexicographic (Morgan–Owens). Useful as a gloss word, not as the narrative noun.
  • pēgma, pēgmatis n. — framework, stage machinerynoun, third declension · also used · classicalAnother ancient framework/machinery noun, especially for theatrical stage machinery and board fixtures. Its ancient examples do not by themselves establish the modern tube-and-clamp construction sense; māchina has the clearer explicit builder’s-scaffold entry.

Examples

  • Operārius in māchinā stat.The worker is standing on the scaffold. composed
  • Māchinam juxtā domum cōnstruunt.They are assembling the scaffolding beside the house. composed
  • Dē plānō lūde, nōn in māchinā.Play on the ground, not on the scaffold (after the Digest’s dē plānō). composed

See also upright, crossbar, scaffold pole, scaffold platform, framework, scaffold worker, assemble, dismantle.

Sources & evidence

Lewis & Short: machina · Lewis & Short: compages · Lewis & Short: pegma · Lewis & Short: planus · Morgan–Owens: scaffolding

living room noun draft

  • exedra, exedrae f.noun, first declension · classical · Vitruvius 5.11.2: exhedrae spatiōsae, habentēs sēdēs (so spelt in the Latin Library text); Cicero, de Or. 3.17; N.D. 1.15 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 125Classically a room furnished with seats, for conversation; in Cicero the room where the speakers of a dialogue sit and talk. See also top floor, furniture, armchair, sofa.

  1. Traupman (pp. 124–125) gives sessōrium for “living room”, but its ancient senses are “seat, stool” (Caelius Aurelianus) and, in a single passage, “dwelling” (Petronius 77.4 vīperae hujus sessōrium) (Lewis & Short). Ruling: exedra for the sitting room

About this lexicon

Macrons, usage and evidence

Macrons mark long vowels; short vowels are left plain. A heavy syllable is not automatically a long vowel. Consonantal i is written j (jam, ejus, conjungō), and the vowel before intervocalic j is left unmarked (major); search treats i and j alike. Inflected examples, genitives, principal parts and Latin headings are included in the review.

For ancient vocabulary, the main references are Lewis & Short and Lewis’s Elementary Latin Dictionary through Perseus and Logeion, with Dickinson’s core list for cross-checking. Hidden quantities are also compared against Bennett’s discussion with Michelson’s corrections and notes on Allen. Dictionary omissions are not automatically proof of shortness; disputed lengths are identified where relevant.

The lexicon is English–Latin. Another language is cited only where it helps to explain a Latin word, its meaning or its form.

For modern words, the classical lengths of inherited roots and regular Latin endings are retained where justified. Loanword stem quantities that the checked sources do not establish are explicitly labelled. “Reading convention” marks an adopted reconstruction, rather than an attested ancient pronunciation.

Ancient Latin means the word and its relevant basic sense are ancient. Lexicographic evidence means a modern dictionary records the expression; it does not imply universal acceptance. Modern extension applies an older word to a modern object. Working formation identifies our own phrase or name adaptation.

Example sentences are composed for everyday conversation, many of them with a small child. They are not quotations unless an author and passage are identified. Noun genitives and genders, important sense distinctions, and known alternative forms are supplied where useful.

Words in the new record format have a page of their own. Each Latin form is labelled with its period, and numbered notes give the reason wherever we depart from Lewis & Short or a source. Each Latin word that heads a term has a page too, which lists every entry that uses it. Our rulings on disputed words are kept, with their evidence and history, on the rulings page; the rules behind them are on How we decide.

Review notes · 8 November 2026

All 53 original grouped entries were reviewed; 39 household and family entries were added. Quantities, examples, definitions and attestation labels were checked separately. The review also removes unsupported precise dates, unsourced principal parts and blanket “attested” tags.

5 October 2026 addition: three family-play entries cover trampoline jumping, Sīmius et arbor and Nauta et undae. The game titles and spoken prompts are our own; modern senses are labelled. The plural genua has short u.

7 October 2026 addition: ausum is the preferred ancient word for “adventure” in the sense of a daring undertaking or venture; adventūra is retained as a medieval/modern alternative, with its semantic development explicitly noted.

11 October 2026 addition: seven workshop-and-repair entries distinguish ancient tool vocabulary from later technical Latin and our own descriptive formations. The review replaces the earlier unsupported cochleārius for “screwdriver” with lexicographically attested vertitōrium, prefers forceps for pliers, records variable vowel quantity in cochlea and terebra, and distinguishes a “dowel” (scalmus) from a wall plug. For the latter, ancora mūrālis plastica is explicitly marked as our provisional descriptive formation, not as an attested traditional term.

18 October 2026 addition: 27 grouped entries cover the family smoothie guide: ingredients, equipment, materials, measurements, preparation verbs and phrases for cooking with a child. Traupman’s uploaded Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, Morgan–Owens and ancient dictionaries were compared. Recorded modern terms, older words with modern senses, uncertain quantities and our composed descriptions are labelled separately. Start with smoothie ingredients · Source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover construction, house layout, furnishings, trowels, a crowbar, extension leads, cable reels and sheet-metal shears. Existing workshop entries were extended with the recorded tape-measure phrase. Descriptive formations and uncertain ancient senses remain explicit. Construction vocabulary source audit.

24 October 2026 addition: 17 grouped entries cover hooks, swinging, pipes, gravel, movement, flips, trenches, dirt, heaps, squeezing/crushing, crashes, missions/quests, caps, scaffolding and its parts/actions. Eight existing entries were extended or cross-linked for rods/bars, blankets, lids, planks, wiping and food-preparation verbs. This batch adds English–Latin vocabulary only. Physical senses, modern applications and our composed descriptions remain distinct. Site and play vocabulary source audit.

25 October 2026: a dedicated Lūdī et lūdibria category adds 14 grouped playground/toy entries and brings the existing swing entry into the same filter. Playground source audit.

26 October 2026: classical sources and corrections for the site and construction vocabulary. Two entries are added: the adze, ascia, and ground level, basement, terrace, wing and extension. Scaffolding now leads with māchina and Vitruvius’s arrēctāria / trānsversāria; norma is written without a macron; coctilis has a short i. tabula spūmea is our working formation for EPS board. Site vocabulary corrections.

29 October 2026: the sitting room is exedra (Vitruvius, Cicero; Traupman p. 125), not sessōrium, whose ancient senses are “seat” and, in one passage of Petronius, “dwelling”; concrete is opus caementīcium, after Vitruvius’s caementīcius, not Traupman’s concrētum; jentāculum and jentō have a short e, as Lewis & Short leaves them.

29 October 2026 addition: the daily-life vocabulary of the seven fābulae Theodōrus et pater (I Iter in Lūsitāniam to VII Diēs ūnus Osoitsae), first proposed on 23 October and rebased on the revised texts: 75 grouped entries (entry-196 to entry-270) cover travel, town and shops, place names, weather and landscape, trees, animals, market food, kitchen work, the house and its rebuilding, and phrases for the day. A new category, Urbs, vīcus et loca, holds town, shop and place-name vocabulary. Where a proposed card duplicated an existing one (body parts, vegetables, playground, slide, swing, sandpit, ball games, balance bike, rooms, builders, building timber, family, and the adze card of 26 October), its new words and examples were added to that card instead. Every example marked “Fābula” was re-quoted from the texts as revised on 29 October, in their j orthography. The fork is furcilla (not fuscinula), and mantēle leads with its classical sense, the hand towel. Corrections made on 23 October: jentāculum (short e), būtȳrum, pōtiō, lac, lacūna, īnstrūmentum, vēsīca īnflāta and ēlectricus; alternatives were added to the coffee, tram, trampoline, stick, back, balloon, wake-up, hug, pepper, pumpkin, cutting-board, peel and berry entries. Search libelli to see the addition.

29 October 2026 addition: the everyday words worked into the fābulae in the 29 October vocabulary pass, with an everyday-vocabulary survey of the texts. 14 grouped entries (entry-271 to entry-284) cover electric light and sockets, kitchen appliances, the bathroom, the car, getting about, Dad’s bag, fine weather, geography, time, exclamations and spoken phrases, quiet and gestures, and cooking words from the Culīna Theodōrī; 42 existing entries gain words and examples (family, sleep, bed, clothes, towels, teeth, body, feelings, rooms, cupboards, stairs, doors and shutters, ball games, birds, shops, the table). Every example is quoted from the current texts; Traupman pages were checked in the book. The bath towel is linteum and the hand towel mantēle (not gausapina or manutergium); trulla is also the ladle; the toothbrush is pēniculus dentārius beside pēnicillus; lābellum has a long ā (de Vaan). Search vocabulary to see the addition.

7 November 2026: the Theodōrus et pater readers are cited as Libellī I–VII (Ad Larem avītum), the name on their covers, not as fābulae, which now means only the tales told inside them; their entries’ anchors change accordingly (#fabulae-265 is now #libelli-265). All of the roughly 400 examples quoted from the libellī were checked again against the texts as they stand on 7 November, and 76 that later revisions had changed were re-quoted or replaced. Pyjamas are vestis nocturna, the household word; Traupman’s synthesis dormītōria is noted but not used. The high chair, which has left the texts, is dropped from the furniture entry. Dad’s hip bag is sacculus scorteus; the tablecloth in the libellī is linteum; the heel of a shoe is fulmenta (Plautus), beside Traupman’s fulmentum. Search libelli to see the entries.

8 November 2026: the lexicon is now English–Latin throughout; the Bulgarian glosses, labels and search terms were removed.

8 November 2026: the first 23 words move to the new record format, one record per concept with its own page: hiccups, burping and tickling; “perhaps”; twelve swimming words; seven pots and kitchen utensils. Their notes give the evidence for lutra, caccabus and fortasse against Lewis & Short, and the rulings behind them are collected on the rulings page. The conversation category is now Sermō cotīdiānus: personal names belong in example sentences, not in categories or tags. pōculum ānsātum now has its long a, like olla ānsāta.

Selected quantity corrections
  • ramus / ramulus / ramos → rāmus / rāmulus / rāmōs
  • gravedō / gravedinis → gravēdō / gravēdinis
  • involucrum / manubrium → involūcrum / manūbrium
  • scabī / vesīca / semita → scābī / vēsīca / sēmita
  • vaccinium / morum → vaccīnium / mōrum
  • frīgeō / algēō / fervēō / languēō → frīgeō / algeō / ferveō / langueō
  • elaborātiō / recognitiō → ēlabōrātiō / recōgnitiō
  • program(m)ātum as a noun genitive plural → programmatum; verbal programmātum is a different form
Usage corrections

Ancient fermentō, fermentēscō and vapōrō are no longer called exclusively later inventions. Berry names distinguish modern botanical use from uncertain ancient identification. Totoro, the magnetic-toy phrase and specific Git phrases are labelled as our own adaptations.

The kettle expression and unsupported yogurt or coffee stem quantities are described with their actual level of evidence. Source links appear inside each entry.
